topics.title: Aberration
topics.description: A failure of light rays to converge at one focus due to limitations or defects in a lens or mirror.

topics.title: Aberrations
topics.description: Aberrations are imperfections in image formation caused by the limitations of optical systems, such as lenses or mirrors.

topics.title: Absolute Pressure
topics.description: Absolute pressure is the total pressure in a fluid, which is the sum of gauge pressure and atmospheric pressure.

topics.title: Absolute Temperature
topics.description: Absolute temperature is the temperature measured in Kelvins, which is an absolute temperature scale measured in terms of the number of degrees above absolute zero.

topics.title: Absolute Zero
topics.description: The lowest possible temperature; the temperature at which all molecular motion ceases.

topics.title: Absorption and Reflection of Light
topics.description: The true color of an object is determined by its absorption or reflection of light, with different wavelengths being absorbed or reflected to produce the perceived color.

topics.title: Absorption Spectrum
topics.description: A spectrum of light absorbed by a substance, showing dark lines at specific wavelengths corresponding to energy transitions in the atoms.

topics.title: AC Current
topics.description: Current that fluctuates sinusoidally with time, expressed as I = I0 sin 2πft.

topics.title: AC Power Transmission
topics.description: AC power is used for power transmission because it can be easily transformed to higher voltages, reducing power loss over long distances.

topics.title: AC Voltage
topics.description: Voltage that fluctuates sinusoidally with time, expressed as V = V0 sin 2.πft.

topics.title: Acceleration
topics.description: Acceleration is the rate at which an object's velocity changes over time.

topics.title: Acceleration Direction
topics.description: Acceleration is a vector in the same direction as the change in velocity, which can be due to a change in speed, direction, or both.

topics.title: Acceleration Due to Gravity (g)
topics.description: Acceleration of an object as a result of gravity.

topics.title: Acceleration in Elevator Systems
topics.description: The change in velocity of an object in an elevator, which affects the normal force and scale reading experienced by a person inside.

topics.title: Acceleration in SHM
topics.description: Acceleration in simple harmonic motion is directly proportional to the displacement and directed toward the equilibrium position, varying sinusoidally with time.

topics.title: Acceleration Opposite to Velocity
topics.description: Acceleration in the opposite direction of velocity means the object is slowing down.

topics.title: Accommodation
topics.description: The eye's ability to adjust its focal length to focus on objects at different distances.

topics.title: Accommodation of the Eye
topics.description: Accommodation is the process by which the eye adjusts the power of its lens to focus images on the retina for objects at different distances.

topics.title: Accretion Disk
topics.description: An accretion disk is a disk of gas and dust that orbits a black hole, heating up and emitting X-rays as it falls into the black hole.

topics.title: Accuracy
topics.description: Accuracy is how close a measurement is to the correct or true value for that measurement.

topics.title: Accuracy and Precision
topics.description: Accuracy refers to how close a measured value is to the true value, while precision refers to how consistent repeated measurements are.

topics.title: Achromatic Doublet
topics.description: An achromatic doublet is a lens system composed of two lenses made from different materials that work together to reduce chromatic aberration.

topics.title: Acoustic Impedance
topics.description: Acoustic impedance is a measure of the resistance to the propagation of sound in a medium, defined as the product of the medium's density and the speed of sound in that medium.

topics.title: Acoustics
topics.description: Acoustics is the study of sound, including how sound waves are produced, transmitted, and perceived.

topics.title: Action Potential
topics.description: An action potential is a brief voltage pulse that travels along a neuron's axon, caused by the rapid movement of ions across the cell membrane during depolarization and repolarization.

topics.title: Action-Reaction Force Pairs
topics.description: When one object exerts a force on another, the second object simultaneously exerts an equal and opposite force on the first.

topics.title: Action-Reaction Pairs
topics.description: Action-reaction pairs are forces that occur in pairs, where one object exerts a force on another, and the second object exerts an equal and opposite force on the first.

topics.title: Active Galactic Nucleus
topics.description: An active galactic nucleus is a compact region at the center of a galaxy that has a very high luminosity, often powered by a supermassive black hole.

topics.title: Active Transport
topics.description: Active transport is a process in which a living membrane expends energy to move substances across it.

topics.title: Adaptive Optics
topics.description: Optical technology that uses computers to adjust lenses and mirrors to correct image distortions.

topics.title: Addition of Velocities
topics.description: The method of combining velocities from different reference frames to determine the resultant velocity.

topics.title: Additive and Subtractive Color Mixing
topics.description: Additive color mixing involves combining different colored lights, while subtractive color mixing involves combining pigments or dyes to produce colors.

topics.title: Adhesive Forces
topics.description: Adhesive forces are attractive forces between molecules of different types.

topics.title: Adiabatic Process
topics.description: An adiabatic process is a thermodynamic process in which no heat transfer occurs between the system and its surroundings, meaning the internal energy change is solely due to work done.

topics.title: Air Columns
topics.description: Air columns are regions of air that can vibrate and produce sound waves, often found in wind instruments.

topics.title: Air Infiltration
topics.description: Air infiltration is the process by which outside air leaks into a building through cracks and gaps, contributing to heat transfer.

topics.title: Air Resistance
topics.description: A frictional force that slows the motion of objects as they travel through the air.

topics.title: Albert Einstein
topics.description: Albert Einstein was a physicist who developed modern relativity and made significant contributions to quantum mechanics.

topics.title: Alpha Decay
topics.description: A type of radioactive decay in which an atomic nucleus emits an alpha particle.

topics.title: Alpha Decay Equation
topics.description: Alpha decay involves the emission of a helium nucleus from an atom, reducing its atomic number by two and its mass number by four.

topics.title: Alpha Rays
topics.description: One of the types of rays emitted from the nucleus of an atom.

topics.title: Alternating Current
topics.description: Electric current whose direction alternates back and forth at regular intervals.

topics.title: Alternating Current (AC)
topics.description: Alternating current is an electric current that periodically reverses direction and varies in magnitude.

topics.title: Alternating Current (AC) and Frequency
topics.description: Alternating current (AC) is an electric current that periodically reverses direction, and its frequency is the number of cycles per second, commonly used in power distribution systems.

topics.title: Ammeter
topics.description: An instrument that measures current.

topics.title: Ammeter Connection
topics.description: An ammeter must be connected in series with the circuit to measure the current flowing through a component.

topics.title: Ampere
topics.description: The ampere is the SI unit of electric current, defined as one coulomb per second.

topics.title: Ampere (Amp)
topics.description: The SI unit for current; 1 A = 1 C/s.

topics.title: Ampere’s Law
topics.description: Ampere’s Law is a fundamental law that relates the magnetic field around a closed loop to the current passing through the loop, providing a general way to calculate magnetic fields created by currents.

topics.title: Ampere’s Law (Modified by Maxwell)
topics.description: Magnetic fields are generated by moving charges or by changing electric fields, extending Ampere’s law to include the effect of changing electric fields.

topics.title: Amplitude
topics.description: The maximum displacement from the equilibrium position of an object oscillating around the equilibrium position.

topics.title: Amplitude and Energy of Waves
topics.description: The energy carried by a wave is proportional to the square of its amplitude, which for electromagnetic waves corresponds to the square of the electric or magnetic field strength.

topics.title: Amplitude Modulation (AM)
topics.description: A method for placing information on electromagnetic waves by modulating the amplitude of a carrier wave with an audio signal, resulting in a wave with constant frequency but varying amplitude.

topics.title: Amplitude of a Sound Wave
topics.description: The amplitude of a sound wave is the maximum displacement of particles from their equilibrium position, which corresponds to the loudness of the sound.

topics.title: Amplitude of Oscillation
topics.description: Amplitude of oscillation is the maximum displacement of a system from its equilibrium position during oscillatory motion.

topics.title: Analog Meter
topics.description: A measuring instrument that gives a readout in the form of a needle movement over a marked gauge.

topics.title: Analytical Addition and Subtraction of Vectors
topics.description: Analytical addition and subtraction of vectors involve using mathematical equations to represent and combine vectors.

topics.title: Analytical Method
topics.description: A method of determining the magnitude and direction of a resultant vector using the Pythagorean theorem and trigonometric identities.

topics.title: Analytical Method of Vector Addition
topics.description: The analytical method of vector addition uses trigonometry to calculate the resultant vector by breaking vectors into their x and y components and then adding them.

topics.title: Analytical Method of Vector Subtraction
topics.description: The analytical method of vector subtraction involves adding the negative of a vector, which is done by negating its components and then using the analytical method of addition.

topics.title: Analytical Methods for Velocity Addition
topics.description: Analytical methods involve using trigonometric equations to find the magnitude and direction of a velocity vector from its components or to determine components from magnitude and direction.

topics.title: Analytical Methods of Vector Addition and Subtraction
topics.description: Techniques that use mathematical calculations, such as components and trigonometry, to add or subtract vectors.

topics.title: Aneroid Gauge
topics.description: An aneroid gauge is a mechanical pressure gauge that uses a flexible bellows and spring arrangement to measure pressure and display it on a calibrated scale.

topics.title: Anger Camera
topics.description: A medical imaging device that uses a scintillator connected to a series of photomultipliers.

topics.title: Anger Camera (Gamma Camera)
topics.description: An Anger camera, or gamma camera, is a device that detects gamma rays emitted by radiopharmaceuticals to produce images of internal body structures.

topics.title: Angle of Displacement
topics.description: The angle of displacement calculated as the inverse tangent of the ratio of the vertical displacement to the horizontal displacement.

topics.title: Angle of Incidence
topics.description: The angle between the incoming light ray and the perpendicular to the surface at the point of incidence.

topics.title: Angle of Reflection
topics.description: The angle, with respect to the normal, at which a ray leaves a reflective surface.

topics.title: Angle of Refraction
topics.description: The angle between the normal and the refracted ray.

topics.title: Angle of Rotation
topics.description: The angle through which an object rotates about a fixed axis, measured in radians.

topics.title: Angle of Velocity
topics.description: The direction of velocity determined by the inverse tangent of the ratio of the vertical component of velocity to the horizontal component of velocity.

topics.title: Angular Acceleration
topics.description: The rate of change of angular velocity with time.

topics.title: Angular Displacement
topics.description: Angular displacement is the angle through which an object rotates, measured in radians.

topics.title: Angular Magnification
topics.description: Angular magnification is the ratio of the angle subtended by an object as viewed through a telescope to the angle subtended by the object as viewed by the unaided eye.

topics.title: Angular Momentum
topics.description: Angular momentum is a vector quantity that represents the product of an object's moment of inertia and its angular velocity.

topics.title: Angular Momentum Projection Quantum Number
topics.description: The angular momentum projection quantum number (m_l) specifies the z-component of angular momentum and can take integer values from −l to +l.

topics.title: Angular Momentum Quantum Number
topics.description: The angular momentum quantum number (l) defines the magnitude of angular momentum for a given energy state and can take integer values from 0 to n−1.

topics.title: Angular Resolution
topics.description: Angular resolution is the ability of an optical instrument to distinguish between two closely spaced objects, determined by the Rayleigh criterion and expressed as the angle theta = 1.22 lambda / D, where lambda is the wavelength and D is the diameter of the aperture.

topics.title: Angular Velocity
topics.description: Angular velocity is the rate at which an object rotates about an axis, measured in radians per second.

topics.title: Angular Velocity and Centripetal Acceleration
topics.description: Centripetal acceleration can also be expressed in terms of angular velocity using the formula $ a_c = r	heta^2 $, where $ r $ is the radius and $ 	heta $ is the angular velocity.

topics.title: Angular velocity and emf
topics.description: The angular velocity of a rotating coil in a generator directly affects the induced emf, with higher angular velocity resulting in a greater peak emf.

topics.title: Annihilation
topics.description: Annihilation is the process where a particle and its antiparticle interact and convert their mass into energy.

topics.title: Antimatter
topics.description: Composed of antiparticles.

topics.title: Antinode
topics.description: A point of maximum displacement in a wave.

topics.title: Antinodes
topics.description: Antinodes are points in a standing wave where the amplitude of the wave is maximum, indicating the location of maximum vibration.

topics.title: Antiquark
topics.description: An antiquark is the antiparticle of a quark, with opposite quantum numbers such as charge and baryon number.

topics.title: Aphelion
topics.description: Aphelion is the point in a planet's orbit where it is farthest from the sun.

topics.title: Application of Physical Principles to Real-World Situations
topics.description: Using fundamental physics principles and equations to analyze and solve practical problems, ensuring the solution aligns with real-world expectations.

topics.title: Applications of Atomic Excitations and De-Excitations
topics.description: Atomic excitations and de-excitations involve the absorption and emission of energy by atoms, which have practical applications in technology and science.

topics.title: Applications of Atomic Knowledge
topics.description: Understanding atoms and their properties helps explain and improve our knowledge of geology, biology, and the natural world.

topics.title: Applications of Electrostatics
topics.description: Applications of electrostatics include devices like photocopiers, air cleaners, and electrostatic precipitators.

topics.title: Applications of Magnetic Damping
topics.description: Applications of magnetic damping include sensitive laboratory balances, recycling centers separating metals, and braking systems in trains and roller coasters.

topics.title: Applications of Magnetism
topics.description: Applications of magnetism include technologies like electric motors, generators, MRI machines, and computer hard drives, which rely on magnetic fields for their operation.

topics.title: Applications of Nuclear Physics
topics.description: Applications of nuclear physics refer to the practical uses of nuclear processes in various fields such as medicine, energy production, and other areas of modern life.

topics.title: Applications of Physics
topics.description: Physics has numerous applications in other sciences and technologies, such as biology, chemistry, geology, and everyday technology like GPS, smartphones, and medical imaging.

topics.title: Applications of RC Circuits
topics.description: RC circuits are used in various applications such as timing circuits, flash photography, heart defibrillators, and intermittent wiper systems in cars.

topics.title: Applications of Statics
topics.description: Applications of statics involve using the principles of equilibrium to analyze and solve real-world problems involving forces and torques.

topics.title: Approximation
topics.description: An estimated value based on prior experience and reasoning.

topics.title: Arc Length
topics.description: Arc length is the distance traveled along a circular path, calculated as the product of the radius and the rotation angle.

topics.title: Archimedes’ Principle
topics.description: Archimedes’ Principle states that the buoyant force on an object submerged in a fluid is equal to the weight of the fluid displaced by the object.

topics.title: Area of an Ellipse
topics.description: The area of an ellipse is calculated by multiplying pi by the lengths of its semi-major and semi-minor axes.

topics.title: Area Under Velocity vs. Time Graphs
topics.description: The area under a velocity vs. time graph represents the displacement of an object.

topics.title: Arrangement of Atoms in Gases
topics.description: In gases, atoms are separated by large distances and move freely, allowing them to expand to fill their container.

topics.title: Arrangement of Atoms in Liquids
topics.description: In liquids, atoms are in close contact but can slide past one another, allowing the liquid to flow while maintaining a definite volume.

topics.title: Arrangement of Atoms in Solids
topics.description: In solids, atoms are in close contact and arranged in a fixed lattice structure, allowing them to vibrate but not move freely.

topics.title: Artificial Hip Joint
topics.description: An artificial hip joint is a medical device used to replace a damaged hip joint, consisting of a ball and socket design to mimic natural joint movement.

topics.title: Artificial Joint Dimensions
topics.description: The dimensions of an artificial hip device can be estimated from a photograph, which helps in understanding the scale and design of such medical implants.

topics.title: Artificial Pacemakers and RC Circuits
topics.description: Artificial pacemakers use RC circuits to control heart rate by adjusting the time constant (τ = RC) to deliver electrical signals at the appropriate intervals.

topics.title: Astigmatism
topics.description: A condition where the cornea cannot properly focus an image onto the retina.

topics.title: Atom
topics.description: An atom is the smallest unit of a chemical element that retains the properties of that element.

topics.title: Atomic De-Excitation
topics.description: The process by which an atom transfers from an excited electronic state back to the ground state electronic configuration, often by emitting a photon.

topics.title: Atomic Excitation
topics.description: A state in which an atom or ion gains enough energy to promote one or more of its electrons to higher energy electronic states.

topics.title: Atomic Forces
topics.description: Atomic forces are the forces that hold the subatomic particles together within an atom.

topics.title: Atomic Mass
topics.description: The total mass of the protons, neutrons, and electrons in a single atom.

topics.title: Atomic Number
topics.description: The atomic number is the number of protons in the nucleus of an atom, which determines the element.

topics.title: Atomic Spectra
topics.description: Atomic spectra are the discrete wavelengths of light emitted or absorbed by atoms, indicating quantized energy levels within the atom.

topics.title: Atomic Structure
topics.description: Atomic structure refers to the arrangement and composition of subatomic particles within an atom.

topics.title: Aurora Borealis
topics.description: The Aurora Borealis, or northern lights, is a natural light display in the sky, primarily caused by charged particles from the sun interacting with Earth's magnetic field and atmosphere.

topics.title: Availability of Energy
topics.description: Availability of energy refers to the portion of energy that can be converted into work, which decreases as entropy increases.

topics.title: Average Acceleration
topics.description: The change in velocity divided by the time over which it changes.

topics.title: Average Angular Velocity
topics.description: The average rate of change of rotational angle over time, calculated as the average of initial and final angular velocities.

topics.title: Average Effective Force
topics.description: Average effective force is a constant force that produces the same impulse as a time-varying force over a given time interval.

topics.title: Average Power in AC Circuits
topics.description: Average power in AC circuits is the time-averaged power consumed by a load, calculated using RMS voltage and RMS current.

topics.title: Average Speed
topics.description: Distance traveled divided by time during which motion occurs.

topics.title: Average Velocity
topics.description: Displacement divided by time over which displacement occurs.

topics.title: Average Velocity from a Position vs. Time Graph
topics.description: Average velocity from a position vs. time graph is calculated by dividing the change in position by the change in time.

topics.title: Average Velocity with Constant Acceleration
topics.description: Average velocity of an object under constant acceleration is the arithmetic mean of the initial and final velocities, given by v̄ = (v₀ + v)/2.

topics.title: Avogadro’s Number
topics.description: Avogadro's number is the number of atoms or molecules in one mole of a substance, approximately 6.022 × 10^23.

topics.title: Axions
topics.description: Axions are a type of WIMPs with masses about 10−10 of an electron mass.

topics.title: Axis of a Polarizing Filter
topics.description: The direction along which a polarizing filter allows the electric field of an electromagnetic wave to pass.

topics.title: Back Emf
topics.description: Back emf is the electromotive force generated in a motor that opposes the applied voltage, resulting from the rotation of the motor's coil.

topics.title: Back Strain from Poor Posture
topics.description: Poor posture causes the upper body's center of gravity to shift forward, creating torque around the hips that requires large forces from back muscles.

topics.title: Banked Curve
topics.description: A curve in a road that is sloping in a manner that helps a vehicle negotiate the curve.

topics.title: Barometer
topics.description: A barometer is a device that measures atmospheric pressure, often using a column of mercury where the height of the column indicates the pressure.

topics.title: Baryon
topics.description: Baryons are particles composed of three quarks, such as protons and neutrons.

topics.title: Baryon Number
topics.description: A conserved physical quantity that is zero for mesons and leptons and ±1 for baryons and antibaryons, respectively.

topics.title: Basal Metabolic Rate
topics.description: The total energy conversion rate of a person at rest.

topics.title: Basal Metabolic Rate (BMR)
topics.description: The total energy conversion rate of a person at rest, divided among various systems in the body, primarily the liver, spleen, and brain.

topics.title: Base of Support
topics.description: The base of support is the area beneath an object that is in contact with the ground or surface, which helps determine stability.

topics.title: Base Pairing in DNA
topics.description: Base pairing in DNA refers to the specific pairing of adenine (A) with thymine (T) and cytosine (C) with guanine (G), which ensures accurate genetic information transfer during cell division.

topics.title: Base Quantity
topics.description: A physical quantity chosen by convention and practical considerations such that all other physical quantities can be expressed as algebraic combinations of them.

topics.title: Base Unit
topics.description: A standard for expressing the measurement of a base quantity within a particular system of units; defined by a particular procedure used to measure the corresponding base quantity.

topics.title: Beat
topics.description: A phenomenon produced by the superposition of two waves with slightly different frequencies but the same amplitude.

topics.title: Beat Frequency
topics.description: Beat frequency is the frequency at which the amplitude of the resultant wave fluctuates when two waves of slightly different frequencies interfere.

topics.title: Becquerel
topics.description: The SI unit for the rate of decay of a radioactive material.

topics.title: Behavior of Electromagnetic Radiation
topics.description: The behavior of electromagnetic radiation refers to how electromagnetic waves travel through space and interact with matter, including properties like reflection, refraction, diffraction, and interference.

topics.title: Bernoulli’s Equation
topics.description: Bernoulli’s equation is a statement of the conservation of energy for an incompressible, frictionless fluid, expressing that the sum of pressure, kinetic energy per unit volume, and gravitational potential energy per unit volume is constant.

topics.title: Bernoulli’s Principle
topics.description: Bernoulli’s principle is a specific form of Bernoulli’s equation for fluids at constant depth, stating that an increase in fluid speed results in a decrease in pressure.

topics.title: Beta Decay
topics.description: Beta decay is a type of radioactive decay in which a neutron in the nucleus is transformed into a proton, emitting an electron and an antineutrino.

topics.title: Beta Decay Equation
topics.description: Beta decay involves the emission of an electron and an antineutrino from an atom, increasing its atomic number by one while keeping the mass number the same.

topics.title: Beta Rays
topics.description: One of the types of rays emitted from the nucleus of an atom.

topics.title: Big Bang
topics.description: The theoretical event that marked the beginning of the universe, where all matter and energy were concentrated in an extremely hot and dense state before rapidly expanding.

topics.title: Big Bang Evolution
topics.description: The sequence of events following the Big Bang, including the evolution of fundamental forces and the formation of particles and structures in the early universe.

topics.title: Binding Energy
topics.description: Binding energy is the energy required to separate a nucleus into its individual protons and neutrons.

topics.title: Binding Energy (Work Function)
topics.description: Binding energy, also known as the work function, is the minimum energy required to eject an electron from a material.

topics.title: Binding Energy of an Electron
topics.description: The binding energy of an electron is the minimum energy required to remove an electron from its bound state in a material.

topics.title: Binding Energy per Nucleon
topics.description: Binding energy per nucleon is the binding energy of a nucleus divided by the number of nucleons, and it is greater for medium-mass nuclei.

topics.title: Bioelectrical Energy
topics.description: The energy used to maintain electrical potentials in all living cells, primarily for nerve impulses and cellular processes.

topics.title: Bioelectricity and Wound Healing
topics.description: Bioelectricity refers to the role of electrical signals and ion movements in biological processes, including wound healing and tissue repair.

topics.title: Biological Effects of Ionizing Radiation
topics.description: The impact of ionizing radiation on living tissues, which can be harmful or beneficial depending on the dose and exposure.

topics.title: Biot-Savart Law
topics.description: A physical law that describes the magnetic field generated by an electric current in terms of a specific equation.

topics.title: Birefringent Crystals
topics.description: Crystals that split an unpolarized beam of light into two beams.

topics.title: Black Body Radiation
topics.description: Black body radiation refers to the electromagnetic radiation emitted by an idealized object that absorbs all incident radiation and emits radiation based solely on its temperature.

topics.title: Black Hole
topics.description: A black hole is an object with such strong gravity that not even light can escape its gravitational pull.

topics.title: Blackbody
topics.description: A blackbody is an object that absorbs all radiated energy that strikes it and also emits energy across all wavelengths of the electromagnetic spectrum.

topics.title: Blackbody Radiation
topics.description: Blackbody radiation is the electromagnetic radiation emitted by a perfect blackbody, which absorbs and re-emits all incident radiation, with the intensity and wavelength distribution depending on its temperature.

topics.title: Blackbody Spectrum
topics.description: The distribution of electromagnetic radiation emitted by a blackbody as a function of wavelength or frequency, which is determined by its temperature.

topics.title: Bladder Pressure
topics.description: The pressure inside the bladder as it fills with urine, which triggers the urge to urinate and can be influenced by various physiological factors.

topics.title: Blood Pressure
topics.description: The pressure exerted by blood against the walls of blood vessels, typically measured in millimeters of mercury (mm Hg).

topics.title: Blood Pressure in the Lungs
topics.description: The pressure within the lungs, which fluctuates with breathing and is influenced by muscle action and surface tension.

topics.title: Bohr Model of the Atom
topics.description: A model of the atom where electrons orbit the nucleus in quantized energy levels, and energy is emitted or absorbed when electrons transition between these levels.

topics.title: Bohr Radius
topics.description: The mean radius of the orbit of an electron around the nucleus of a hydrogen atom in its ground state.

topics.title: Bohr’s Model of the Atom
topics.description: Bohr’s model describes the structure of an atom with electrons orbiting the nucleus in specific, quantized energy levels.

topics.title: Bohr’s Theory of the Hydrogen Atom
topics.description: Bohr's theory explains the hydrogen spectrum by proposing that electrons orbit the nucleus in quantized energy levels and emit or absorb photons when transitioning between these levels.

topics.title: Boiling
topics.description: Boiling is the process by which a liquid turns into a gas at its boiling point, which occurs throughout the liquid.

topics.title: Boiling and Vapor Pressure
topics.description: Boiling occurs when the vapor pressure of a liquid equals the atmospheric pressure, allowing bubbles of vapor to form and rise to the surface.

topics.title: Boltzmann Constant
topics.description: The Boltzmann constant is a physical constant relating the average kinetic energy of particles in a gas with the temperature of the gas, with a value of 1.38 × 10^-23 J/K.

topics.title: Boson
topics.description: A particle with zero or an integer value of intrinsic spin.

topics.title: Bottom Quark
topics.description: A quark flavor.

topics.title: Bow Wake
topics.description: A V-shaped disturbance created when the wave source moves faster than the wave propagation speed.

topics.title: Bragg Equation
topics.description: The Bragg equation, nλ = 2d sinθ, describes the condition for constructive interference of waves, such as electrons or X-rays, scattered by the atomic planes of a crystal.

topics.title: Bragg Reflection
topics.description: Bragg reflection is the constructive interference of electrons (or X-rays) scattered by the planes of atoms in a crystal, occurring when the path length difference is an integer multiple of the wavelength.

topics.title: Break-Even
topics.description: A condition in fusion where the power produced equals the heating power input.

topics.title: Breeder Reactor
topics.description: A breeder reactor is a type of nuclear reactor designed to produce more fissionable material than it consumes, typically by converting non-fissionable isotopes into fissionable ones.

topics.title: Breeding
topics.description: Breeding is a process in which neutrons are used to convert non-fissionable isotopes, such as uranium-238, into fissionable isotopes, such as plutonium-239.

topics.title: Breeding Reaction
topics.description: A process that produces 239Pu.

topics.title: Bremsstrahlung
topics.description: Radiation produced when electrons are decelerated.

topics.title: Bremsstrahlung Radiation
topics.description: Bremsstrahlung radiation is x-ray radiation produced when electrons are decelerated upon striking a target material in an x-ray tube.

topics.title: Brewster’s Angle
topics.description: Brewster’s angle is the angle of incidence at which light reflected from a surface is completely polarized, and it is given by the tangent of the angle equal to the ratio of the refractive indices of the two media.

topics.title: Brewster’s Law
topics.description: The relationship between the tangent of Brewster’s angle and the indices of refraction of two media.

topics.title: Bridge Device
topics.description: A device that forms a bridge between two branches of a circuit; some bridge devices are used to make null measurements in circuits.

topics.title: Brownian Motion
topics.description: Brownian motion is the random movement of particles suspended in a fluid, caused by collisions with the fluid's molecules.

topics.title: Bulk Modulus
topics.description: Bulk modulus is a measure of the resistance of a material to uniform compression, defined as the ratio of volumetric stress to volumetric strain.

topics.title: Buoyant Force
topics.description: The upward force exerted by a fluid on an object submerged in it.

topics.title: Calculating Magnitude of a Resultant Vector
topics.description: The magnitude of a resultant vector is calculated using the Pythagorean theorem, which relates the magnitudes of the perpendicular components to the resultant vector.

topics.title: Calculation of Force from Pressure and Area
topics.description: Force can be calculated by multiplying the pressure by the area over which it is applied.

topics.title: Calorie
topics.description: A calorie (cal) is the energy needed to change the temperature of 1.00 g of water by 1.00 °C.

topics.title: Capacitance
topics.description: Capacitance is the ability of a system to store electric charge per unit voltage, measured in farads.

topics.title: Capacitance Formula
topics.description: The formula relating capacitance, charge, and voltage, expressed as C = Q/V.

topics.title: Capacitance of a Parallel Plate Capacitor
topics.description: The capacitance of a parallel plate capacitor is directly proportional to the area of the plates and inversely proportional to the distance between them, given by C = ε₀A/d.

topics.title: Capacitive Reactance
topics.description: The opposition a capacitor provides to a change in current, calculated by X_C = 1/(2πfC).

topics.title: Capacitor
topics.description: An electrical component used to store energy by separating electric charge on two opposing plates.

topics.title: Capacitor Charging
topics.description: A capacitor charges when a voltage is applied across its plates, causing equal and opposite charges to accumulate on each plate.

topics.title: Capacitor Charging in an RC Circuit
topics.description: In an RC circuit, a capacitor charges over time, with the voltage across it increasing exponentially until it reaches the maximum voltage of the source.

topics.title: Capacitor Discharging in an RC Circuit
topics.description: In an RC circuit, a capacitor discharges over time, with the voltage across it decreasing exponentially until it approaches zero.

topics.title: Capacitor Energy Equations
topics.description: The energy stored in a capacitor can be calculated using three equivalent formulas: $ E_{\text{cap}} = \frac{QV}{2} $, $ E_{\text{cap}} = \frac{1}{2} CV^2 $, and $ E_{\text{cap}} = \frac{Q^2}{2C} $.

topics.title: Capacitors
topics.description: A capacitor is a device that stores electric charge and electric potential energy in an electric field.

topics.title: Capacitors and Dielectrics
topics.description: A capacitor is a device that stores electric charge, and a dielectric is an insulating material that increases the capacitance when placed between the plates.

topics.title: Capacitors in Parallel
topics.description: Capacitors connected in parallel are arranged so that the same voltage is applied across each capacitor, and the total charge stored is the sum of the charges stored on each capacitor.

topics.title: Capacitors in Series
topics.description: Capacitors connected in series are arranged so that the same charge accumulates on each capacitor, and the total voltage across the combination is the sum of the voltages across each capacitor.

topics.title: Capacitors in Series and Parallel
topics.description: Capacitors in series have the same charge but different voltages, while capacitors in parallel have the same voltage but different charges.

topics.title: Capillary Action
topics.description: Capillary action is the tendency of a fluid to be raised or suppressed in a narrow tube, or capillary tube, due to the balance between cohesive and adhesive forces.

topics.title: Carbon Nanotubes
topics.description: Cylindrical structures made of carbon atoms arranged in a hexagonal lattice, known for their unique mechanical and electrical properties.

topics.title: Carbon-14 Dating
topics.description: A specific type of radioactive dating that uses the decay of carbon-14 to estimate the age of organic materials.

topics.title: Carnot Cycle
topics.description: A Carnot cycle is a theoretical thermodynamic cycle that consists of two isothermal and two adiabatic processes, and is the most efficient cyclical process possible for a heat engine.

topics.title: Carnot Efficiency
topics.description: Carnot efficiency is the maximum theoretical efficiency of a heat engine operating between two temperatures, calculated as 1 minus the ratio of the cold reservoir temperature to the hot reservoir temperature in kelvins.

topics.title: Carnot Engine
topics.description: A heat engine that uses a Carnot cycle.

topics.title: Carnot Heat Engine
topics.description: A Carnot heat engine is an idealized heat engine that operates between two thermal reservoirs at different temperatures and achieves the maximum possible efficiency for those temperatures.

topics.title: Carrier Wave
topics.description: An electromagnetic wave that carries a signal by modulation of its amplitude or frequency.

topics.title: Case 1 Image for Mirrors
topics.description: A case 1 image for mirrors is formed when the object is placed beyond the focal point of a concave mirror, resulting in a real, inverted, and smaller image.

topics.title: Case 2 Image for Mirrors
topics.description: A case 2 image for mirrors is formed when the object is placed between the focal point and the mirror surface of a concave mirror, resulting in a virtual, upright, and enlarged image.

topics.title: Case 3 Image for Mirrors
topics.description: A case 3 image for mirrors is formed when the object is placed in front of a convex mirror, resulting in a virtual, upright, and diminished image.

topics.title: Cathode-Ray Tube
topics.description: A vacuum tube containing a source of electrons and a screen to view images.

topics.title: Cause and Effect in Physics
topics.description: Cause and effect in physics refers to the relationship between an action (cause) and its resulting effect, which is central to understanding how forces influence motion.

topics.title: Cavendish Experiment
topics.description: An experiment conducted by Henry Cavendish to measure the gravitational constant G by observing the gravitational attraction between two masses.

topics.title: Celsius Scale
topics.description: A temperature scale in which the freezing point of water is 0 °C and the boiling point is 100 °C.

topics.title: Celsius to Fahrenheit Conversion
topics.description: The formula to convert temperature from Celsius to Fahrenheit is T°F = (9/5)T°C + 32.

topics.title: Celsius to Kelvin Conversion
topics.description: The formula to convert temperature from Celsius to Kelvin is T(K) = T°C + 273.15.

topics.title: Center of Gravity
topics.description: The center of gravity is the point where the entire weight of an object can be considered to act.

topics.title: Center of Mass
topics.description: The average position of the mass in an object or system, used to simplify the analysis of gravitational interactions.

topics.title: Central Axis
topics.description: A line perpendicular to the center of a lens or mirror extending in both directions.

topics.title: Central Maximum in Single Slit Diffraction
topics.description: The brightest and widest maximum in a single slit diffraction pattern, located at the center and formed by constructive interference of light waves.

topics.title: Centrifugal Force
topics.description: Centrifugal force is a fictitious force that appears in rotating frames of reference, pushing objects outward from the center of rotation.

topics.title: Centrifuge
topics.description: A centrifuge is a device that uses high-speed rotation to generate large centripetal accelerations, used to separate substances of different densities.

topics.title: Centrip,etal Force
topics.description: Centripetal force is the net force required to keep an object moving in a circular path, directed toward the center of the circle.

topics.title: Centripetal Acceleration
topics.description: Centripetal acceleration is the acceleration experienced by an object moving in a circular path, directed toward the center of the circle.

topics.title: Centripetal Force
topics.description: The net force required to keep an object moving in a circular path, directed toward the center of the circle.

topics.title: Centripetal Force in Magnetic Fields
topics.description: The magnetic force acting on a moving charge can act as the centripetal force, causing the charge to move in a circular path.

topics.title: Centripetal Force Provided by Magnetic Field
topics.description: The magnetic force acting on a moving charge can act as the centripetal force, causing the charge to move in a circular path.

topics.title: Cerebrospinal Fluid Pressure
topics.description: The pressure exerted by the fluid surrounding the brain and spinal cord, which helps support and protect these organs.

topics.title: Cesium-137
topics.description: Cesium-137 is a radioactive isotope used as a source of gamma rays in food irradiation, with an energy of 0.67 MeV and less penetrating power than Cobalt-60.

topics.title: Chain Reaction
topics.description: A chain reaction is a self-sustaining sequence of nuclear reactions where neutrons released from one reaction trigger more reactions.

topics.title: Change in Angular Velocity
topics.description: The difference between final and initial values of angular velocity.

topics.title: Change in Entropy
topics.description: The ratio of heat transfer to temperature.

topics.title: Change in Momentum
topics.description: Change in momentum is the difference between the final and initial momentum of an object, which is equal to the impulse applied to the object.

topics.title: Change of Wavelength with Index of Refraction
topics.description: The wavelength of light in a medium is equal to the wavelength in a vacuum divided by the index of refraction of the medium.

topics.title: Chaos
topics.description: Chaos describes systems whose outcomes are extremely sensitive to initial conditions.

topics.title: Chaotic Behavior
topics.description: Chaotic behavior refers to the unpredictable and sensitive dependence on initial conditions in certain systems, making long-term predictions difficult.

topics.title: Characteristic Time Constant
topics.description: The time constant τ of an RL circuit, calculated by τ = L/R, where L is inductance and R is resistance.

topics.title: Characteristic Time Constant of an RL Circuit
topics.description: The characteristic time constant of an RL circuit is the time it takes for the current to reach approximately 63.2% of its final value.

topics.title: Characteristic X-Ray
topics.description: Characteristic x rays are electromagnetic radiation emitted by an atom when an inner-shell vacancy is filled by an electron transitioning from a higher energy level.

topics.title: Charge Carrier Sign Determination
topics.description: The Hall effect can be used to determine whether the charge carriers in a material are positive or negative by observing the direction of the Hall emf.

topics.title: Charge Concentration on Sharp Points
topics.description: Excess charges on a nonuniform conductor become most concentrated at the location of greatest curvature, such as sharp points.

topics.title: Charge Concentration on Sharp Points of Conductors
topics.description: Excess charges on a nonuniform conductor become most concentrated at the location of greatest curvature, such as sharp points.

topics.title: Charge Properties of Particles
topics.description: Charge properties of particles refer to the electric charge characteristics of fundamental particles like quarks and leptons.

topics.title: Charge Repulsion
topics.description: Charge repulsion is the phenomenon where like charges (such as two positive charges) push each other away.

topics.title: Charge Separation
topics.description: Charge separation is the process by which charges are divided between two objects, often due to friction, resulting in one object having a net positive charge and the other a net negative charge.

topics.title: Charge Separation in DNA
topics.description: DNA is a highly charged molecule with base pairs held together by electrostatic forces, which contribute to its structure and function.

topics.title: Charging by Contact
topics.description: Charging by contact is a method where an object is charged directly by touching it with another charged object, transferring charge through physical contact.

topics.title: Charging by Induction
topics.description: Charging by induction is a method where an object is charged without direct contact by bringing a charged object near it, causing a redistribution of charges in the object.

topics.title: Charm Quark
topics.description: A quark flavor, which is the counterpart of the strange quark.

topics.title: Chart of the Nuclides
topics.description: A table comprising stable and unstable nuclei.

topics.title: Chemical Energy
topics.description: The energy in a substance stored in the bonds between atoms and molecules that can be released in a chemical reaction.

topics.title: Chromatic Aberration
topics.description: Chromatic aberration is a distortion in an image caused by different wavelengths of light being refracted by different amounts through a lens.

topics.title: Circuit Breaker
topics.description: A safety device that protects against thermal overload by interrupting the circuit if the current exceeds a safe level.

topics.title: Circuit Diagram
topics.description: A schematic drawing of an electrical circuit including all circuit elements.

topics.title: Circular Aperture Diffraction
topics.description: Circular aperture diffraction refers to the spreading of light passing through a circular aperture, producing a diffraction pattern with a central bright spot surrounded by concentric rings, where the first minimum occurs at an angle theta = 1.22 lambda / D.

topics.title: Circular Motion
topics.description: Circular motion is the movement of an object along a circular path.

topics.title: Classical Limit
topics.description: The classical limit refers to the condition where objects are large and moving at speeds much slower than the speed of light, making relativistic mechanics indistinguishable from classical mechanics.

topics.title: Classical Mechanics
topics.description: Classical mechanics is the realm of physics where Newton’s laws of motion apply, typically to objects moving at speeds much less than the speed of light and larger than most molecules.

topics.title: Classical Physics
topics.description: Classical physics is the branch of physics that describes the behavior of objects moving at speeds much slower than the speed of light and in weak gravitational fields.

topics.title: Classical Relativity
topics.description: The study of relative velocities in situations where speeds are less than about 1% of the speed of light.

topics.title: Classical Velocity Addition
topics.description: The method of adding velocities when the speed is much less than the speed of light, where velocities add like regular numbers in one-dimensional motion.

topics.title: Closed Magnetic Field Lines
topics.description: Magnetic field lines form continuous closed loops, indicating that magnetic fields have no beginning or end and always form complete circuits.

topics.title: Closed-Pipe Resonator
topics.description: A closed-pipe resonator is a tube closed at one end that supports standing waves with resonant frequencies that are odd multiples of the fundamental frequency.

topics.title: Cobalt-60
topics.description: Cobalt-60 is a radioactive isotope used as a source of gamma rays in food irradiation, with an average energy of 1.25 MeV.

topics.title: Coefficient of Friction
topics.description: A dimensionless quantity that represents the ratio of the frictional force between two surfaces to the normal force pressing them together.

topics.title: Coefficient of Kinetic Friction
topics.description: The coefficient of kinetic friction is a unitless quantity that represents the ratio of the kinetic friction force to the normal force between two surfaces.

topics.title: Coefficient of Linear Expansion
topics.description: The change in length per unit length per 1 °C change in temperature, used to calculate linear expansion.

topics.title: Coefficient of Performance
topics.description: The ratio of heat transfer at the output (the hot reservoir) to the work supplied for a heat pump, or the ratio of heat transfer from the cold reservoir to the work supplied for a refrigerator or air conditioner.

topics.title: Coefficient of Performance (COP) for Heat Pumps
topics.description: The coefficient of performance (COP) for a heat pump is the ratio of the heat transferred to the hot reservoir (Q_h) to the work input (W), expressed as COP_hp = Q_h / W.

topics.title: Coefficient of Static Friction
topics.description: The coefficient of static friction is a unitless quantity that represents the ratio of the maximum static friction force to the normal force between two surfaces.

topics.title: Coefficient of Volume Expansion
topics.description: The change in volume per unit volume per 1 °C change in temperature.

topics.title: Coherence
topics.description: Coherence refers to the property of waves that enables them to maintain a constant phase difference, allowing for stable interference patterns.

topics.title: Coherent Sources
topics.description: Coherent sources are sources of waves that maintain a constant phase relationship over time.

topics.title: Coherent Waves
topics.description: Waves that are in phase or have a definite phase relationship.

topics.title: Cohesion and Adhesion in Liquids: Surface Tension and Capillary Action
topics.description: Cohesion is the attraction between molecules of the same substance, while adhesion is the attraction between different substances, leading to surface tension and capillary action.

topics.title: Cohesive Forces
topics.description: Cohesive forces are attractive forces between molecules of the same type.

topics.title: Cold Reservoir
topics.description: A cold reservoir is a low-temperature object or environment that absorbs heat from a heat engine or heat pump.

topics.title: Colliding Beam Accelerators
topics.description: Colliding beam accelerators are particle accelerators that use beams of particles moving in opposite directions to reduce energy loss and create particles with high energy and mass.

topics.title: Colliding Beams
topics.description: Head-on collisions between particles moving in opposite directions.

topics.title: Collimator
topics.description: A collimator is a device with holes that allows gamma rays to pass through in specific directions, helping to focus and direct radiation for imaging purposes.

topics.title: Collisions in Two Dimensions
topics.description: Collisions in two dimensions involve objects colliding in a plane, requiring analysis of momentum components along both axes.

topics.title: Collisions of Extended Bodies in Two Dimensions
topics.description: Collisions of extended bodies in two dimensions involve the conservation of angular momentum and linear momentum during collisions between objects.

topics.title: Color and Color Vision
topics.description: Color and color vision refer to the ability to perceive different wavelengths of light as distinct colors.

topics.title: Color Charge
topics.description: Color charge is a property of quarks that is responsible for the strong nuclear force interactions between them.

topics.title: Color Constancy
topics.description: Color constancy is the ability of the eye-brain system to perceive the true color of an object under varying lighting conditions.

topics.title: Color Perception
topics.description: Color perception is the ability of the human eye to detect and interpret different wavelengths of visible light, which is determined by the response of specialized cells in the eye called cones.

topics.title: Color Vision
topics.description: Color vision is the ability of the human eye to perceive different wavelengths of light as distinct colors.

topics.title: Coma
topics.description: Coma is an optical aberration that occurs when an object is off-center, causing the image to appear pear-shaped due to rays not converging at a single focal point.

topics.title: Coma Aberration
topics.description: Coma aberration is an optical distortion that occurs when an object is off-center, resulting in a pear-shaped image.

topics.title: Combination of Series and Parallel Resistors
topics.description: A combination circuit contains both series and parallel connections, which can be reduced to a single equivalent resistance by simplifying step-by-step.

topics.title: Common Phases of Matter
topics.description: The common phases of matter are solid, liquid, gas, and plasma, which are the states in which matter typically exists.

topics.title: Commutative
topics.description: Refers to the interchangeability of order in a function; vector addition is commutative because the order in which vectors are added does not affect the final sum.

topics.title: Comparison of Densities
topics.description: Different substances have different densities, which can be used to identify their composition.

topics.title: Comparison of Electrostatic and Gravitational Forces
topics.description: The electrostatic force between charged particles is significantly stronger than the gravitational force between the same particles, especially at the subatomic level.

topics.title: Competitive Binding
topics.description: Competitive binding is a principle in radioimmunoassay where a radioactive isotope competes with a non-radioactive substance for binding sites on antibodies, allowing the measurement of the target substance.

topics.title: Complex Adaptive Systems
topics.description: A complex adaptive system is a system that can adapt, learn, and evolve over time, often through interactions among its components.

topics.title: Complex Machine
topics.description: A complex machine is a combination of two or more simple machines working together to perform a task.

topics.title: Complex Systems
topics.description: A complex system is a system composed of many interacting parts that exhibit behaviors and patterns that cannot be easily predicted from the properties of the individual parts.

topics.title: Complexity
topics.description: Complexity is an emerging field devoted to the study of complex systems.

topics.title: Complexity and Chaos
topics.description: The study of complex systems and chaotic behavior, where small changes can lead to vastly different outcomes in dynamic systems.

topics.title: Component (of a 2-D Vector)
topics.description: A piece of a vector that points in either the vertical or horizontal direction; every 2-D vector can be expressed as a sum of two vertical and horizontal components.

topics.title: Component (of a 2-Dimensional Vector)
topics.description: A piece of a vector that points in a particular direction, usually in the direction of one of the axes of a chosen coordinate system.

topics.title: Component Analysis of Forces
topics.description: Breaking down forces into components along chosen axes to simplify two-dimensional force problems into one-dimensional problems.

topics.title: Components of Vectors
topics.description: The x and y components of a vector are the projections of the vector along the x- and y-axes, respectively.

topics.title: Compound Microscope
topics.description: A compound microscope is an optical instrument that uses two or more lenses to magnify small objects, with the first lens forming an image that serves as the object for the second lens.

topics.title: Compression
topics.description: Compression is a region in a longitudinal wave where the particles of the medium are pushed together, resulting in higher pressure.

topics.title: Compression and Rarefaction
topics.description: Compression is a region of high pressure in a sound wave, while rarefaction is a region of low pressure.

topics.title: Compression of Matter
topics.description: Compression refers to the ability of a substance to decrease in volume under pressure, with solids and liquids resisting compression more than gases.

topics.title: Compressive Deformation
topics.description: Compressive deformation is the shortening of a material when subjected to a force pushing it together, resulting in a change in length.

topics.title: Compton Effect
topics.description: The Compton effect is the scattering of X-ray photons by electrons, where both energy and momentum are conserved, resulting in a decrease in the photon's energy and a change in its direction.

topics.title: Compton Wavelength
topics.description: The Compton wavelength is a fundamental property of a particle that represents the wavelength shift observed when a photon collides with a particle, such as an electron.

topics.title: Computed Tomography (CT) Scanner
topics.description: A computed tomography (CT) scanner is a medical imaging device that uses x rays and computer processing to create detailed cross-sectional images of the body.

topics.title: Concave Mirror
topics.description: A concave mirror is a mirror that curves inward, and can form real or virtual images depending on the object's position relative to the focal point.

topics.title: Concave Mirror Behavior
topics.description: A concave mirror is a converging mirror that can form both real and virtual images depending on the object's position relative to its focal length.

topics.title: Concentration of Waves
topics.description: Concentrating a wave onto a smaller area increases its intensity, as intensity is defined as power per unit area.

topics.title: Condensation
topics.description: A phase change from gas to liquid.

topics.title: Conditions for Equilibrium
topics.description: The two conditions for equilibrium are that the net force acting on an object must be zero and the net torque acting on the object must also be zero.

topics.title: Conduction
topics.description: Conduction is the transfer of heat through stationary matter by physical contact, where energy is transferred between particles due to their thermal motion.

topics.title: Conduction in Collisions
topics.description: Conduction occurs through molecular collisions, where energy is transferred from molecules with higher kinetic energy to those with lower kinetic energy.

topics.title: Conductive Heat Transfer
topics.description: Conductive heat transfer is the process by which heat is transferred through a material due to the collisions of molecules, moving from hotter regions to colder regions.

topics.title: Conductor
topics.description: A conductor is a material that allows electric charge to move freely through it due to the presence of free electrons or ions.

topics.title: Conductor as a Faraday Cage in a Car
topics.description: A metal car acts as a Faraday cage, protecting passengers from dangerous electric fields caused by a downed line touching the car.

topics.title: Conductor as an Equipotential Surface
topics.description: A conductor in electrostatic equilibrium is an equipotential surface, meaning the electric potential is the same at all points on its surface.

topics.title: Conductors
topics.description: Conductors are materials that allow electric charges to move freely through them.

topics.title: Conductors and Insulators
topics.description: Conductors are materials that allow charge to move freely, while insulators are materials that restrict the movement of charge.

topics.title: Cones and Color Perception
topics.description: Cones are photoreceptors in the retina that are sensitive to different ranges of wavelengths, enabling the perception of various colors through their stimulation.

topics.title: Confocal Microscopy
topics.description: Confocal microscopy produces three-dimensional images by using pinholes to exclude out-of-focus light and capturing light from a single focal plane.

topics.title: Consequences of Special Relativity
topics.description: The observable effects or outcomes that arise from the postulates of special relativity, such as time dilation, length contraction, and the equivalence of mass and energy.

topics.title: Conservation Laws
topics.description: Principles stating that certain physical quantities, such as energy, momentum, and charge, remain constant in isolated systems.

topics.title: Conservation of Angular Momentum
topics.description: The conservation of angular momentum states that if no external torque acts on a system, the total angular momentum of the system remains constant.

topics.title: Conservation of Charge
topics.description: The conservation of charge is the principle that the total electric charge in an isolated system remains constant.

topics.title: Conservation of Charge in Circuits
topics.description: Charge is conserved in a circuit, meaning the total charge entering a junction equals the total charge leaving it.

topics.title: Conservation of Energy
topics.description: Conservation of energy states that energy cannot be created or destroyed, only transformed from one form to another.

topics.title: Conservation of Energy in Circuits
topics.description: Energy is conserved in a circuit, meaning the total energy supplied by voltage sources equals the total energy dissipated by resistors.

topics.title: Conservation of Energy in Thermodynamics
topics.description: Conservation of energy in thermodynamics relates to the first law, stating that energy cannot be created or destroyed, only converted from one form to another.

topics.title: Conservation of Internal Kinetic Energy
topics.description: Conservation of internal kinetic energy states that the total internal kinetic energy of a system remains constant in an elastic collision.

topics.title: Conservation of Mechanical Energy
topics.description: The principle that the total mechanical energy (kinetic plus potential) of a system remains constant when only conservative forces are acting.

topics.title: Conservation of Mechanical Energy with Nonconservative Forces
topics.description: When nonconservative forces act, the total mechanical energy of a system changes by the amount of work done by these forces.

topics.title: Conservation of Momentum
topics.description: Conservation of momentum states that the total momentum of a closed system remains constant if no external forces act on the system.

topics.title: Conservation of Momentum for Two Objects
topics.description: In a closed system with two objects, the total momentum before and after a collision remains the same.

topics.title: Conservation of Momentum in Photon Absorption
topics.description: The principle that the momentum of a photon absorbed by a particle is transferred to the particle, leading to a recoil velocity as described by the conservation of momentum.

topics.title: Conservation of Momentum in Two Dimensions
topics.description: The total momentum along the x-axis and y-axis is conserved in two-dimensional collisions.

topics.title: Conservation of Momentum Principle
topics.description: The total momentum of a system remains constant if the net external force acting on it is zero.

topics.title: Conservation of Total Baryon Number
topics.description: A general rule based on the observation that the total number of nucleons was always conserved in nuclear reactions and decays.

topics.title: Conservation of Total Electron Family Number
topics.description: A general rule stating that the total electron family number stays the same through an interaction.

topics.title: Conservation of Total Muon Family Number
topics.description: A general rule stating that the total muon family number stays the same through an interaction.

topics.title: Conservative Force
topics.description: A force for which the work done by or against it depends only on the starting and ending points of a motion and not on the path taken.

topics.title: Constant
topics.description: A quantity that does not change.

topics.title: Constant Acceleration
topics.description: Acceleration that does not change with respect to time.

topics.title: Constant for Satellites Orbiting the Same Massive Object
topics.description: The constant for satellites orbiting the same massive object relates the cube of the orbital radius to the square of the orbital period, and is proportional to the mass of the central body.

topics.title: Constructive Interference
topics.description: Constructive interference occurs when waves arrive at the same point in phase, resulting in a wave with a larger amplitude.

topics.title: Constructive Interference and Intensity
topics.description: When two identical waves interfere perfectly constructively, the resulting wave's intensity is four times the intensity of each individual wave.

topics.title: Constructive Interference for a Double Slit
topics.description: The condition where light waves from a double slit reinforce each other, creating a bright spot.

topics.title: Constructive Interference in a Diffraction Grating
topics.description: Constructive interference in a diffraction grating occurs when light waves from different slits arrive in phase at a point on a screen, creating a bright region.

topics.title: Constructive Interference in Atomic Orbits
topics.description: Constructive interference in atomic orbits occurs when an electron's wavelength fits perfectly into the circumference of its orbit, allowing it to exist in that orbit.

topics.title: Constructive Interference in Thin Films
topics.description: Constructive interference in thin films occurs when the path length difference between two reflected rays is an integral multiple of the wavelength in the medium.

topics.title: Contact Angle
topics.description: The angle between the tangent to a liquid surface and the surface it contacts, indicating the wetting behavior of the liquid.

topics.title: Contact Lenses
topics.description: Contact lenses are corrective lenses that rest directly on the cornea, providing superior peripheral vision and correcting some corneal astigmatism by filling in irregularities with a tear layer.

topics.title: Contrast
topics.description: The difference in intensity between objects and the background on which they are observed.

topics.title: Controlled Chain Reaction
topics.description: A controlled chain reaction is a process in which neutrons from one fission event cause subsequent fission events in a controlled manner, maintaining a steady energy output.

topics.title: Controlled Nuclear Fusion
topics.description: Controlled nuclear fusion is the process of combining light atomic nuclei to release energy, which is considered a potential future energy source.

topics.title: Convection
topics.description: Convection is the transfer of heat by the large-scale movement of fluids or gases.

topics.title: Convection in Insulation
topics.description: Convection in insulation refers to the role of air movement in determining whether air acts as an insulator or conductor, depending on the available space for airflow.

topics.title: Conventional Current
topics.description: Conventional current is the direction that positive charge would flow in a conductor, which is opposite to the direction of electron flow.

topics.title: Converging Lens
topics.description: A converging lens is a lens that causes parallel light rays to converge at a single point on the opposite side of the lens.

topics.title: Converging Mirror
topics.description: A concave mirror that causes parallel light rays to converge at one or more points along its axis.

topics.title: Conversion Factor
topics.description: A ratio expressing how many of one unit are equal to another unit.

topics.title: Conversion of Chemical Energy to Useful Work
topics.description: The process of transforming chemical energy from food into useful work, which can be calculated based on energy consumption rates and activity levels.

topics.title: Conversion of Potential Energy to Kinetic Energy
topics.description: Gravitational potential energy can be converted into kinetic energy when an object falls, with the energy transformation governed by the work-energy theorem.

topics.title: Convex Mirror
topics.description: A convex mirror is a mirror that curves outward, and always forms virtual images, with the image appearing behind the mirror.

topics.title: Convex Mirror Behavior
topics.description: A convex mirror is a diverging mirror that always forms virtual, upright, and reduced images, regardless of the object's position.

topics.title: Coordinate Axes
topics.description: A set of perpendicular lines used to describe the direction and magnitude of forces in a problem, often chosen to simplify calculations.

topics.title: Coordinate System
topics.description: A coordinate system is a framework used to describe the position and direction of motion in a given reference frame.

topics.title: Coordinate System for Free Fall
topics.description: A coordinate system for free fall defines the direction of motion, typically with upward as positive and downward as negative, which affects the sign of acceleration due to gravity.

topics.title: Copernican Model
topics.description: A model of the solar system where the Sun is at the center and all planets orbit around it.

topics.title: Coriolis Force
topics.description: The fictitious force causing the apparent deflection of moving objects when viewed in a rotating frame of reference.

topics.title: Corner Reflector
topics.description: An object with two perpendicular reflecting surfaces that reflects light back parallel to its incoming direction.

topics.title: Correspondence Principle
topics.description: In the classical limit, quantum mechanics becomes the same as classical physics.

topics.title: Cosmic Microwave Background
topics.description: The cosmic microwave background is the spectrum of microwave radiation of cosmic origin.

topics.title: Cosmic Microwave Background Radiation (CMBR)
topics.description: The faint glow of microwave radiation that fills the universe, a remnant of the intense heat from the Big Bang, which has cooled over time.

topics.title: Cosmic Questions in Physics
topics.description: Cosmic questions in physics are fundamental inquiries about the universe's structure, origin, and behavior on the largest scales.

topics.title: Cosmological Constant
topics.description: The cosmological constant is a theoretical construct intimately related to the expansion and closure of the universe.

topics.title: Cosmological Red Shift
topics.description: A shift in the wavelength of light from distant galaxies due to the expansion of space, indicating that galaxies are moving away from us.

topics.title: Cosmology
topics.description: Cosmology is the study of the character and evolution of the universe.

topics.title: Cosmology and Particle Physics
topics.description: The study of the universe's origin, structure, and evolution, along with the fundamental particles that make up matter.

topics.title: Cost of Electricity
topics.description: The cost of electricity is determined by multiplying the energy consumed (in kilowatt-hours) by the cost per kilowatt-hour.

topics.title: Cost of Energy
topics.description: The cost of energy is calculated by multiplying the power consumption rate by the time of use.

topics.title: Cost of Energy Consumption
topics.description: The cost of energy consumed is calculated by multiplying the power consumption rate by the time of use.

topics.title: Coulomb Repulsion
topics.description: Coulomb repulsion is the repulsive force between positively charged nuclei that must be overcome for fusion to occur.

topics.title: Coulomb's Constant
topics.description: Coulomb's constant is a proportionality constant in Coulomb's law, with a value of 8.99 × 10⁹ N·m²/C² in SI units.

topics.title: Coulomb’s Law
topics.description: Coulomb’s Law describes the force between two point charges in terms of their magnitudes and the distance between them.

topics.title: Crank
topics.description: A crank is a type of lever that can be rotated 360° about its pivot, used to convert rotational motion into linear motion or vice versa.

topics.title: Critical Angle
topics.description: The critical angle is the incident angle at which the angle of refraction is exactly 90 degrees, leading to total internal reflection.

topics.title: Critical Damping
topics.description: The condition in which the damping of an oscillator causes it to return as quickly as possible to its equilibrium position without oscillating back and forth about this position.

topics.title: Critical Density
topics.description: Critical density is the density needed to just halt universal expansion in a universe with no cosmological constant, estimated to be about 10^-26 kg/m³.

topics.title: Critical Mass
topics.description: Critical mass is the minimum amount of fissionable material required to sustain a self-sustaining chain reaction.

topics.title: Critical Point
topics.description: The temperature above which a liquid cannot exist.

topics.title: Critical Pressure
topics.description: The minimum pressure needed for a liquid to exist at the critical temperature.

topics.title: Critical Temperature
topics.description: Critical temperature is the temperature at which and below which a material becomes a superconductor.

topics.title: Criticality
topics.description: A condition where a chain reaction easily becomes self-sustaining.

topics.title: Critically Damped System
topics.description: A critically damped system is one where the damping is just sufficient to return the system to equilibrium as quickly as possible without overshooting.

topics.title: Curie
topics.description: The activity of 1g of radium-226, equal to 3.70 × 10^10 becquerels.

topics.title: Curie Temperature
topics.description: The temperature above which a ferromagnetic material cannot be magnetized.

topics.title: Current
topics.description: The flow of charge through an electric circuit past a given point of measurement.

topics.title: Current Division in Parallel
topics.description: In a parallel circuit, the total current is the sum of the currents through each resistor.

topics.title: Current in Parallel Circuits
topics.description: In a parallel circuit, the total current is the sum of the currents through each branch, and the current through each resistor depends on its resistance.

topics.title: Current Sensitivity
topics.description: The maximum current that a galvanometer can read.

topics.title: Current Sensitivity of a Galvanometer
topics.description: The current sensitivity of a galvanometer is the current that causes a full-scale deflection of its needle.

topics.title: Current Thresholds for Electrical Shock
topics.description: The effects of electrical shock depend on the current level, with specific thresholds for sensation, muscle contraction, ventricular fibrillation, and burns.

topics.title: Curved Path Motion
topics.description: Motion along a curved path is two- or three-dimensional motion that can be described using similar principles to one-dimensional motion.

topics.title: Cyclical Process
topics.description: A cyclical process is a process in which a system returns to its initial state after completing a cycle, with no net change in internal energy.

topics.title: Cyclotron
topics.description: An accelerator that uses fixed-frequency alternating electric fields and fixed magnets to accelerate particles in a circular spiral path.

topics.title: Cyclotron Accelerator
topics.description: An accelerator that uses fixed-frequency alternating electric fields and fixed magnets to accelerate particles in a circular spiral path.

topics.title: Dalton’s Law
topics.description: The total pressure of a gas mixture is the sum of the partial pressures of each individual gas in the mixture.

topics.title: Dalton’s Law of Partial Pressures
topics.description: The physical law that states the total pressure of a gas is the sum of the partial pressures of its component gases.

topics.title: Damped Harmonic Motion
topics.description: Damped harmonic motion is the oscillatory motion of a system where energy is gradually removed by non-conservative forces, causing the amplitude to decrease over time.

topics.title: Damped Harmonic Oscillator
topics.description: A damped harmonic oscillator is a system that oscillates with decreasing amplitude due to energy loss from damping forces.

topics.title: Damping
topics.description: Damping is the process by which energy is removed from an oscillating system, typically due to friction or resistance, causing the amplitude of oscillations to decrease over time.

topics.title: Dark Matter
topics.description: Dark matter is indirectly observed non-luminous matter.

topics.title: Dark Matter and Closure
