topics.description: The study of dark matter, which is invisible matter that influences the universe's structure, and closure, which refers to whether the universe will eventually stop expanding.

topics.title: Data Analysis
topics.description: Data analysis is the process of inspecting, cleaning, transforming, and modeling data to discover useful information and support decision-making.

topics.title: Daughter
topics.description: The nucleus obtained when a parent nucleus decays and produces another nucleus following the rules and the conservation laws.

topics.title: Davisson-Germer Experiment
topics.description: The Davisson-Germer experiment demonstrated the wave nature of electrons by showing that electrons can produce diffraction patterns when scattered by a crystal, confirming de Broglie's hypothesis.

topics.title: DC Circuits Containing Resistors and Capacitors
topics.description: DC circuits containing resistors and capacitors involve the charging and discharging of capacitors through resistors, with the current and voltage changing over time.

topics.title: DC Instruments
topics.description: DC instruments are devices used to measure electrical quantities such as voltage and current in direct current (DC) circuits.

topics.title: DC Voltmeters and Ammeters
topics.description: DC voltmeters measure voltage across a component and are connected in parallel, while DC ammeters measure current through a component and are connected in series.

topics.title: De Broglie Relationship
topics.description: The relationship that connects the wavelength of a particle to its momentum, expressed as lambda = h/p, where h is Planck's constant and p is the momentum.

topics.title: De Broglie Wavelength
topics.description: The de Broglie wavelength is the wavelength associated with a particle, given by the equation λ = h/p, where h is Planck's constant and p is the particle's momentum.

topics.title: Decay
topics.description: The process by which an atomic nucleus of an unstable atom loses mass and energy by emitting ionizing particles.

topics.title: Decay Constant
topics.description: A quantity that is inversely proportional to the half-life and used in the equation for the number of nuclei as a function of time.

topics.title: Decay Equation
topics.description: The equation to find out how much of a radioactive material is left after a given period of time.

topics.title: Decay Series
topics.description: A process whereby subsequent nuclides decay until a stable nuclide is produced.

topics.title: Deceleration
topics.description: Acceleration in the direction opposite to velocity; acceleration that results in a decrease in velocity.

topics.title: Decibel
topics.description: A unit used to describe sound intensity levels.

topics.title: Decibel Scale
topics.description: A logarithmic scale used to measure the intensity of sound, where each 10 dB increase represents a tenfold increase in sound intensity.

topics.title: Defibrillator
topics.description: A machine used to provide an electrical shock to a heart attack victim's heart in order to restore the heart's normal rhythmic pattern.

topics.title: Defibrillator Function
topics.description: A defibrillator is a medical device that delivers a controlled electric shock to the heart to restore normal cardiac rhythm during life-threatening arrhythmias.

topics.title: Deformation
topics.description: Deformation is the change in shape or size of an object due to the application of an external force.

topics.title: Degree Celsius
topics.description: A unit on the Celsius temperature scale.

topics.title: Degree Fahrenheit
topics.description: A unit on the Fahrenheit temperature scale.

topics.title: Density
topics.description: Density is the mass per unit volume of a substance or object.

topics.title: Density and Buoyancy
topics.description: The density of an object relative to the density of the fluid determines whether it floats, sinks, or remains suspended.

topics.title: Density Calculation from Pressure and Altitude
topics.description: Density of a fluid can be calculated using the relationship between pressure, depth, and gravitational acceleration.

topics.title: Dependent Variable
topics.description: The variable that is being measured; usually plotted along the y-axis.

topics.title: Depolarization
topics.description: Depolarization is the process by which the inside of a neuron's membrane becomes less negative, allowing an action potential to be generated.

topics.title: Depolarization and Repolarization
topics.description: Depolarization is the process by which a neuron's membrane potential becomes less negative, allowing an action potential to be generated, while repolarization is the return to the resting potential after depolarization.

topics.title: Depolarizing Wave
topics.description: A depolarizing wave is a change in the charge of the egg membrane upon fusion with a sperm cell, which prevents multiple sperm from fertilizing the egg.

topics.title: Derived Quantity
topics.description: A physical quantity defined using algebraic combinations of base quantities.

topics.title: Derived Units
topics.description: Derived units are units of measurement that are defined in terms of fundamental units, such as speed, which is length divided by time.

topics.title: Deriving Acceleration from a Velocity vs. Time Graph
topics.description: An acceleration vs. time graph can be derived from a velocity vs. time graph by calculating the slope of the velocity vs. time graph at various points.

topics.title: Deriving Velocity from a Position vs. Time Graph
topics.description: A velocity vs. time graph can be derived from a position vs. time graph by calculating the slope of the position vs. time graph at various points.

topics.title: Destructive Interference
topics.description: Destructive interference occurs when two identical waves arrive at the same point exactly out of phase, resulting in complete cancellation of the waves.

topics.title: Destructive Interference for a Double Slit
topics.description: The condition where light waves from a double slit cancel each other, creating a dark spot.

topics.title: Destructive Interference for a Single Slit
topics.description: The condition where light waves from a single slit cancel each other, creating a dark spot.

topics.title: Destructive Interference in Single Slit Diffraction
topics.description: A condition where light waves from different parts of a single slit interfere destructively, resulting in a minimum in intensity at specific angles.

topics.title: Destructive Interference in Thin Films
topics.description: Destructive interference in thin films occurs when the path length difference between two reflected rays is a half-integral multiple of the wavelength in the medium.

topics.title: Determining Direction of a Resultant Vector
topics.description: Determining the direction of a resultant vector involves using the inverse tangent function to find the angle of the vector relative to the x-axis from its perpendicular components.

topics.title: Determining Magnitude of a Resultant Vector
topics.description: Determining the magnitude of a resultant vector involves using the Pythagorean theorem to calculate the length of the vector from its perpendicular components.

topics.title: Development of Force Concept
topics.description: The evolution of the understanding of force from ancient ideas to modern physics.

topics.title: Dew Point
topics.description: The temperature at which air becomes saturated with water vapor, leading to condensation and the formation of dew or fog.

topics.title: Diagnostic Imaging
topics.description: Diagnostic imaging is the use of radioactive materials to create images of internal body structures for medical diagnosis.

topics.title: Diagnostics and Medical Imaging
topics.description: The use of ionizing radiation to create images of the body for diagnostic purposes.

topics.title: Dialysis
topics.description: Dialysis is the transport of any other molecule through a semipermeable membrane due to its concentration difference.

topics.title: Diamond Sparkle
topics.description: Diamonds sparkle due to total internal reflection, which occurs because their critical angle for light exiting into air is very small, causing most light to reflect internally.

topics.title: Diastolic Blood Pressure
topics.description: The minimum pressure in the arteries when the heart relaxes between beats, also measured in millimeters of mercury (mm Hg).

topics.title: Diastolic Pressure
topics.description: Diastolic pressure is the minimum blood pressure in the arteries, measured when the heart relaxes between beats.

topics.title: Dielectric
topics.description: An insulating material.

topics.title: Dielectric Constant
topics.description: A dimensionless constant that represents how much a dielectric material increases the capacitance of a capacitor compared to when it is in a vacuum.

topics.title: Dielectric Strength
topics.description: The maximum electric field above which an insulating material begins to break down and conduct.

topics.title: Dielectrics
topics.description: Dielectrics are insulating materials that, when placed between the plates of a capacitor, increase its capacitance.

topics.title: Difference Between Heat Pumps and Refrigerators
topics.description: A heat pump is designed to transfer heat into a warm environment, while a refrigerator transfers heat from a cool environment to a warmer one, with both requiring work input.

topics.title: Differential Interference Contrast
topics.description: A technique that uses polarized light split into two beams to create an interference pattern, enhancing contrast and shadowing in images.

topics.title: Diffraction
topics.description: The bending of a wave around the edges of an opening or an obstacle.

topics.title: Diffraction Grating
topics.description: A large number of evenly spaced parallel slits that produce interference patterns.

topics.title: Diffraction Grating Constructive Interference
topics.description: Constructive interference in a diffraction grating occurs when the path difference between adjacent slits is an integer multiple of the wavelength.

topics.title: Diffraction Grating Dispersion
topics.description: Diffraction grating dispersion refers to the ability of a grating to spread out different wavelengths of light into a spectrum, creating a rainbow-like effect.

topics.title: Diffraction Grating Equation
topics.description: The diffraction grating equation, d sin(theta) = m lambda, relates the distance between slits (d), the wavelength of light (lambda), the angle of the maximum (theta), and the order of the maximum (m).

topics.title: Diffraction Grating Maxima
topics.description: Diffraction grating maxima are the bright regions formed on a screen when light waves from different slits interfere constructively at specific angles.

topics.title: Diffraction Limit
topics.description: The diffraction limit is the fundamental limit to the resolution of an optical system, caused by the wave nature of light, which results in spreading of light through an aperture and blurring of images.

topics.title: Diffraction of Electrons
topics.description: Diffraction of electrons is the phenomenon where electrons, when interacting with a crystal, produce interference patterns similar to light waves interacting with a diffraction grating.

topics.title: Diffraction of Light
topics.description: Diffraction is the bending and spreading of light waves around obstacles or through openings, which results in the formation of patterns of light and dark regions.

topics.title: Diffraction Pattern
topics.description: A diffraction pattern is the interference pattern produced when light passes through an aperture or around an obstacle, characterized by a central bright maximum surrounded by alternating dark and bright rings.

topics.title: Diffuse Reflection
topics.description: Diffuse reflection is the reflection of light from a rough surface, where light is scattered in many different directions, allowing objects to be seen from various angles.

topics.title: Diffused Reflection
topics.description: Diffused reflection is the type of reflection that occurs from rough surfaces, where light rays reflect in many different directions, allowing objects to be seen from various angles.

topics.title: Diffusion
topics.description: Diffusion is the movement of substances due to random thermal molecular motion.

topics.title: Diffusion Constant
topics.description: The diffusion constant is a quantity that determines the rate of diffusion for a particular molecule in a specific medium.

topics.title: Digital Meter
topics.description: A measuring instrument that gives a readout in a digital form.

topics.title: Dimensional Analysis
topics.description: Dimensional analysis is a method used to check if the units in a physics calculation are correct by treating units like numbers.

topics.title: Dipole
topics.description: A dipole is a molecule with two centers of equal and opposite charges, creating an electric dipole moment.

topics.title: Direct Current
topics.description: Electric current that flows in a single direction.

topics.title: Direct Current (DC)
topics.description: Direct current is an electric current that flows in one direction and maintains a constant magnitude.

topics.title: Direction in One-Dimensional Motion
topics.description: Direction in one-dimensional motion is indicated by a positive or negative sign, with the chosen positive direction defining the reference for motion.

topics.title: Direction of a Resultant Vector
topics.description: The direction of a resultant vector is determined using the inverse tangent function, which relates the y and x components of the vector.

topics.title: Direction of a Vector
topics.description: The orientation of a vector in space.

topics.title: Direction of Acceleration
topics.description: The direction of acceleration is the same as the direction of the change in velocity, which may not always align with the direction of velocity itself.

topics.title: Direction of Angular Momentum
topics.description: The direction of angular momentum is perpendicular to the plane of rotation, determined by the right-hand rule, and points along the axis of rotation.

topics.title: Direction of Centripetal Acceleration
topics.description: The direction of centripetal acceleration is always toward the center of the circular path, perpendicular to the velocity vector.

topics.title: Direction of Electrostatic Force
topics.description: The direction of the electrostatic force between two charges is along the line joining their centers, and it is attractive if the charges are opposite and repulsive if they are the same.

topics.title: Direction of Force Due to Pressure
topics.description: The force exerted by a fluid due to pressure is always perpendicular to the surface it acts upon.

topics.title: Direction of Friction
topics.description: Friction always acts in the direction opposite to the motion or attempted motion of an object relative to the surface it is in contact with.

topics.title: Direction of Magnetic Field Lines
topics.description: The direction that the north end of a compass needle points.

topics.title: Direction of Magnetic Force Between Parallel Conductors
topics.description: The direction of the magnetic force between two parallel conductors is attractive if the currents are in the same direction and repulsive if the currents are in opposite directions.

topics.title: Direction of Polarization
topics.description: The direction parallel to the electric field for electromagnetic waves.

topics.title: Direction of Torque
topics.description: Torque has a direction, either clockwise or counterclockwise, relative to the chosen pivot point, depending on the direction of the applied force.

topics.title: Discovery of Electrons
topics.description: Electrons were discovered through experiments with gas discharge tubes, where cathode rays were observed to be deflected by electric and magnetic fields, indicating they are negatively charged particles.

topics.title: Discovery of the Atom
topics.description: The discovery of the atom refers to the historical process of understanding that matter is composed of discrete, indivisible particles called atoms.

topics.title: Discovery of the Parts of the Atom
topics.description: The discovery of the parts of the atom involves identifying the subatomic particles, such as electrons and nuclei, that make up atoms.

topics.title: Disorder
topics.description: Disorder is a measure of the randomness or lack of structure in a system, and entropy is a measure of this disorder.

topics.title: Disorder and Order
topics.description: Disorder refers to a state with a high number of microstates, while order refers to a state with a low number of microstates, making disorder vastly more likely.

topics.title: Disorder and Order in Systems
topics.description: Disorder is vastly more likely than order in systems, as there are exponentially more ways to achieve disordered states compared to ordered ones.

topics.title: Disorder in Thermodynamics
topics.description: Disorder in thermodynamics is a measure of the randomness or lack of structure in a system, which is directly related to entropy.

topics.title: Dispersion
topics.description: Dispersion is the spreading of white light into its full spectrum of wavelengths.

topics.title: Dispersion of Light
topics.description: Dispersion is the phenomenon where white light is split into a spectrum of colors, such as a rainbow, when passing through a narrow slit or a prism.

topics.title: Displacement
topics.description: Displacement is the change in position of an object, measured as the straight-line distance and direction from the initial to the final position.

topics.title: Displacement and Force Relationship
topics.description: For work to be done, there must be a displacement of the object in the direction of the applied force.

topics.title: Displacement Components
topics.description: The horizontal and vertical parts of a projectile's displacement, which can be calculated using trigonometric functions of the launch angle.

topics.title: Displacement for Work
topics.description: For work to be done, there must be a displacement of the object in the direction of the applied force.

topics.title: Displacement with Constant Acceleration
topics.description: Displacement of an object under constant acceleration can be calculated using the equation x = x₀ + v₀t + ½at², where x is the final position, x₀ is the initial position, v₀ is the initial velocity, a is the acceleration, and t is the time.

topics.title: Displacement with Constant Velocity
topics.description: Displacement of an object moving at a constant velocity can be calculated using the equation x = x₀ + v̄t, where x is the final position, x₀ is the initial position, v̄ is the average velocity, and t is the time.

topics.title: Displacement-Time Graph
topics.description: A displacement-time graph shows how displacement changes with time, and its slope represents velocity.

topics.title: Dissipative Processes
topics.description: Dissipative processes are irreversible processes that involve energy loss due to factors like friction or turbulence, which reduce the efficiency of a heat engine by transferring heat to the environment.

topics.title: Distance
topics.description: Distance is a scalar quantity that describes the total length of the path traveled between two points, without considering direction.

topics.title: Distance Traveled
topics.description: The total length of the path traveled between two positions.

topics.title: Distribution of Molecular Speeds
topics.description: The speeds of molecules in a gas follow a distribution called the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution, which depends on the temperature of the gas.

topics.title: Diverging Lens
topics.description: A concave lens that causes parallel light rays to bend away from its axis.

topics.title: Diverging Mirror
topics.description: A convex mirror that causes parallel light rays to bend away from its axis.

topics.title: DNA Structure and Charge
topics.description: DNA is a highly charged molecule with a double-helical structure, where the electrostatic force helps maintain its structure and genetic information.

topics.title: Domain
topics.description: A region within a magnetic material where the magnetic poles of individual atoms are aligned.

topics.title: Domains
topics.description: Regions within a material that behave like small bar magnets.

topics.title: Doppler Effect
topics.description: The Doppler effect is the change in frequency of a wave in relation to an observer who is moving relative to the wave source.

topics.title: Doppler Shift
topics.description: The Doppler shift is the actual change in frequency caused by the relative motion between the source and the observer.

topics.title: Doppler-Shifted Ultrasound
topics.description: A medical technique to detect motion and determine velocity through the Doppler shift of an echo.

topics.title: Dose Calculation
topics.description: The process of determining the radiation dose by dividing the energy deposited in tissue by the mass of the tissue, and then adjusting for the relative biological effectiveness (RBE).

topics.title: Double Slit Interference
topics.description: Double slit interference is the phenomenon where light waves passing through two closely spaced slits create an interference pattern of bright and dark fringes on a screen.

topics.title: Double-Slit Interference
topics.description: An experiment in which waves or particles from a single source impinge upon two slits, producing an interference pattern.

topics.title: Down Quark
topics.description: The second-lightest of all quarks.

topics.title: Drag Coefficient
topics.description: A dimensionless quantity that depends on the shape and size of an object, representing how much drag it experiences in a fluid.

topics.title: Drag Force
topics.description: A force proportional to the square of the speed of an object, calculated as F_d = ½CρAv², where C is the drag coefficient, A is the area facing the fluid, and ρ is the fluid density.

topics.title: Drag Force and Frictional Resistance
topics.description: A force exerted by a fluid (like water or air) that opposes the motion of an object through that fluid.

topics.title: Drag Force Equation
topics.description: The mathematical expression for drag force is F_D = ½ CρAv², where C is the drag coefficient, ρ is the fluid density, A is the cross-sectional area, and v is the velocity.

topics.title: Drag Force Proportional to Velocity Squared
topics.description: The drag force on an object moving at high speeds in a fluid is proportional to the square of its velocity.

topics.title: Drift Velocity
topics.description: Drift velocity is the average velocity at which free charges move through a conductor under the influence of an electric field.

topics.title: Driving Frequency
topics.description: Driving frequency is the frequency at which an external force is applied to a system to cause it to oscillate.

topics.title: Dual Nature of Light
topics.description: Light has both wave-like and particle-like properties, known as wave-particle duality.

topics.title: Dynamic Equilibrium
topics.description: A state of equilibrium in which the net external force and torque on a system moving with constant velocity are zero.

topics.title: Dynamics
topics.description: The study of how forces affect the motion of objects and systems.

topics.title: Eardrum Pressure
topics.description: The pressure exerted on the eardrum, which can be affected by changes in the middle ear and can lead to rupture if too high.

topics.title: Eardrum Vibration
topics.description: Eardrum vibration is the movement of the eardrum caused by the pressure variations of a sound wave, which is essential for hearing.

topics.title: Earth's Interior Structure
topics.description: The Earth's interior structure refers to the layered composition of the Earth, including the solid inner core, liquid outer core, and molten mantle.

topics.title: Earth's Magnetic Field
topics.description: Earth behaves like a large bar magnet with its magnetic south pole near the geographic North Pole and its magnetic north pole near the geographic South Pole.

topics.title: Earth/Ground Connection
topics.description: A low-resistance path directly to the earth that ensures the neutral wire and appliance case are at zero volts, making them safe to touch.

topics.title: Eccentricity
topics.description: A measure of how much an ellipse deviates from being a perfect circle.

topics.title: Eccentricity of an Ellipse
topics.description: Eccentricity is a measure of how much an ellipse deviates from being a circle, calculated as the ratio of the distance from the center to a focus and the distance from the center to a vertex.

topics.title: ECG Waveforms
topics.description: ECG waveforms, such as the P wave, QRS complex, and T wave, represent specific electrical events in the heart, including atrial depolarization, ventricular depolarization, and ventricular repolarization.

topics.title: Eddy Current
topics.description: A current loop in a conductor caused by motional electromotive force (emf).

topics.title: Effect of Gravity on Light
topics.description: Gravity can bend the path of light, causing it to curve toward massive objects.

topics.title: Effect of Internal Resistance on Terminal Voltage
topics.description: As internal resistance increases, the terminal voltage of a voltage source decreases, even if the emf remains constant.

topics.title: Effect of Medium on Speed of Sound
topics.description: The speed of sound varies significantly depending on the medium, with sound traveling faster in solids and liquids than in gases.

topics.title: Effect of Nonconservative Forces on Mechanical Energy
topics.description: Nonconservative forces add or remove mechanical energy from a system, often converting it into other forms like thermal energy.

topics.title: Effect of Temperature on Speed of Sound
topics.description: The speed of sound in a gas increases with temperature, following the relationship v_w = 331 m/s × √(T/273 K).

topics.title: Efficiency
topics.description: A measure of the effectiveness of the input of energy to do work; useful energy or work divided by the total input of energy.

topics.title: Efficiency of Energy Conversion
topics.description: Efficiency is the ratio of useful energy or work output to the total energy input in a conversion process.

topics.title: Effort Arm
topics.description: The effort arm is the part of a lever between the fulcrum and the point where the effort force is applied.

topics.title: Einstein’s Equivalence Principle
topics.description: The principle that acceleration and gravity are indistinguishable in their effects, forming the basis of Einstein’s theory of general relativity.

topics.title: Einstein’s First Postulate
topics.description: The laws of physics are the same and can be stated in their simplest form in all inertial frames of reference.

topics.title: Einstein’s Postulates
topics.description: Einstein’s postulates are the foundational principles of special relativity, stating that the laws of physics are the same for all inertial frames and the speed of light is constant in all inertial frames.

topics.title: Einstein’s Second Postulate
topics.description: The speed of light in a vacuum is a constant, independent of the relative motion of the source.

topics.title: Einstein’s Theory of General Relativity
topics.description: A theory that describes gravity as the curvature of spacetime caused by mass.

topics.title: Elapsed Time
topics.description: Elapsed time is the difference between the ending time and beginning time, calculated as Δt = t_f − t_0.

topics.title: Elastic Collision
topics.description: An elastic collision is a collision in which both momentum and kinetic energy are conserved.

topics.title: Elastic Collisions with Equal Mass
topics.description: Collisions where two objects of equal mass collide elastically, resulting in specific kinematic outcomes.

topics.title: Elastic Deformation
topics.description: Elastic deformation is a reversible change in shape or size of a material caused by an applied force, which returns to its original state when the force is removed.

topics.title: Elastic Potential Energy
topics.description: Potential energy stored as a result of deformation of an elastic object, such as the stretching of a spring.

topics.title: Elasticity
topics.description: Elasticity is the property of a material to deform under stress and return to its original shape when the stress is removed.

topics.title: Electric and Magnetic Force Unification
topics.description: Electric and magnetic forces are different manifestations of the same fundamental force, known as the electromagnetic force.

topics.title: Electric Charge
topics.description: Electric charge is a physical quantity that describes the property of matter that causes it to experience a force when placed in an electromagnetic field.

topics.title: Electric Charge Distribution
topics.description: Electric charge distributes itself equally between two conducting spheres of the same size when they are in contact.

topics.title: Electric Circuit
topics.description: An electric circuit is a closed path through which electric current can flow, typically consisting of components like batteries, resistors, and wires.

topics.title: Electric Current
topics.description: Electric current is the movement of electric charge through a conductor.

topics.title: Electric Current Effects on the Human Body
topics.description: Electric current through the human body can cause a range of effects, from harmless sensations to severe muscle contractions, heart fibrillation, and even death, depending on the current's magnitude, path, duration, and frequency.

topics.title: Electric Energy
topics.description: Electric energy is the capacity to do work that is supplied by an electric current over time.

topics.title: Electric Energy Transmission
topics.description: Electric energy is transmitted through the movement of charge, which is known as electric current.

topics.title: Electric Eye
topics.description: An electric eye is a group of devices that use the photoelectric effect for detection.

topics.title: Electric Field
topics.description: The electric field is a vector field that represents the force per unit charge exerted on a positive test charge at a given point in space.

topics.title: Electric Field and Distance Relationship
topics.description: The electric field due to a point charge decreases with the square of the distance from the charge.

topics.title: Electric Field and Equipotential Relationship
topics.description: Electric field lines are always perpendicular to equipotential lines, indicating that the electric field direction is perpendicular to the direction of constant potential.

topics.title: Electric Field and Potential Relationship
topics.description: The electric field can be expressed as the rate of change of electric potential with distance.

topics.title: Electric Field Around Earth
topics.description: A near-uniform electric field of approximately 150 N/C, directed downward, surrounds Earth, with the magnitude increasing slightly as we get closer to the surface.

topics.title: Electric Field as a Gradient of Electric Potential
topics.description: The electric field is the rate of change of electric potential with distance, pointing in the direction of decreasing potential.

topics.title: Electric Field as Voltage Gradient
topics.description: The electric field is the rate of change of electric potential with distance, indicating that the field points in the direction of decreasing potential.

topics.title: Electric Field Diagrams for Multiple Charges
topics.description: Electric field diagrams for multiple charges show how field lines interact, with lines repelling from like charges and attracting between opposite charges.

topics.title: Electric Field Direction
topics.description: The direction of the electric field is the direction in which a positive test charge would move in the field, pointing away from positive charges and toward negative charges.

topics.title: Electric Field Direction and Potential
topics.description: The electric field points in the direction of decreasing electric potential, indicating the direction a positive charge would move under the influence of the field.

topics.title: Electric Field Direction for Point Charges
topics.description: Electric field lines point away from positive charges and toward negative charges, indicating the direction a positive test charge would move in the field.

topics.title: Electric Field Due to a Point Charge
topics.description: The electric field created by a point charge is the force per unit charge experienced by a test charge placed at a distance from the point charge, and its magnitude is given by the equation E = k|Q|/r².

topics.title: Electric Field in a Capacitor
topics.description: The electric field in a capacitor is directly proportional to the charge stored and inversely proportional to the distance between the plates.

topics.title: Electric Field Inside a Conductor
topics.description: The electric field inside a conductor in electrostatic equilibrium is zero.

topics.title: Electric Field Line Representation
topics.description: Electric field lines are a visual representation of electric fields, where the direction of the field is indicated by the direction of the lines and their density indicates the field strength.

topics.title: Electric Field Lines
topics.description: Electric field lines are a visual representation of the electric field, where the direction of the lines indicates the direction of the force on a positive test charge, and the density of the lines indicates the strength of the field.

topics.title: Electric Field Lines Between Like Charges
topics.description: Electric field lines between two like charges (both positive or both negative) repel each other, resulting in field lines that diverge from each other.

topics.title: Electric Field Lines Between Opposite Charges
topics.description: Electric field lines between opposite charges (positive and negative) converge, indicating the field lines start from the positive charge and end at the negative charge.

topics.title: Electric Field Perpendicular to Conductor Surface
topics.description: Just outside a conductor, the electric field lines are perpendicular to its surface, ending or beginning on charges on the surface.

topics.title: Electric Field Strength
topics.description: Electric field strength is the magnitude of the electric field at a point, measured in newtons per coulomb (N/C), and is calculated as the force on a test charge divided by the charge.

topics.title: Electric Field Strength and Line Density
topics.description: The strength of an electric field is proportional to the number of field lines per unit area, with closer lines indicating a stronger field.

topics.title: Electric Field Strength Calculation
topics.description: Electric field strength in a uniform electric field can be calculated by dividing the potential difference (voltage) by the distance between the plates.

topics.title: Electric Field Units
topics.description: The electric field can be expressed in volts per meter (V/m), which is equivalent to newtons per coulomb (N/C).

topics.title: Electric Field Vector Addition
topics.description: The total electric field at a point due to multiple charges is the vector sum of the individual electric fields created by each charge.

topics.title: Electric Force Balance with Magnetic Force
topics.description: Electric force balance with magnetic force occurs when the electric force created by charge separation in a conductor equals the magnetic force on the moving charges, resulting in equilibrium.

topics.title: Electric Forces
topics.description: Electric forces are the forces that act between electrically charged particles.

topics.title: Electric Forces in Biology
topics.description: Electric forces play a role in biological processes, such as the function of nerves and muscles.

topics.title: Electric Generator
topics.description: An electric generator is a device that converts mechanical energy into electrical energy by rotating a coil in a magnetic field.

topics.title: Electric Hazards
topics.description: Electric hazards refer to the risks associated with electric shock and the potential for injury or death from electrical currents.

topics.title: Electric Motor
topics.description: A device that converts electrical energy into mechanical energy.

topics.title: Electric Motor Operation
topics.description: An electric motor converts electrical energy into mechanical energy by using the magnetic force on current-carrying wires to produce torque, which rotates a shaft.

topics.title: Electric Polarization
topics.description: Electric polarization is the process by which a neutral object develops regions of positive and negative charge due to the influence of an external electric field.

topics.title: Electric Potential
topics.description: Potential energy per unit charge.

topics.title: Electric Potential and Distance Relationship
topics.description: The electric potential due to a point charge decreases with increasing distance from the charge.

topics.title: Electric Potential and Electric Field Relationship
topics.description: Electric potential (ΔV) and electric field (E) are related such that the electric field in a uniform field is the potential difference divided by the distance between the plates.

topics.title: Electric Potential at Infinity
topics.description: The electric potential at infinity is defined as zero, which serves as a reference point for calculating electric potential due to a point charge.

topics.title: Electric Potential Decreases with Distance
topics.description: The electric potential due to a point charge decreases as the distance from the charge increases, while the electric field decreases with the square of the distance.

topics.title: Electric Potential Difference
topics.description: The difference in electric potential between two points, calculated as the work done per unit charge to move a charge between those points.

topics.title: Electric Potential Due to a Point Charge
topics.description: The electric potential created by a point charge is the work done per unit charge to bring a test charge from infinity to a point in the electric field of the point charge.

topics.title: Electric Potential Energy
topics.description: The energy a charge possesses due to its position in an electric field.

topics.title: Electric Potential Formula for a Point Charge
topics.description: The electric potential $ V $ due to a point charge $ Q $ at a distance $ r $ is given by $ V = kQ / r $, where $ k $ is Coulomb's constant.

topics.title: Electric Potential from Multiple Charges
topics.description: The electric potential at a point due to multiple charges is the algebraic sum of the potentials due to each individual charge.

topics.title: Electric Potential in a Uniform Electric Field
topics.description: The electric potential at a point in a uniform electric field is the work done per unit charge to move a charge from a reference point to that point.

topics.title: Electric Potential vs. Electric Field
topics.description: Electric potential is a scalar quantity that represents the potential energy per unit charge at a point in an electric field, while electric field is a vector quantity that represents the force per unit charge at a point.

topics.title: Electric Power
topics.description: Electric power is the rate at which electrical energy is converted into other forms of energy, such as heat or light.

topics.title: Electrical Conductivity
topics.description: Electrical conductivity is the ability of a material to allow the flow of electric charge.

topics.title: Electrical Energy
topics.description: The energy carried by a flow of charge.

topics.title: Electrical Potential Due to a Point Charge
topics.description: The electric potential at a point due to a point charge is the work done per unit charge to bring a test charge from infinity to that point.

topics.title: Electrical Resistance and Shock Severity
topics.description: The severity of an electrical shock depends on the combination of voltage and resistance, with lower resistance leading to higher current and greater risk.

topics.title: Electrical Safety Devices (Fuses and Circuit Breakers)
topics.description: Fuses and circuit breakers are safety devices that automatically open a circuit when excessive current flows, preventing overheating and potential fires.

topics.title: Electrical Safety Systems
topics.description: Electrical safety systems are devices and practices designed to protect people and equipment from electrical hazards.

topics.title: Electrical Signals in Nerve Conduction
topics.description: Electrical signals in nerve conduction are critical for transmitting information through the nervous system, involving changes in the electrical properties of cell membranes.

topics.title: Electricity
topics.description: Electricity is the presence and flow of electric charge, which can be harnessed to perform work and power devices.

topics.title: Electricity and Magnetism
topics.description: Electricity and magnetism are branches of physics that study electric charges, their movements, and the magnetic fields created by electric currents.

topics.title: Electrocardiogram (ECG)
topics.description: A record of voltages created by depolarization and repolarization, especially in the heart.

topics.title: Electromagnet
topics.description: An object that is temporarily magnetic when an electrical current is passed through it.

topics.title: Electromagnetic Force
topics.description: One of the four fundamental forces of nature; the electromagnetic force consists of static electricity, moving electricity and magnetism.

topics.title: Electromagnetic Induction
topics.description: Electromagnetic induction is the process by which a changing magnetic field induces an electromotive force (emf) in a conductor.

topics.title: Electromagnetic Induction in Safety
topics.description: The phenomenon where AC currents in appliances can induce an emf on the case, which is mitigated by grounding the case to keep its voltage near zero.

topics.title: Electromagnetic Radiation
topics.description: Electromagnetic radiation is a form of energy that travels through space as waves, including visible light, radio waves, and X-rays.

topics.title: Electromagnetic Spectrum
topics.description: The electromagnetic spectrum is the range of all types of electromagnetic radiation, including radio waves, microwaves, infrared, visible light, ultraviolet, X-rays, and gamma rays.

topics.title: Electromagnetic Wave Applications in Medicine
topics.description: Electromagnetic waves are used in medical applications such as MRI, X-ray imaging, and radiation therapy for diagnosing and treating diseases.

topics.title: Electromagnetic Wave Equation
topics.description: The speed of light in a vacuum is related to its frequency and wavelength by the equation c = fλ.

topics.title: Electromagnetic Wave Intensity and Field Strength
topics.description: The average intensity of an electromagnetic wave is proportional to the square of the maximum electric field strength.

topics.title: Electromagnetic Wave Interaction with Matter
topics.description: Electromagnetic waves can interact with matter through transmission, reflection, or absorption, depending on the material's properties and the wave's frequency.

topics.title: Electromagnetic Wave Penetration
topics.description: The ability of electromagnetic waves to penetrate materials depends on their wavelength, with shorter wavelengths penetrating more deeply.

topics.title: Electromagnetic Wave Propagation
topics.description: Electromagnetic waves propagate through space at the speed of light, with their speed, frequency, and wavelength related by the equation c = fλ.

topics.title: Electromagnetic Waves
topics.description: Electromagnetic waves are waves that consist of oscillating electric and magnetic fields, which propagate through space at the speed of light.

topics.title: Electromagnetic Waves vs. Sound Waves
topics.description: Electromagnetic waves differ from sound waves because they do not require a medium to travel and are not related to pressure variations in matter.

topics.title: Electromagnetism
topics.description: The use of electrical currents to induce magnetism.

topics.title: Electromotive Force
topics.description: Electromotive force (emf) is the energy per unit charge that a source, such as a battery, provides to move charges through a circuit.

topics.title: Electromotive Force (emf)
topics.description: Electromotive force is the potential difference of a source when no current is flowing, measured in volts.

topics.title: Electromotive Force (emf) in a Generator
topics.description: The electromotive force (emf) in a generator is the voltage induced in a coil rotating in a magnetic field, calculated by the equation epsilon = N A B omega sine omega t.

topics.title: Electromotive Force (emf) Induced by Changing Magnetic Flux
topics.description: The electromotive force induced in a coil is proportional to the rate of change of magnetic flux through the coil and the number of turns in the coil.

topics.title: Electron
topics.description: A particle orbiting the nucleus of an atom and carrying the smallest unit of negative charge.

topics.title: Electron Capture
topics.description: The process in which a proton-rich nuclide absorbs an inner atomic electron and simultaneously emits a neutrino.

topics.title: Electron Capture Equation
topics.description: Electron capture is a beta-decay process in which a nucleus absorbs an inner-shell electron and emits an electron neutrino; the nuclide changes according to \({}^{A}_{Z}X_{N}+e^{-}\rightarrow{}^{A}_{Z-1}Y_{N+1}+\nu_e\).

topics.title: Electron Clouds
topics.description: Electron clouds are regions around the nucleus where electrons are likely to be found, representing the probabilistic nature of their positions in quantum mechanics.

topics.title: Electron Configuration
topics.description: The arrangement of electrons in an atom's shells and subshells, determined by the Pauli exclusion principle and quantum numbers, is called the electron configuration.

topics.title: Electron Energy in Hydrogen-Like Atoms
topics.description: The energy of an electron in a hydrogen atom's orbital is inversely proportional to the square of its principal quantum number.

topics.title: Electron Energy Levels
topics.description: Electron energy levels are the specific, quantized energy states that an electron in an atom can occupy, with each level corresponding to a particular orbit.

topics.title: Electron Family Number
topics.description: The number ±1 assigned to all members of the electron family, or the number 0 assigned to all particles not in the electron family.

topics.title: Electron Orbital Energies
topics.description: Electron orbital energies are the specific energy levels an electron can occupy in an atom, which are quantized and depend on the principal quantum number.

topics.title: Electron Shell and Subshell Symbols
topics.description: Electron shells and subshells are denoted by the symbols n (principal quantum number) and l (azimuthal quantum number), with l represented by letters s, p, d, f, g, h, etc., corresponding to l = 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, etc.

topics.title: Electron Shell Filling
topics.description: Electron shells fill starting from the lowest energy level (n = 1) to higher levels, with subshells within each shell filling in order of increasing l (from s to p, d, f, etc.).

topics.title: Electron Transfer
topics.description: Electron transfer is the movement of electrons from one object to another, resulting in a net positive or negative charge on the objects.

topics.title: Electron Volt
topics.description: A unit of energy equal to the energy gained by a fundamental charge accelerated through a potential difference of 1 volt.

topics.title: Electron’s Antineutrino
topics.description: The antiparticle of the electron’s neutrino.

topics.title: Electron’s Neutrino
topics.description: A subatomic elementary particle which has no net electric charge.

topics.title: Electrons
topics.description: Electrons are subatomic particles used in food irradiation, accelerated to energies up to 10 MeV to create ionizing radiation.

topics.title: Electrostatic Attraction and Repulsion
topics.description: The forces between charged objects where like charges repel and opposite charges attract, based on the principles of electrostatics.

topics.title: Electrostatic Charge and Force
topics.description: The force exerted on a charged particle by an electric field, calculated using the equation F = qE.

topics.title: Electrostatic Deflection
topics.description: The use of electric fields to direct charged particles, such as ink droplets in inkjet printers, to specific positions on a page.

topics.title: Electrostatic Equilibrium
topics.description: An electrostatically balanced state in which all free electrical charges have stopped moving about.

topics.title: Electrostatic Force
topics.description: Another term for the electrostatic force.

topics.title: Electrostatic Induction
topics.description: The process by which an electrically charged object brought near a neutral object creates a charge in that object.

topics.title: Electrostatic Painting
topics.description: A technique that uses electrostatic charge to spray paint onto surfaces, allowing even coverage and reaching difficult areas.

topics.title: Electrostatic Precipitator
topics.description: A device that uses electrostatic forces to remove particles from air, commonly used in industrial and home air cleaning systems.

topics.title: Electrostatic Repulsion
topics.description: The phenomenon of two objects with like charges repelling each other.

topics.title: Electrostatic Screening
topics.description: Electrostatic screening is the reduction of the electrostatic force between charges due to the presence of other charges in the environment.

topics.title: Electrostatics
topics.description: The study of electric forces that are static or slow-moving.

topics.title: Electroweak Epoch
topics.description: A period in the early universe when the electromagnetic and weak nuclear forces were unified into a single electroweak force, which later separated.

topics.title: Electroweak Theory
topics.description: A gauge theory that unifies the electromagnetic and weak nuclear forces, predicting the existence of specific carrier particles like W⁺, W⁻, and Z⁰.

topics.title: Elliptical Orbit
topics.description: An elliptical orbit is a path that an object follows around another object, where the shape is an ellipse with the central object located at one of the foci.

topics.title: EMF
topics.description: The rate at which energy is drawn from a source per unit current flowing through a circuit.

topics.title: Emf Induced in a Generator Coil
topics.description: The emf generated in a generator coil, given by emf = NABω sin(ωt), where N is the number of turns, A is the area, B is the magnetic field, and ω is the angular velocity.

topics.title: Emission Spectra of Light Sources
topics.description: The color of a light source is defined by the wavelengths it produces, as illustrated by the emission spectra of different light sources.

topics.title: Emission Spectrum
topics.description: A spectrum of light emitted by a substance when its atoms are excited, showing discrete wavelengths corresponding to specific energy transitions.

topics.title: Emissivity
topics.description: Emissivity is a measure of how well an object radiates energy, with black bodies having an emissivity of 1 and perfect reflectors having an emissivity of 0.

topics.title: Enabling Science
topics.description: An enabling science is a field that provides the fundamental understanding and models needed to develop new techniques and instruments in other areas.

topics.title: Energies of Hydrogen-Like Atoms
topics.description: The Bohr formula for the energies of electron states in hydrogen-like atoms.

topics.title: Energy
topics.description: Energy is the capacity to do work, and it can exist in various forms such as kinetic, potential, and thermal energy.

topics.title: Energy and Amplitude Relationship
topics.description: The energy of a wave is directly proportional to the square of its amplitude, meaning larger amplitude waves carry more energy.

topics.title: Energy and Oxygen Consumption Rates
topics.description: The rate at which energy and oxygen are consumed during various physical activities, measured in watts and liters of oxygen per minute, respectively.

topics.title: Energy and Oxygen Consumption Relationship
topics.description: Energy consumption is directly proportional to oxygen consumption because the digestive process involves oxidizing food.

topics.title: Energy as the Ability to Do Work
topics.description: Energy is defined as the ability to do work, though not all energy is always available to do work.

topics.title: Energy Conservation
topics.description: Energy conservation is the practice of reducing energy use through decreased activities or increased efficiency in energy conversion processes.

topics.title: Energy Conservation in Simple Harmonic Motion
topics.description: The total mechanical energy in a simple harmonic oscillator remains constant, oscillating between kinetic and potential energy.

topics.title: Energy Consumption Rate
topics.description: Energy consumption rate is the amount of energy used per unit time, often measured in watts.

topics.title: Energy Conversion
topics.description: Energy conversion is the process of changing energy from one form to another.

topics.title: Energy Conversion in the Human Body
topics.description: The process by which the chemical energy stored in food is converted into work, thermal energy, and/or stored chemical energy in fatty tissue.

topics.title: Energy Emitted During Nuclear Decay
topics.description: The energy emitted during nuclear decay is the difference in mass between the parent nucleus and the decay products, converted into energy via Einstein's equation E = Δm c².

topics.title: Energy Expenditure and Fat Storage
topics.description: When a person consumes more energy than needed for work and warmth, the excess energy is stored as body fat.

topics.title: Energy Expenditure During Physical Activities
topics.description: The rate at which energy is used during various activities, measured in watts, which varies depending on the type and intensity of the activity.

topics.title: Energy in Electromagnetic Waves
topics.description: Electromagnetic waves carry energy through their electric and magnetic fields, which can exert forces and do work on charges in a system.

topics.title: Energy in Simple Harmonic Motion
topics.description: Energy in simple harmonic motion is the sum of kinetic and potential energy, which remains constant if there is no damping.

topics.title: Energy Levels in Atoms
topics.description: Specific discrete energy states that electrons in atoms can occupy, leading to the emission or absorption of specific wavelengths of light.

topics.title: Energy of a Photon
topics.description: The energy of a photon is directly proportional to its frequency and is given by the equation E = hf, where h is Planck’s constant and f is the frequency of the photon.

topics.title: Energy Release in Atomic Processes
topics.description: Energy is released when the structure of atoms is altered, such as through nuclear reactions.

topics.title: Energy Resource Sustainability
topics.description: Energy resource sustainability involves using energy in a way that meets current needs without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs.

topics.title: Energy Stored in a Capacitor
topics.description: The energy stored in a capacitor is the work done to move charge onto the capacitor plates, calculated as one-half the capacitance multiplied by the square of the voltage.

topics.title: Energy Stored in an Inductor
topics.description: The energy stored in an inductor, calculated by E_ind = ½LI², where L is inductance and I is current.

topics.title: Energy Transfer
topics.description: Energy can be transferred to or from a system through heat or work.

topics.title: Energy Transfer in Waves
topics.description: The energy transferred by a wave depends on both the amplitude of the wave and the time over which the wave interacts with a surface.

topics.title: Energy Transformation
topics.description: Energy transformation is the process of converting energy from one form to another, often resulting in waste heat and less useful forms of energy.

topics.title: Energy Transformation and Waste Heat
topics.description: Energy transformation refers to the process of converting energy from one form to another, often resulting in waste heat that is less useful for doing work.

topics.title: Energy Transformation in Simple Harmonic Motion
topics.description: Energy in a simple harmonic oscillator continuously transforms between potential and kinetic energy as the system oscillates.

topics.title: Energy Unit Conversion
topics.description: Energy unit conversion refers to the relationship between different units of energy, such as calories and joules.

topics.title: Energy Unit: Joule
topics.description: The joule (J) is the SI unit of energy, used to measure heat and work.

topics.title: Energy-Level Diagram
topics.description: An energy-level diagram is a visual representation of the allowed energy states of an atom, with energy increasing vertically and transitions between states shown as arrows.

topics.title: Energy-Mass Conversion
topics.description: Energy and mass are interchangeable, with energy equal to mass multiplied by the speed of light squared.

topics.title: English Units
topics.description: A system of measurement used in the United States; includes units of measurement such as feet, gallons, and pounds.

topics.title: Entrainment
topics.description: Entrainment is the process by which a high-velocity fluid creates a region of low pressure, causing other fluids to be drawn into the high-velocity stream.

topics.title: Entrance Pupil
topics.description: The entrance pupil is the effective aperture of an optical system that controls the amount of light entering and helps reduce aberrations.

topics.title: Entropy
topics.description: Entropy is a measure of disorder or randomness in a system, and it quantifies the unavailability of energy to do work.

topics.title: Entropy and Probability
topics.description: Entropy is related to the probability of a state; the more likely a state is, the greater its entropy, as it corresponds to a larger number of microstates.

topics.title: Entropy and Work
topics.description: Entropy is related to the unavailability of energy to do work, as higher entropy indicates less energy is available for work.

topics.title: Entropy Change
topics.description: Entropy change is the measure of the change in disorder of a system, calculated as the heat transfer divided by the absolute temperature for a reversible process.

topics.title: Equation of Continuity
topics.description: The equation of continuity states that the flow rate remains constant throughout a fluid system, meaning the product of cross-sectional area and velocity is constant.

topics.title: Equation of State
topics.description: An equation of state is a mathematical relationship that describes the behavior of a physical system in terms of its thermodynamic properties.

topics.title: Equilibrium
topics.description: Equilibrium is a state where the net external force on an object is zero, meaning the object is either stationary or moving at a constant velocity.

topics.title: Equilibrium Between Phases
topics.description: A state where the rates of molecules transitioning between two phases (e.g., liquid and gas) are equal, resulting in no net change in the amount of each phase.

topics.title: Equilibrium Conditions
topics.description: The conditions for a system to be in equilibrium, which are the sum of forces equals zero and the sum of torques equals zero.

topics.title: Equilibrium in Force Systems
topics.description: A state where the net force acting on an object is zero, resulting in no acceleration.

topics.title: Equilibrium in Musculoskeletal Systems
topics.description: Equilibrium in the musculoskeletal system is achieved when the net torque and net force are both zero, balancing the forces and torques exerted by muscles, bones, and joints.

topics.title: Equilibrium of Forces
topics.description: A state where the net force acting on an object is zero, resulting in no acceleration.

topics.title: Equilibrium Position
topics.description: The equilibrium position is the position of a system where the net force acting on it is zero, and it remains at rest unless disturbed by an external force.

topics.title: Equipotential Line
topics.description: A line along which the electric potential is constant.

topics.title: Equipotential Surfaces
topics.description: Equipotential surfaces are three-dimensional versions of equipotential lines, representing regions in space where the electric potential is the same at every point.

topics.title: Equivalent Resistance
topics.description: The total resistance of a group of resistors connected in series, which is the sum of their individual resistances.

topics.title: Equivalent Resistance in Parallel
topics.description: The equivalent resistance of resistors connected in parallel is the reciprocal of the sum of the reciprocals of their individual resistances.

topics.title: Equivalent Resistance in Series
topics.description: The equivalent resistance of resistors connected in series is the sum of their individual resistances.

topics.title: Equivalent Resistor
topics.description: A single resistor that has the same resistance as a group of resistors combined.

topics.title: Escape Velocity
topics.description: Escape velocity is the takeoff velocity when kinetic energy just cancels gravitational potential energy.

topics.title: Estimation
topics.description: Estimation is the process of making an approximate calculation or judgment about a quantity without exact measurements.

topics.title: Ether
topics.description: A medium once believed to carry light waves, which was later proven not to exist.

topics.title: Ether Frame of Reference
topics.description: A hypothetical medium thought to fill space through which light waves traveled, which was disproven by the Michelson–Morley experiment.

topics.title: Ethical and Moral Implications of Nuclear Physics
topics.description: The ethical and moral implications of nuclear physics refer to the dual nature of nuclear technology, which can be used for both beneficial and harmful purposes, reflecting the ambivalence of its applications.

topics.title: Evaporation
topics.description: Evaporation is the process by which molecules of a liquid change to the gaseous state.

topics.title: Evaporation and Condensation
topics.description: Evaporation is the process by which water molecules transition from liquid to vapor, while condensation is the reverse process, where vapor transitions back to liquid.

topics.title: Evaporation and Cooling
topics.description: Evaporation and cooling involve the removal of heat from the body through the phase change of sweat, which is enhanced by convection to maintain the evaporation process.

topics.title: Event Horizon
topics.description: The event horizon is the boundary around a black hole beyond which nothing, not even light, can escape.

topics.title: Excess Charge on Conductor Surface
topics.description: Any excess charge resides entirely on the surface or surfaces of a conductor.

topics.title: Excited State
topics.description: A state of an atom where an electron has absorbed energy and moved to a higher energy level than its ground state.

topics.title: Existence of Other Fundamental Forces
topics.description: The existence of other fundamental forces refers to the question of whether there are forces beyond the four known fundamental forces, and what implications this might have for physics.

topics.title: Existence of Sound Without Perception
topics.description: Sound exists as a disturbance in a medium even if no one is present to perceive or hear it.

topics.title: Exit Pupil
topics.description: The exit pupil is the effective aperture of an optical system that controls the amount of light exiting and helps reduce aberrations.

topics.title: Experiment
topics.description: A process involved with testing a hypothesis.

topics.title: Exponential Behavior in RL Circuits
topics.description: The current in an RL circuit follows an exponential behavior, either increasing or decreasing over time depending on whether the circuit is being energized or de-energized.

topics.title: Exponential Decay of Current in an RL Circuit
topics.description: The current in an RL circuit decreases exponentially over time when the circuit is de-energized.

topics.title: Exponential Relationship
topics.description: A relation between variables in which a constant change in the independent variable is accompanied by change in the dependent variable that is proportional to the value it already had.

topics.title: External Force
topics.description: A force acting on an object or system that originates outside of the object or system.

topics.title: External Forces and Systems
topics.description: Forces that act on a system from outside are called external forces and can affect the motion of that system.

topics.title: Extremely Low Frequency (ELF)
topics.description: Electromagnetic radiation with wavelengths usually in the range of 0 to 300 Hz, but also about 1kHz.

topics.title: Eyeglasses and Vision Correction
topics.description: Eyeglasses use lenses to correct vision defects such as nearsightedness and farsightedness by adjusting the focal length of light entering the eye.

topics.title: Eyepiece
topics.description: The lens or combination of lenses in an optical instrument closest to the observer's eye.

topics.title: Fahrenheit Scale
topics.description: A temperature scale in which the freezing point of water is 32 °F and the boiling point is 212 °F.

topics.title: Fahrenheit to Celsius Conversion
topics.description: The formula to convert temperature from Fahrenheit to Celsius is T°C = (5/9)(T°F - 32).

topics.title: Fahrenheit to Kelvin Conversion
topics.description: The formula to convert temperature from Fahrenheit to Kelvin is T(K) = (5/9)(T°F - 32) + 273.15.

topics.title: Falling Objects
topics.description: Falling objects are objects that are in motion under the influence of gravity alone, typically near the Earth's surface.

topics.title: Far Point
topics.description: The object point imaged by the eye onto the retina when the eye is unaccommodated.

topics.title: Faraday Cage
topics.description: A Faraday cage is a metal shield that encloses a volume, with all electrical charges residing on the outside surface and no electrical field inside.

topics.title: Faraday Cage Protection
topics.description: A Faraday cage is a metal shield that encloses a volume, with all electrical charges residing on its outside surface and no electrical field inside.

topics.title: Faraday’s Law of Induction
topics.description: The induced electromotive force in a circuit is proportional to the rate of change of magnetic flux through the circuit.

topics.title: Farsightedness
topics.description: A condition where incoming light rays reach the retina before converging into a focused image.

topics.title: Farsightedness (Hyperopia)
topics.description: Farsightedness is the inability to see close objects clearly while distant objects may be clear, caused by the eye underconverging light rays from close objects, making them focus behind the retina.

topics.title: Fermilab’s Accelerator Principle
topics.description: Fermilab’s accelerator uses colliding beams of protons and antiprotons to create new particles, with the total incoming momentum being zero to allow for the creation of particles with high masses.

topics.title: Fermion
topics.description: A particle with a half-integer value of intrinsic spin.

topics.title: Ferromagnet
topics.description: A ferromagnet is a material that can be strongly magnetized and retains its magnetic properties even in the absence of an external magnetic field.

topics.title: Ferromagnetic Material
topics.description: Materials like iron, cobalt, nickel, and gadolinium that exhibit strong magnetic effects.

topics.title: Ferromagnets and Electromagnets
topics.description: Ferromagnets are materials that can be magnetized permanently, while electromagnets are magnets created by electric currents.

topics.title: Feynman Diagram
topics.description: A Feynman diagram is a graphical representation used to visualize the exchange of virtual particles in interactions between subatomic particles.

topics.title: Fiber Optics
topics.description: Fiber optics is the use of thin fibers of plastic or glass to transmit light through total internal reflection, enabling communication and imaging.

topics.title: Fictitious Force
topics.description: A fictitious force is an apparent force that arises in non-inertial frames of reference, giving the illusion of a real force acting on an object.

topics.title: Field
topics.description: A map of the amount and direction of a force acting on other objects, extending out into space.

topics.title: Final Position
topics.description: The position of an object at the end of a given time interval, which can be calculated using initial position, initial velocity, time, and acceleration.

topics.title: Final Velocity
topics.description: The velocity of an object at the end of a given time interval, which can be calculated using initial velocity, acceleration, and time.

topics.title: Final Velocity with Constant Acceleration
topics.description: The final velocity of an object under constant acceleration can be calculated using the equation v = v₀ + at, where v is the final velocity, v₀ is the initial velocity, a is the acceleration, and t is the time.

topics.title: Finding Vector Components
topics.description: Finding vector components involves determining the horizontal and vertical parts of a vector using trigonometric relationships with the vector's magnitude and direction.

topics.title: Fine Structure
topics.description: The splitting of spectral lines of the hydrogen spectrum when examined at very high resolution.

topics.title: Finite Lower Limit to Space
topics.description: The finite lower limit to space suggests that there is a smallest possible size in the universe, beyond which space cannot be divided, potentially related to the size of superstrings.

topics.title: First Condition for Equilibrium
topics.description: The first condition for equilibrium is that the net external force acting on a system must be zero.

topics.title: First Law of Thermodynamics
topics.description: The first law of thermodynamics states that the change in internal energy of a system is equal to the net heat added to the system minus the net work done by the system, expressed as ΔU = Q − W.

topics.title: First Postulate of Special Relativity
topics.description: The idea that the laws of physics are the same and can be stated in their simplest form in all inertial frames of reference.

topics.title: Fission
topics.description: A nuclear reaction in which a heavy atomic nucleus splits into lighter nuclei, releasing energy.

topics.title: Fission Bomb
topics.description: A bomb that uses the process of nuclear fission to release energy by splitting heavy atomic nuclei.

topics.title: Fission Fragments
topics.description: Fission fragments are the two smaller nuclei produced when a heavy nucleus undergoes fission.

topics.title: Fission Fuel
topics.description: Fission fuel is a material that can undergo nuclear fission, such as uranium-235 or plutonium-239.

topics.title: Fission Products
topics.description: Fission products are the smaller nuclei and neutrons produced as a result of a nuclear fission reaction.

topics.title: Fissionable Material
topics.description: A material capable of undergoing nuclear fission when bombarded with neutrons, such as uranium-235 or plutonium-239.

topics.title: Flash Photography and Strobe Lights
topics.description: Flash photography and strobe lights use RC circuits to produce short, intense flashes of light by rapidly discharging a capacitor through a low-resistance path.

topics.title: Flat (Zero Curvature) Universe
topics.description: A flat (zero curvature) universe is a universe that is infinite but not curved.

topics.title: Flat Universe
topics.description: A flat universe is one with zero curvature, meaning that the geometry of space is Euclidean, and it is considered to be very close to the observed universe.

topics.title: Flavor
topics.description: A property of quarks that distinguishes different types of quarks.

topics.title: Flavor of Quark
topics.description: The flavor of a quark refers to its type, such as up (u), down (d), strange (s), charm (c), bottom (b), or top (t).

topics.title: Flavors
topics.description: Quark type.

topics.title: Floating and Sinking
topics.description: An object floats if the buoyant force is greater than its weight, sinks if the buoyant force is less than its weight, and remains suspended if the buoyant force equals its weight.

topics.title: Flow of Fluids
topics.description: The flow of fluids refers to the movement of liquids or gases through a system or medium.

topics.title: Flow Rate
topics.description: Flow rate is the volume of fluid passing through a given area per unit time.

topics.title: Fluid
topics.description: A fluid is a substance that can flow and take the shape of its container, including both liquids and gases.

topics.title: Fluid Dynamics
topics.description: The physics of fluids in motion.

topics.title: Fluid Flow
topics.description: Fluid flow refers to the movement of liquids or gases through a medium, such as water through a hose or air around objects.

topics.title: Fluid Statics
topics.description: Fluid statics is the study of fluids at rest and the forces they exert, including pressure and buoyancy.

topics.title: Fluid Support
topics.description: The ability of a fluid to support the weight of an object submerged in it.

topics.title: Fluids
topics.description: A fluid is a substance that can flow and take the shape of its container, including both liquids and gases.

topics.title: Fluorescence
topics.description: A process in which an atom or molecule, excited by a photon of a given energy, de-excites by emitting a lower-energy photon.

topics.title: Focal Length
topics.description: The distance from the center of a lens or curved mirror to its focal point.

topics.title: Focal Length of Spherical Mirrors
topics.description: The focal length of a concave mirror is the distance from the mirror's center to its focal point, where parallel rays converge after reflection, and it is positive.

topics.title: Focal Point
topics.description: The focal point of a lens is the point where parallel light rays converge (for a converging lens) or appear to diverge from (for a diverging lens).

topics.title: Food Irradiation
topics.description: Food irradiation is the treatment of food with ionizing radiation to reduce pest infestation, delay spoilage, and prevent illness caused by microorganisms.

topics.title: Food Safety
topics.description: Food safety refers to the assurance that food is free from harmful microorganisms, toxins, and contaminants, which is a primary goal of food irradiation.

topics.title: Force
topics.description: A push or pull on an object with a specific magnitude and direction.

topics.title: Force and Area Relationship in Hydraulic Systems
topics.description: In a hydraulic system, the ratio of force to area is constant, meaning a force applied to a smaller area can result in a larger force on a larger area.

topics.title: Force and Time Relationship
topics.description: The effect of a force on an object depends on both the magnitude of the force and the duration for which it acts, with a larger force acting for a shorter time having the same effect as a smaller force acting for a longer time.

topics.title: Force Carrier Particle
topics.description: Particles that mediate the fundamental forces, such as photons for electromagnetism and gluons for the strong nuclear force.

topics.title: Force Carrier Particles
topics.description: Particles such as photons, gluons, and vector bosons that mediate the transfer of forces between objects.

topics.title: Force Constant
topics.description: A constant related to the rigidity of a system: the larger the force constant, the more rigid the system; the force constant is represented by k.

topics.title: Force Constant (Spring Constant)
topics.description: The force constant, or spring constant, is a measure of the stiffness of a spring, defined as the force required to produce a unit displacement.

topics.title: Force Field
topics.description: A region in which a test particle will experience a force.

topics.title: Force in Joints
topics.description: Joints experience large forces due to the mechanical advantage of the system, often resulting in significant stress on the joint structures.

topics.title: Force of Kinetic Friction
topics.description: The force that opposes the motion of an object sliding over a surface, calculated as the product of the coefficient of kinetic friction and the normal force.

topics.title: Force of Static Friction
topics.description: The maximum force that must be overcome to start an object moving, which is less than or equal to the product of the coefficient of static friction and the normal force.

topics.title: Force on a Moving Charge in a Magnetic Field
topics.description: The force on a moving charge in a magnetic field is perpendicular to both the charge's velocity and the magnetic field.

topics.title: Force Per Unit Length Between Parallel Conductors
topics.description: The force per unit length between two parallel current-carrying conductors is calculated using the formula F/l = μ₀I₁I₂/(2πr), where I₁ and I₂ are the currents, r is the distance between the conductors, and μ₀ is the permeability of free space.

topics.title: Force Unification
topics.description: Force unification is the concept that the fundamental forces of nature may be different manifestations of a single force under certain conditions.

topics.title: Force Unit - Newton
topics.description: A newton (N) is the SI unit of force, defined as the force required to accelerate a 1-kg mass at a rate of 1 m/s².

topics.title: Forced Oscillation
topics.description: Forced oscillation occurs when a periodic driving force is applied to a system, causing it to oscillate at the frequency of the driving force rather than its natural frequency.

topics.title: Forced Oscillations and Resonance
topics.description: Forced oscillations occur when an external periodic force is applied to an oscillator, and resonance is the phenomenon where the amplitude of oscillation increases significantly when the frequency of the external force matches the natural frequency of the system.

topics.title: Forces and Torques in Muscles and Joints
