topics.description: Forces and torques in muscles and joints describe how muscles exert forces on bones and joints to produce movement and maintain body stability.

topics.title: Forces on the Hip Joint
topics.description: The forces acting on the hip joint include the weight of the body and the forces exerted by muscles and ligaments to maintain movement and stability.

topics.title: Forms of Energy
topics.description: Energy can exist in various forms such as kinetic, potential, thermal, chemical, electrical, and radiant energy, among others.

topics.title: Fossil Fuels
topics.description: Oil, natural gas, and coal.

topics.title: Four Basic Forces
topics.description: The four fundamental forces that account for all known phenomena in nature are gravitational, electromagnetic, weak nuclear, and strong nuclear forces.

topics.title: Four Fundamental Forces
topics.description: The four fundamental forces are gravity, electromagnetism, weak nuclear force, and strong nuclear force, which are responsible for all interactions known to science.

topics.title: Frame of Reference
topics.description: A point or collection of points arbitrarily chosen, which motion is measured in relation to.

topics.title: Fraunhofer Lines
topics.description: Black lines shown on an absorption spectrum that show the wavelengths absorbed by a gas.

topics.title: Free Body Diagram
topics.description: A visual representation of all forces acting on a system, showing their magnitudes, directions, and points of application.

topics.title: Free Charge
topics.description: An electrical charge (either positive or negative) which can move about separately from its base molecule.

topics.title: Free Electron
topics.description: An electron that is free to move away from its atomic orbit.

topics.title: Free Fall
topics.description: Free fall is the motion of an object where gravity is the only force acting on it, resulting in constant acceleration toward the center of Earth.

topics.title: Free Radicals
topics.description: Free radicals are unstable molecules with unpaired electrons that can cause chemical reactions leading to the breakdown of cell structures.

topics.title: Free-Body Diagram
topics.description: A free-body diagram is a visual representation of all external forces acting on a body, shown as vectors originating from an isolated point.

topics.title: Free-Fall
topics.description: A situation in which the only force acting on an object is the force due to gravity.

topics.title: Freefall
topics.description: A situation in which the only force acting on an object is the force of gravity.

topics.title: Freezing
topics.description: A phase change from liquid to solid.

topics.title: Frequency
topics.description: The number of events per unit of time.

topics.title: Frequency and Electrical Shock Effects
topics.description: The frequency of an electrical current affects the severity of a shock, with the body being most sensitive to frequencies near 50- or 60-Hz AC.

topics.title: Frequency and Wavelength Relationship
topics.description: Frequency and wavelength are inversely proportional properties of electromagnetic waves, meaning as frequency increases, wavelength decreases, and vice versa.

topics.title: Frequency Modulation (FM)
topics.description: A method of placing information on electromagnetic waves by modulating the frequency of a carrier wave with an audio signal, producing a wave of constant amplitude but varying frequency.

topics.title: Frequency Observed by a Moving Observer
topics.description: The frequency observed by a moving observer when the source is stationary is given by the equation f_obs = f_s × ((v_w ± v_obs) / v_w).

topics.title: Frequency Observed by a Moving Observer with a Stationary Source
topics.description: The frequency observed by a moving observer when the source is stationary is given by the equation f_obs = f_s × ((v_w ± v_obs) / v_w).

topics.title: Frequency Observed by a Moving Source
topics.description: The frequency observed by a stationary person when a source is moving is given by the equation f_obs = f_s × (v_w / (v_w ± v_s)).

topics.title: Frequency Observed by a Stationary Observer with a Moving Source
topics.description: The frequency observed by a stationary observer when the source is moving is given by the equation f_obs = f_s × (v_w / (v_w ± v_s)).

topics.title: Frequency of a Wave
topics.description: The number of cycles of a wave that pass a given point per unit time.

topics.title: Frequency of Current and Shock Sensitivity
topics.description: The frequency of an electrical current affects the severity of a shock, with the human body being most sensitive to frequencies near 50- or 60-Hz AC.

topics.title: Frequency of Light
topics.description: The frequency of light remains constant when it travels from one medium to another.

topics.title: Frequency of Simple Harmonic Motion
topics.description: Frequency is the number of oscillations an object completes in one second in simple harmonic motion.

topics.title: Frequency of Sound
topics.description: The frequency of a sound wave is the number of waves that pass a point per unit time, determining the pitch of the sound.

topics.title: Frequency Shift Calculation
topics.description: The frequency shift of sound from a moving object can be calculated using the Doppler shift formula, which relates the observed frequency to the source frequency, the speed of sound, and the speed of the source or observer.

topics.title: Friction
topics.description: Friction is a force that opposes relative motion between surfaces in contact.

topics.title: Friction and Deformation Forces
topics.description: Friction and deformation forces are types of forces that affect the motion, position, and shape of objects, and are important in applying Newton’s laws of motion.

topics.title: Frictional Force Components
topics.description: Frictional force components are the parts of the gravitational force acting on an object on an inclined plane, resolved into perpendicular and parallel directions relative to the plane.

topics.title: Fulcrum
topics.description: A fulcrum is the pivot point of a lever around which the bar rotates.

topics.title: Function of a Space Shuttle
topics.description: The space shuttle is a reusable spacecraft designed to carry astronauts and cargo into space, with components like solid fuel boosters and an external fuel tank.

topics.title: Functional MRI (fMRI)
topics.description: A type of MRI that measures changes in blood flow in the brain to map brain activity associated with specific functions or tasks.

topics.title: Fundamental
topics.description: The lowest-frequency resonance.

topics.title: Fundamental Building Blocks
topics.description: Fundamental building blocks are the smallest particles that make up all matter and have no further substructure.

topics.title: Fundamental Building Blocks of Matter
topics.description: Fundamental building blocks of matter are the smallest particles that cannot be broken down into smaller components.

topics.title: Fundamental Frequency
topics.description: The lowest frequency of a periodic waveform.

topics.title: Fundamental Particle
topics.description: A fundamental particle is a particle that has no substructure and is not made of other particles.

topics.title: Fundamental Particles and Substructure
topics.description: Fundamental particles and substructure questions explore whether particles like quarks and leptons are truly elementary or if they have a more complex internal structure.

topics.title: Fundamental Physical Quantities
topics.description: Fundamental physical quantities are the basic quantities used to describe physical phenomena, including length, mass, time, and electric current.

topics.title: Fundamental Physical Units
topics.description: The seven fundamental physical units in the SI system of units are length, mass, time, electric current, temperature, amount of a substance, and luminous intensity.

topics.title: Fundamental Unit of Charge
topics.description: The fundamental unit of charge is the charge of an electron or proton, which has a magnitude of 1.60 × 10^-19 coulombs.

topics.title: Fundamental Units
topics.description: Units that can only be expressed relative to the procedure used to measure them.

topics.title: Further Applications of Newton’s Laws of Motion
topics.description: The use of Newton’s laws to analyze and solve real-world problems involving forces and motion.

topics.title: Fusion
topics.description: A nuclear reaction in which light atomic nuclei combine to form heavier nuclei, releasing energy in the process.

topics.title: Fusion Fuel
topics.description: Fusion fuel refers to the materials, such as deuterium and tritium, used in fusion reactions to produce energy.

topics.title: Galaxy Formation
topics.description: Galaxy formation refers to the process by which galaxies, like the Milky Way, formed from primordial gas and dark matter in the early universe.

topics.title: Galaxy Red Shift
topics.description: The observed shift in the wavelength of light from galaxies due to their motion away from us, used to determine the expansion of the universe.

topics.title: Galileo's Telescope Design
topics.description: Galileo's telescope design uses a convex objective lens and a concave eyepiece to produce an upright image, commonly used in spyglasses and similar devices.

topics.title: Galvanometer
topics.description: An analog measuring device, denoted by G, that measures current flow using a needle deflection caused by a magnetic field force acting upon a current-carrying wire.

topics.title: Galvanometer as Ammeter
topics.description: A galvanometer can be used as an ammeter by connecting it in parallel with a small resistance, called a shunt resistance.

topics.title: Galvanometer as Voltmeter
topics.description: A galvanometer can be used as a voltmeter by connecting it in series with a large resistance.

topics.title: Gamma (γ)
topics.description: Gamma (γ) is a factor used to calculate the relationship between proper time and the time measured by an observer in motion, defined as γ = 1 / sqrt(1 - v²/c²).

topics.title: Gamma Decay
topics.description: A type of radioactive decay in which an atomic nucleus emits a gamma particle.

topics.title: Gamma Decay Equation
topics.description: Gamma decay involves the emission of high-energy photons from an atom without changing its atomic or mass number.

topics.title: Gamma Ray
topics.description: Extremely high frequency electromagnetic radiation emitted by the nucleus of an atom, either from natural nuclear decay or induced nuclear processes in nuclear reactors and weapons.

topics.title: Gamma Ray Production
topics.description: Gamma rays are produced by nuclear processes, such as radioactive decay, and they are the highest-energy form of electromagnetic radiation.

topics.title: Gamma-Ray Burst Origins
topics.description: Gamma-ray burst origins are questions about the sources of high-energy gamma-ray bursts observed in space, potentially linked to events like neutron star collisions or black hole interactions.

topics.title: Gamma-Ray Bursts
topics.description: Gamma-ray bursts are intense flashes of gamma rays from distant cosmic sources, often associated with supernovae or neutron star mergers.

topics.title: Gauge Boson
topics.description: A particle that carries one of the four forces.

topics.title: Gauge Pressure
topics.description: Gauge pressure is the pressure relative to atmospheric pressure, with positive values indicating pressures above atmospheric pressure and negative values indicating pressures below it.

topics.title: Gauge Pressure, Absolute Pressure, and Pressure Measurement
topics.description: Gauge pressure is the pressure relative to atmospheric pressure, while absolute pressure is the total pressure measured from a perfect vacuum.

topics.title: Gauss
topics.description: The unit of the magnetic field strength, where 1 G = 10^-4 T.

topics.title: Gauss’s Law for Electricity
topics.description: A principle stating that the electric flux through a closed surface is proportional to the enclosed electric charge.

topics.title: Gauss’s Law for Magnetism
topics.description: A principle stating that the magnetic flux through a closed surface is always zero, indicating there are no magnetic monopoles.

topics.title: Geiger Tube
topics.description: A very common radiation detector that usually gives an audio output.

topics.title: General Conservation of Energy Equation
topics.description: The total energy in a system, including kinetic, potential, work done by nonconservative forces, and other energy, remains constant and can be expressed as KE_i + PE_i + W_nc + OE_i = KE_f + PE_f + OE_f.

topics.title: General Relativity
topics.description: A theory by Einstein that describes gravity as the curvature of spacetime caused by mass, rather than a force acting at a distance.

topics.title: General Relativity and Quantum Gravity
topics.description: The attempt to unify Einstein's theory of general relativity, which describes gravity, with quantum mechanics to explain gravity at the smallest scales.

topics.title: Generator
topics.description: A device that converts mechanical energy into electrical energy.

topics.title: Generator operation
topics.description: A generator converts mechanical energy into electrical energy by using the motion of a coil in a magnetic field to induce an electromotive force (emf) through electromagnetic induction.

topics.title: Generator Principle
topics.description: The generator principle describes how mechanical energy is converted into electrical energy by rotating a coil of wire within a magnetic field.

topics.title: Generators
topics.description: A generator is a device that converts mechanical energy into electrical energy through electromagnetic induction.

topics.title: Geometric Optics
topics.description: Geometric optics is the branch of optics that describes the behavior of light using rays and the principles of geometry and trigonometry.

topics.title: Giant Magnetoresistance
topics.description: Giant magnetoresistance is a phenomenon where a small change in a magnetic field can cause a significant change in electrical resistance, which is crucial for advancements in computer memory technology.

topics.title: Glaucoma
topics.description: A condition caused by the buildup of fluid pressure in the eye.

topics.title: Global Heating
topics.description: Global heating refers to the increase in Earth's temperature due to the accumulation of heat-trapping gases in the atmosphere.

topics.title: Global Positioning Systems (GPS)
topics.description: Global Positioning Systems are networks of satellites that provide location and time information, requiring adjustments for relativistic effects to function accurately.

topics.title: Gluon
topics.description: A particle that mediates the strong nuclear force between quarks.

topics.title: Gluons
topics.description: Massless, spin-1 particles that mediate the strong nuclear force between quarks and carry color charge.

topics.title: Graded Index (GRIN) Lenses
topics.description: Graded index (GRIN) lenses are lenses with a refractive index that varies gradually across the lens, allowing for more precise control of light refraction and correction of optical aberrations.

topics.title: Grand Unification Epoch
topics.description: A period in the early universe when the electromagnetic, weak, and strong nuclear forces were unified into a single force, as predicted by Grand Unified Theories.

topics.title: Grand Unified Theories (GUTs)
topics.description: Theoretical frameworks that attempt to unify the strong, weak, and electromagnetic forces into a single force at high energies.

topics.title: Grand Unified Theory
topics.description: A theoretical framework that proposes the unification of the strong nuclear, weak nuclear, and electromagnetic forces into a single force.

topics.title: Graphical Addition and Subtraction of Vectors
topics.description: Graphical addition and subtraction of vectors involve using drawings to represent and combine vectors.

topics.title: Graphical Analysis of Motion
topics.description: Graphical analysis of motion involves using graphs to represent and analyze the relationships between displacement, velocity, and time.

topics.title: Graphical Method
topics.description: A method of adding vectors by drawing them on a graph using the head-to-tail method.

topics.title: Graphical Methods of Vector Addition and Subtraction
topics.description: Techniques that use diagrams and geometric constructions to add or subtract vectors.

topics.title: Graphical Representation of Motion
topics.description: Graphical representation of motion involves using visual tools like velocity-time graphs to show how velocity and acceleration change over time.

topics.title: Graphical Representation of Vectors
topics.description: A vector is represented graphically as an arrow with a length proportional to its magnitude and a direction indicated by the angle it makes with a reference axis.

topics.title: Graphical Vector Addition
topics.description: Graphical vector addition is a method of adding vectors by drawing them head-to-tail on a diagram and then drawing the resultant vector from the tail of the first vector to the head of the last vector.

topics.title: Graphs and Relationships
topics.description: Graphs are used to visually represent relationships between variables, such as linear, quadratic, inverse, and exponential relationships.

topics.title: Gravitational Acceleration
topics.description: The acceleration experienced by an object due to the gravitational force exerted by a massive body, such as Earth.

topics.title: Gravitational Field
topics.description: The region around a mass where another mass experiences a gravitational force, with strength determined by the gravitational constant and the mass of the source.

topics.title: Gravitational Force
topics.description: The force of attraction between all masses in the universe, which is always attractive and acts over an infinite range.

topics.title: Gravitational Lensing
topics.description: The bending of light by massive objects due to the curvature of spacetime, as predicted by general relativity.

topics.title: Gravitational Orbits
topics.description: The motion of objects under the influence of gravitational force, where a smaller mass orbits a larger mass.

topics.title: Gravitational Potential Energy
topics.description: Gravitational potential energy is the energy an object has due to its position in a gravitational field.

topics.title: Gravitational Potential Energy per Unit Volume
topics.description: Gravitational potential energy per unit volume is the energy associated with the height of a fluid in a gravitational field, represented by the term ρgh in Bernoulli’s equation.

topics.title: Gravitational Waves
topics.description: Gravitational waves are ripples in spacetime caused by the acceleration of massive objects, predicted by general relativity.

topics.title: Graviton
topics.description: The graviton is the proposed carrier particle for gravity, which has not yet been found but is theorized to be massless and travel at the speed of light.

topics.title: Gravity
topics.description: Gravity is the force that attracts objects with mass towards each other.

topics.title: Gray (Gy)
topics.description: The SI unit for radiation dose, defined as 1 J/kg or 100 rad.

topics.title: Greenhouse Effect
topics.description: The warming of the Earth due to gases like carbon dioxide and methane that absorb infrared radiation and reradiate it back toward the surface.

topics.title: Greenhouse Gases
topics.description: Greenhouse gases are gases in the atmosphere that trap heat, contributing to the warming of the Earth.

topics.title: Ground Fault Interrupter (GFI)
topics.description: A safety device that compares the currents in the live/hot and neutral wires and trips if their difference exceeds a safe value, preventing hazardous leakage currents.

topics.title: Ground State
topics.description: The lowest energy state of an atom, where an electron is in its most stable configuration.

topics.title: Grounded
topics.description: Connected to the ground with a conductor, so that charge flows freely to and from the Earth to the grounded object.

topics.title: Grounding
topics.description: Fixing a conductor at zero volts by connecting it to the earth or ground.

topics.title: GUT Epoch
topics.description: The GUT epoch is the time period from 10−43 to 10−34 after the Big Bang, when Grand Unification Theory governed the universe.

topics.title: Gyroscopic Effect
topics.description: The gyroscopic effect is the phenomenon where a spinning object resists changes to the direction of its angular momentum, causing it to precess rather than simply fall over.

topics.title: Hadron Composition
topics.description: The structure of hadrons, which are composed of either three quarks (baryons) or a quark-antiquark pair (mesons).

topics.title: Hadrons
topics.description: Hadrons are particles that interact via the strong nuclear force and are composed of quarks.

topics.title: Hadrons and Leptons
topics.description: Hadrons are particles that feel the strong nuclear force, while leptons are particles that do not feel the strong nuclear force.

topics.title: Half-Life
topics.description: The half-life is the time it takes for half of the radioactive nuclei in a sample to decay.

topics.title: Half-Life and Activity
topics.description: Half-life is the time required for half of a sample of a radioactive substance to decay, while activity is the rate at which a radioactive substance decays.

topics.title: Hall Effect
topics.description: The creation of voltage across a current-carrying conductor by a magnetic field.

topics.title: Hall Effect Voltage Calculation
topics.description: The Hall emf can be calculated using the formula epsilon = Blv, where B is the magnetic field, l is the width of the conductor, and v is the velocity of the charges, provided B, v, and l are mutually perpendicular.

topics.title: Hall Voltage Calculation
topics.description: Hall voltage calculation involves determining the Hall emf using the formula epsilon = Blv, where B is the magnetic field, l is the width of the conductor, and v is the velocity of the charges.

topics.title: Harmonic Motion
topics.description: Harmonic motion is a type of periodic motion where an object oscillates back and forth around an equilibrium position.

topics.title: Harmonics
topics.description: Resonant frequencies of a system that are integer multiples of the fundamental frequency, including the fundamental itself.

topics.title: Head (of a Vector)
topics.description: The end point of a vector; the location of the tip of the vector’s arrowhead.

topics.title: Head-to-Tail Method
topics.description: A method of adding vectors in which the tail of each vector is placed at the head of the previous vector.

topics.title: Hearing
topics.description: The perception of sound.

topics.title: Hearing as Perception
topics.description: Hearing is the perception of sound, which occurs when a sound wave is detected by the human ear and interpreted by the brain.

topics.title: Heat
topics.description: Heat is the transfer of thermal energy between objects due to a temperature difference.

topics.title: Heat and Energy
topics.description: Heat is a form of energy that is transferred between objects or systems due to a temperature difference.

topics.title: Heat Capacity
topics.description: Heat capacity is the amount of heat required to change the temperature of a substance by a certain amount, and it depends on the mass and specific heat of the substance.

topics.title: Heat Conduction
topics.description: Heat conduction is the transfer of thermal energy between molecules in a material due to collisions, moving from regions of higher temperature to lower temperature.

topics.title: Heat Engine
topics.description: A heat engine is a device that converts thermal energy into mechanical work by absorbing heat from a high-temperature source and expelling heat to a low-temperature sink.

topics.title: Heat Engine Reversed
topics.description: A heat pump operates as a heat engine run backward, transferring heat from a cold reservoir to a hot reservoir with work input.

topics.title: Heat of Sublimation
topics.description: The energy required to change a substance from the solid phase to the vapor phase.

topics.title: Heat Pump
topics.description: A heat pump is a device that transfers energy by heat from a cold reservoir to a warm reservoir, requiring work input to achieve this.

topics.title: Heat Pump Operation
topics.description: A heat pump is a device that transfers heat from a cold reservoir to a hot reservoir using work input, effectively operating a heat engine in reverse.

topics.title: Heat Pumps and Refrigerators
topics.description: Heat pumps and refrigerators are devices that transfer heat from a colder reservoir to a hotter reservoir by doing work on the system.

topics.title: Heat Transfer
topics.description: Heat transfer is the process by which thermal energy moves from a region of higher temperature to a region of lower temperature.

topics.title: Heat Transfer by Radiation
topics.description: Heat transfer by radiation is the process by which energy is transferred through electromagnetic waves, without requiring a medium.

topics.title: Heat Transfer During Melting/Freezing
topics.description: The heat transfer during melting or freezing is calculated using the formula Q = mL_f, where Q is the heat transferred, m is the mass, and L_f is the latent heat of fusion.

topics.title: Heat Transfer During Phase Change
topics.description: Heat transfer during a phase change involves energy exchange that changes the state of a substance without altering its temperature.

topics.title: Heat Transfer During Vaporization/Condensation
topics.description: The heat transfer during vaporization or condensation is calculated using the formula Q = mL_v, where Q is the heat transferred, m is the mass, and L_v is the latent heat of vaporization.

topics.title: Heat Transfer from Hot to Cold
topics.description: Heat transfers energy spontaneously from higher-temperature objects to lower-temperature objects, increasing the total entropy of the system.

topics.title: Heat Transfer in Heat Pumps
topics.description: Heat transfer in a heat pump involves moving heat from a cold reservoir to a hot reservoir, requiring work input to overcome the natural direction of heat flow.

topics.title: Heat Transfer in the Human Body
topics.description: Heat transfer in the human body through convection involves the movement of blood to the skin to release heat, which is regulated by the dilation and constriction of blood vessels.

topics.title: Heat Transfer Methods
topics.description: Heat transfer methods are the different ways thermal energy moves from one place to another.

topics.title: Heat Transfer Rate
topics.description: Heat transfer rate is the amount of heat transferred per unit time, calculated by dividing the total heat transferred by the time taken.

topics.title: Heat-Engine Efficiency
topics.description: The efficiency of a heat engine is the ratio of the work output to the heat input, indicating how effectively the engine converts heat into work.

topics.title: Heisenberg Uncertainty Principle
topics.description: A fundamental limit to the precision with which pairs of quantities (momentum and position, and energy and time) can be measured.

topics.title: Helical Motion of a Charged Particle in a Magnetic Field
topics.description: When a charged particle moves at an angle to a magnetic field, its path becomes spiral due to the combination of circular motion and motion parallel to the field.

topics.title: Henry
topics.description: The unit of inductance, defined as 1 H = 1 Ω·s.

topics.title: Hertz
topics.description: An SI unit denoting the frequency of an electromagnetic wave, in cycles per second.

topics.title: Hertz’s Experiments
topics.description: Experiments conducted by Heinrich Hertz that confirmed the existence of electromagnetic waves and verified their speed matches the speed of light.

topics.title: Hierarchy of Matter Structures
topics.description: The hierarchy of matter structures describes how larger structures like solids are composed of smaller structures such as molecules, atoms, nuclei, nucleons, and quarks.

topics.title: Higgs Boson
topics.description: A massive particle that, if observed, would give validity to the theory that carrier particles are identical under certain circumstances.

topics.title: Higgs Field
topics.description: The Higgs field permeates space, and elementary particles acquire mass through their interactions with it. The Higgs boson is an excitation of this field.

topics.title: High Dose
topics.description: A dose greater than 1 Sv (100 rem).

topics.title: High Dose Irradiation
topics.description: High dose irradiation refers to the use of ionizing radiation at doses greater than 10,000 Gy, which is used for sterilization and can cause significant chemical changes in food.

topics.title: High-Temperature Superconductors
topics.description: High-temperature superconductors are materials that become superconductors at temperatures higher than traditional superconductors, often above 77 K (liquid nitrogen temperature).

topics.title: High-Z Nuclei
topics.description: High-Z nuclei are atomic nuclei with a very high atomic number, which are studied to understand the limits of nuclear stability and forces.

topics.title: Hologram
topics.description: A three-dimensional image produced from the Greek word 'holo,' meaning holistic.

topics.title: Holography
topics.description: The process of producing holograms.

topics.title: Hooke’s Law
topics.description: A proportional relationship between the force applied to a material and the deformation it causes, expressed as F = kΔL.

topics.title: Horizontal and Vertical Motion Independence
topics.description: Horizontal and vertical motions in projectile motion are independent, meaning they do not influence each other.

topics.title: Horizontal Motion
topics.description: The motion of a projectile along the horizontal axis, characterized by constant velocity when air resistance is negligible.

topics.title: Hormesis
topics.description: A term describing generally favorable biological responses to low exposures of toxins or radiation.

topics.title: Horsepower
topics.description: An older non-SI unit of power, with 1 hp = 746 W.

topics.title: Hot Reservoir
topics.description: A hot reservoir is a high-temperature object or environment that provides heat to a heat engine or heat pump.

topics.title: Hubble Constant
topics.description: The Hubble constant is a central concept in cosmology determined by the slope of a velocity versus distance graph from red shift measurements.

topics.title: Hues
topics.description: The identity of a color as it relates specifically to the spectrum.

topics.title: Human Hearing Range
topics.description: The range of frequencies humans can typically hear, from approximately 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz.

topics.title: Human Metabolism
topics.description: The conversion of food into heat transfer, work, and stored fat.

topics.title: Humidity
topics.description: Humidity is the amount of water vapor present in the air.

topics.title: Humidity and Comfort
topics.description: High humidity inhibits evaporation, making hot weather feel hotter, while low humidity can cause discomfort due to excessive drying of body tissues.

topics.title: Huygens's Principle
topics.description: Huygens's principle states that every point on a wavefront is a source of wavelets that spread out in the forward direction at the same speed as the wave itself, and the new wavefront is a line tangent to all of these wavelets.

topics.title: Hydraulic Systems
topics.description: Hydraulic systems are enclosed fluid systems used to exert forces, often converting a small force into a larger force through the application of pressure.

topics.title: Hydrogen Spectrum Series
topics.description: Hydrogen spectrum series are sets of spectral lines corresponding to electron transitions ending at specific energy levels, such as the Lyman, Balmer, and Paschen series.

topics.title: Hydrogen Spectrum Wavelengths
topics.description: The wavelengths of visible light from hydrogen, calculated using a specific equation.

topics.title: Hydrogen-like Atom
topics.description: Any atom with only a single electron.

topics.title: Hyperopia
topics.description: A condition where incoming light rays reach the retina before converging into a focused image.

topics.title: Hypothesis
topics.description: A hypothesis is a testable statement that explains how something in the natural world works, often based on observations and prior knowledge.

topics.title: Ideal Angle
topics.description: The angle at which a car can turn safely on a steep curve, which is in proportion to the ideal speed.

topics.title: Ideal Banking
topics.description: The sloping of a curve in a road, where the angle of the slope allows the vehicle to negotiate the curve at a certain speed without the aid of friction between the tires and the road.

topics.title: Ideal Banking Angle
topics.description: The angle of a banked curve that allows a vehicle to navigate the curve at a specific speed without the need for friction.

topics.title: Ideal Gas Law
topics.description: A physical law that relates the pressure and volume of a gas to the number of gas molecules or moles and the temperature of the gas.

topics.title: Ideal Gas Law in Terms of Molecular Mass and Velocity
topics.description: The ideal gas law can be expressed using the average molecular speed squared and the mass of a molecule, relating pressure, volume, number of molecules, and temperature.

topics.title: Ideal Mechanical Advantage
topics.description: Ideal mechanical advantage is the mechanical advantage of a perfect machine with no energy loss due to friction.

topics.title: Ideal Speed
topics.description: The maximum safe speed at which a vehicle can turn on a curve without the aid of friction between the tire and the road.

topics.title: Identifying Knowns and Unknowns in a Problem
topics.description: Distinguishing between the given information and the quantities that need to be determined in a physics problem to guide the solution process.

topics.title: Ignition
topics.description: A condition in fusion where a reaction produces enough energy to be self-sustaining after external energy input is cut off.

topics.title: Illuminance
topics.description: Illuminance is the amount of luminous flux per unit area, measured in lux.

topics.title: Image Formation by Lenses
topics.description: Lenses bend light rays to form images by converging or diverging the light based on their shape and the material's refractive index.

topics.title: Image Formation by Mirrors
topics.description: Mirrors reflect light rays to form images based on the curvature of the mirror and the position of the object relative to the mirror.

topics.title: Image Formation by the Eye
topics.description: The eye forms images by focusing light rays from objects onto the retina using the cornea and lens, which act as a single thin lens.

topics.title: Image Formation in a Flat Mirror
topics.description: An image formed by a flat mirror is virtual, upright, and the same size as the object, located behind the mirror at the same distance as the object.

topics.title: Image Formation in a Microscope
topics.description: In a compound microscope, the objective lens forms a real, inverted image of the object, which then serves as the object for the eyepiece, which further magnifies the image.

topics.title: Image Formation in Mirrors
topics.description: Image formation in mirrors occurs when light rays reflect off a smooth surface and appear to originate from a point behind the mirror, creating a virtual image.

topics.title: Impedance
topics.description: The AC equivalent of resistance in a DC circuit, combining resistance, inductive reactance, and capacitive reactance as Z = √(R² + (X_L − X_C)²).

topics.title: Impedance in an RLC Circuit
topics.description: Impedance is the AC analog of resistance in a DC circuit, representing the total opposition to current in an RLC series circuit.

topics.title: Impulse
topics.description: Impulse is the product of the average force applied to an object and the time interval during which the force acts.

topics.title: Impulse-Momentum Theorem
topics.description: The impulse-momentum theorem states that the impulse applied to an object equals the change in its linear momentum.

topics.title: Impulse–Momentum Theorem
topics.description: The impulse, or change in momentum, is the product of the net external force and the time over which the force acts.

topics.title: In Parallel
topics.description: Resistors connected side by side with their top and bottom ends connected together by wires.

topics.title: In Series
topics.description: Elements in a circuit connected one after the other in the same branch.

topics.title: In-Phase Electric and Magnetic Fields
topics.description: In an electromagnetic wave, the electric and magnetic fields are in phase, meaning they reach their maximum and minimum values at the same time.

topics.title: In-Phase Voltage and Current
topics.description: In an AC circuit, voltage and current are said to be in phase if they reach their peak values at the same time.

topics.title: Incident Ray
topics.description: The incoming light ray that strikes a boundary between two media.

topics.title: Inclined Plane
topics.description: An inclined plane is a simple machine that allows a force to be applied over a longer distance to lift an object, reducing the force needed compared to lifting it vertically.

topics.title: Inclined Plane Problems
topics.description: Inclined plane problems involve analyzing motion along a surface that is tilted relative to the horizontal.

topics.title: Incoherent Waves
topics.description: Waves that have random phase relationships.

topics.title: Incompressible Fluids
topics.description: Incompressible fluids are substances that do not change volume under pressure, such as liquids.

topics.title: Independence of Horizontal and Vertical Motion
topics.description: The horizontal and vertical components of motion in two dimensions are independent of each other, meaning motion in one direction does not affect motion in the perpendicular direction.

topics.title: Independence of Motion
topics.description: The principle that horizontal and vertical motions of a projectile are independent and can be analyzed separately.

topics.title: Independent Variable
topics.description: The variable that the dependent variable is measured with respect to; usually plotted along the x-axis.

topics.title: Index of Refraction
topics.description: The index of refraction of a material is the ratio of the speed of light in a vacuum to the speed of light in the material.

topics.title: Index of Refraction and Wavelength
topics.description: The index of refraction of a medium depends on the wavelength of light, with shorter wavelengths having a higher index of refraction.

topics.title: Induced Current
topics.description: An induced current is a current that is generated in a conductor due to a changing magnetic field.

topics.title: Induced Electric Field
topics.description: An electric field produced by a changing magnetic field, as described by Faraday's law of induction.

topics.title: Induced Electromotive Force (emf)
topics.description: The voltage generated in a conductor when there is a change in the magnetic flux through the conductor.

topics.title: Induced Emf
topics.description: The electromotive force generated in a conductor when there is a change in magnetic flux through the conductor.

topics.title: Induced emf in a generator
topics.description: The electromotive force (emf) generated in a generator is produced by rotating a coil in a magnetic field, which induces a voltage due to changing magnetic flux.

topics.title: Induced EMF in an Inductor
topics.description: The electromotive force (emf) generated in an inductor is proportional to the rate of change of current through it.

topics.title: Induced Magnetic Field
topics.description: An induced magnetic field is a magnetic field created by an induced current, which opposes the change in magnetic flux that caused the current.

topics.title: Inductance
topics.description: The property of a coil that opposes changes in current flowing through it, measured by the ratio of the induced electromotive force to the rate of change of current.

topics.title: Inductive Reactance
topics.description: The opposition an inductor provides to a change in current, calculated by X_L = 2πfL.

topics.title: Inductor
topics.description: A device that exhibits significant self-inductance.

topics.title: Inductor Opposition to Current Change
topics.description: An inductor opposes changes in current by inducing an electromotive force (emf) that counteracts the change in current.

topics.title: Inelastic Collision
topics.description: An inelastic collision is a collision in which momentum is conserved but kinetic energy is not.

topics.title: Inertia
topics.description: Inertia is the property of a body to remain at rest or to remain in motion with constant velocity unless acted upon by a net external force.

topics.title: Inertial Confinement
topics.description: Inertial confinement is a technique that uses high-energy lasers or other methods to compress and heat fusion fuel, achieving the conditions necessary for fusion.

topics.title: Inertial Frame of Reference
topics.description: A reference frame in which a body at rest remains at rest and a body in motion moves at a constant speed in a straight line unless acted on by an outside force.

topics.title: Inertial Reference Frame
topics.description: A frame of reference where all objects follow Newton’s first law of motion, meaning objects at rest remain at rest, and objects in motion continue at a constant velocity unless acted upon by an external force.

topics.title: Inflationary Epoch
topics.description: The rapid expansion of the universe by an incredible factor of 10^−50 for the brief time from 10^−35 to about 10^−32 seconds.

topics.title: Inflationary Scenario
topics.description: A rapid exponential expansion of the universe in the first fraction of a second after the Big Bang, proposed to explain the uniformity of the cosmic microwave background.

topics.title: Infrared Radiation
topics.description: Infrared radiation is a type of electromagnetic wave with longer wavelengths than visible light, often associated with heat transfer.

topics.title: Infrared Radiation (IR)
topics.description: A region of the electromagnetic spectrum with a frequency range that extends from just below the red region of the visible light spectrum up to the microwave region.

topics.title: Infrasound
topics.description: Infrasound refers to sound waves with frequencies below 20 Hz, which are not perceived by the human ear.

topics.title: Infrasound and Ultrasound
topics.description: Sounds below 20 Hz are called infrasound, and those above 20,000 Hz are called ultrasound, both outside the range of human hearing.

topics.title: Initial Velocity
topics.description: The velocity of an object at the beginning of a given time interval.

topics.title: Ink Jet Printer
topics.description: A printing technology that uses electrostatic charge to direct ink droplets precisely onto paper to form text and images.

topics.title: Input Work
topics.description: Input work is the work done on a machine by the input force.

topics.title: Instantaneous Acceleration
topics.description: The rate of change of velocity at a specific instant in time.

topics.title: Instantaneous Acceleration from a Velocity vs. Time Graph
topics.description: Instantaneous acceleration at a point on a velocity vs. time graph is the slope of the tangent line to the curve at that point.

topics.title: Instantaneous Speed
topics.description: The speed of an object at a specific instant in time.

topics.title: Instantaneous Velocity
topics.description: Instantaneous velocity is the velocity at a specific instant in time, representing the average velocity over an infinitesimally small time interval.

topics.title: Instantaneous Velocity from a Position vs. Time Graph
topics.description: Instantaneous velocity at a point on a position vs. time graph is the slope of the tangent line to the curve at that point.

topics.title: Insulation and Heat Transfer
topics.description: Insulation reduces heat transfer by using materials with low thermal conductivity and increasing the thickness of the insulating layer.

topics.title: Insulator
topics.description: An insulator is a material that does not allow electric charge to move freely through it because its electrons and ions are tightly bound in the structure.

topics.title: Insulators
topics.description: Insulators are materials that do not allow electric charges to move freely through them.

topics.title: Integral Multiples of Charge
topics.description: All observed charges in nature are integral multiples of the fundamental unit of charge, which is the charge of an electron or proton.

topics.title: Integrated Concepts in Physics
topics.description: A problem-solving approach that combines multiple physics topics, such as electric fields, forces, and motion, to solve complex real-world problems.

topics.title: Integration of Kinematics and Dynamics
topics.description: The application of kinematic principles (like acceleration and velocity) with dynamic principles (like forces and Newton’s laws) to solve complex motion problems.

topics.title: Intensity
topics.description: Power per unit area.

topics.title: Intensity and Area Relationship
topics.description: The intensity of a wave decreases as the area over which the wave spreads increases, indicating that intensity is inversely proportional to area.

topics.title: Intensity of Electromagnetic Waves
topics.description: The intensity of an electromagnetic wave is the power it carries per unit area, measured in watts per square meter.

topics.title: Intensity of Waves
topics.description: Intensity is the power per unit area carried by a wave, measured in watts per square meter (W/m²).

topics.title: Intensity Reflection Coefficient
topics.description: A measure of the ratio of the intensity of the wave reflected off a boundary between two media relative to the intensity of the incident wave.

topics.title: Interaction Between Magnetic Fields and Electric Currents
topics.description: The way magnetic fields and electric currents influence each other, leading to phenomena such as electromagnetic induction.

topics.title: Interaction of Magnetic Poles
topics.description: Magnetic poles interact such that like poles repel each other and unlike poles attract each other.

topics.title: Interference
topics.description: Interference is the phenomenon where waves overlap and combine to produce a resultant wave with a different amplitude.

topics.title: Interference Fringes
topics.description: Interference fringes are the alternating bright and dark lines formed on a screen due to the constructive and destructive interference of light waves.

topics.title: Interference Microscopes
topics.description: Microscopes that enhance contrast between objects and background by superimposing a reference beam of light upon the light emerging from the sample.

topics.title: Interference Microscopy
topics.description: Interference microscopy enhances contrast by superimposing a reference beam of light with the light emerging from the sample.

topics.title: Interference Microscopy Enhances Contrast
topics.description: Interference microscopes use the superposition of light beams to create contrast by producing constructive and destructive interference patterns.

topics.title: Interference of Light
topics.description: Interference is a wave phenomenon where light waves superpose to form patterns of constructive and destructive interference.

topics.title: Internal Energy
topics.description: The sum of the kinetic and potential energies of a system’s atoms and molecules.

topics.title: Internal Forces
topics.description: Forces that act between components within a system are called internal forces and do not affect the motion of the system as a whole.

topics.title: Internal Kinetic Energy
topics.description: Internal kinetic energy is the sum of the kinetic energies of the objects within a system.

topics.title: Internal Resistance
topics.description: Internal resistance is the resistance within a voltage source that affects the terminal voltage, and it is a factor in determining the electromotive force (emf) of a battery.

topics.title: Interrelated Measurement System
topics.description: An interrelated measurement system is a set of units and standards that are connected and used together to describe physical quantities.

topics.title: Intraocular Pressure
topics.description: The fluid pressure inside the eye that maintains its shape, and when abnormally high, can lead to glaucoma.

topics.title: Intrinsic Magnetic Field
topics.description: The magnetic field generated due to the intrinsic spin of electrons.

topics.title: Intrinsic Spin
topics.description: Intrinsic spin is the internal angular momentum of an electron, which is quantized in magnitude and direction, and contributes to the electron's intrinsic magnetic field.

topics.title: Inverse Proportionality
topics.description: A relation between two variables expressible by an equation of the form y = k divided by x, where k stays constant when x and y change; the special form of inverse relationship that satisfies this equation.

topics.title: Inverse Relationship
topics.description: Any relation between variables where one variable decreases as the other variable increases.

topics.title: Inverse Square Law
topics.description: The electrostatic force decreases with the square of the distance between two charges, meaning it is inversely proportional to the square of the distance.

topics.title: Inverse-Square Law
topics.description: An inverse-square law is a relationship where the magnitude of a physical quantity, such as force, decreases proportionally to the square of the distance from the source.

topics.title: Inversion
topics.description: A vertical flipping of a wave after reflection from a fixed end.

topics.title: Inverted Image in Telescopes
topics.description: Most telescopes produce an inverted image, which is not a problem for astronomical observations but can be an issue for other applications requiring an upright image.

topics.title: Ionization
topics.description: Ionization is the phase change from gas to plasma, which involves separating electrons from atoms to form a ionized gas.

topics.title: Ionization of Radiation
topics.description: The process by which radiation removes electrons from atoms, creating ions and causing damage to materials.

topics.title: Ionizing Radiation
topics.description: Ionizing radiation is radiation with enough energy to remove tightly bound electrons from atoms, creating ions and free radicals.

topics.title: Ionosphere
topics.description: A layer of charged particles located around 100 km above the surface of Earth, which is responsible for a range of phenomena including the electric field surrounding Earth.

topics.title: Iridescence
topics.description: Iridescence is the phenomenon of displaying a range of colors due to the interference of light waves reflecting off surfaces with microscopic structures.

topics.title: Irradiation Plant
topics.description: An irradiation plant is a facility where food is exposed to ionizing radiation using specialized equipment and shielding to ensure safety and effectiveness.

topics.title: Irreversible Process
topics.description: An irreversible process is one that cannot be reversed without leaving some change in the system or its surroundings, and it results in an increase in the total entropy of the universe.

topics.title: Isobaric Process
topics.description: A constant-pressure process in which a gas does work.

topics.title: Isochoric Process
topics.description: A constant-volume process.

topics.title: Isolated System
topics.description: A system where the net external force is zero, allowing the total momentum to remain constant.

topics.title: Isolation Transformer
topics.description: A device that puts a large resistance between the original voltage source and the device, preventing a complete circuit through a person even if they touch one of its output wires.

topics.title: Isothermal Process
topics.description: A constant-temperature process.

topics.title: Isotope
topics.description: An isotope is a variant of an element that has the same number of protons but a different number of neutrons, resulting in a different mass number.

topics.title: Isotopes
topics.description: Isotopes are atoms of the same element that have the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons.

topics.title: James Clerk Maxwell's Theory
topics.description: James Clerk Maxwell formulated a theory in the mid-19th century that predicted the existence of electromagnetic waves.

topics.title: Jet Emission from Black Holes
topics.description: Jet emission from black holes refers to the process by which high-energy particles and radiation are ejected at high speeds from the vicinity of a black hole.

topics.title: Jets from Black Holes
topics.description: Jets from black holes are high-energy streams of particles ejected at nearly the speed of light from the vicinity of a black hole, often aligned with its rotational axis.

topics.title: Joint Forces and Levers
topics.description: Joints act as pivot points, and the forces exerted by muscles and bones create lever systems that can produce large forces at the joints.

topics.title: Joule
topics.description: The SI unit of work and energy, equal to one newton-meter.

topics.title: Joule’s Law
topics.description: The relationship between potential electrical power, voltage, and resistance in an electrical circuit, given by: P_e = IV.

topics.title: Junction Rule
topics.description: Kirchhoff’s first rule, which applies the conservation of charge to a junction; current is the flow of charge; thus, whatever charge flows into the junction must flow out.

topics.title: Kelvin
topics.description: A unit on the Kelvin temperature scale; it is never referred to in terms of 'degrees' Kelvin.

topics.title: Kelvin Scale
topics.description: A temperature scale in which 0 K is the lowest possible temperature, representing absolute zero.

topics.title: Kelvin to Celsius Conversion
topics.description: The formula to convert temperature from Kelvin to Celsius is T°C = T(K) - 273.15.

topics.title: Kelvin to Fahrenheit Conversion
topics.description: The formula to convert temperature from Kelvin to Fahrenheit is T°F = (9/5)(T(K) - 273.15) + 32.

topics.title: Kepler’s First Law
topics.description: The orbit of a planet around the Sun is an ellipse with the Sun at one focus.

topics.title: Kepler’s Laws
topics.description: Kepler’s laws are three scientific laws that describe the motion of planets around the Sun, including the elliptical shape of orbits, equal areas swept in equal times, and the relationship between orbital period and distance.

topics.title: Kepler's Laws of Planetary Motion
topics.description: Kepler's laws are three scientific laws that describe the motion of planets around the Sun, including the elliptical shape of orbits, equal areas in equal times, and the relationship between orbital period and distance.

topics.title: Kepler’s Second Law
topics.description: A line from the Sun to a planet sweeps out equal areas in equal times as the planet orbits.

topics.title: Kepler’s Third Law
topics.description: The square of the orbital period of a planet is proportional to the cube of the semi-major axis of its orbit.

topics.title: Kilocalorie
topics.description: A unit of energy equal to 1000 calories.

topics.title: Kilogram
topics.description: The SI unit for mass, abbreviated (kg).

topics.title: Kilowatt-Hour
topics.description: A kilowatt-hour is a unit of energy equal to the energy consumed by a 1-kilowatt device operating for 1 hour.

topics.title: Kinematic Equations
topics.description: A set of equations used to describe the motion of objects under constant acceleration, relating displacement, velocity, acceleration, and time.

topics.title: Kinematic Equations for Free Fall
topics.description: Kinematic equations for free fall are mathematical formulas used to calculate the position and velocity of an object in free fall, assuming negligible air resistance.

topics.title: Kinematic Equations for Projectile Motion
topics.description: Kinematic equations for projectile motion are used to analyze the horizontal and vertical components of motion separately, with horizontal acceleration being zero and vertical acceleration being -g.

topics.title: Kinematics
topics.description: The study of motion without considering its causes.

topics.title: Kinematics in Two Dimensions
topics.description: The study of motion in two dimensions, involving both horizontal and vertical components.

topics.title: Kinematics of Rotational Motion
topics.description: Describes the relationships among rotation angle, angular velocity, angular acceleration, and time.

topics.title: Kinetic Energy
topics.description: Kinetic energy is the energy an object possesses due to its motion.

topics.title: Kinetic Energy in Simple Harmonic Motion
topics.description: Kinetic energy in a simple harmonic oscillator is the energy associated with the motion of the object and is proportional to the square of its velocity.

topics.title: Kinetic Energy Loss
topics.description: Kinetic energy loss is the reduction in the internal kinetic energy of a system during a collision, which occurs when internal forces do work to transform kinetic energy into other forms such as heat or sound.

topics.title: Kinetic Energy of a Gas Molecule
topics.description: The kinetic energy of a gas molecule is the average translational kinetic energy, which depends on its temperature.

topics.title: Kinetic Energy per Unit Volume
topics.description: Kinetic energy per unit volume is the energy associated with the motion of a fluid, represented by the term (1/2)ρv² in Bernoulli’s equation.

topics.title: Kinetic Friction
topics.description: A force that opposes the motion of two systems that are in contact and moving relative to one another.

topics.title: Kinetic Theory
topics.description: Kinetic theory explains the behavior of gases by considering the motion of their molecules.

topics.title: Kinetic Theory of Gases
topics.description: The kinetic theory of gases explains the behavior of gases in terms of the motion of their molecules, assuming they are in constant random motion.

topics.title: Kirchhoff’s First Rule (Junction Rule)
topics.description: The sum of all currents entering a junction must equal the sum of all currents leaving the junction.

topics.title: Kirchhoff’s Rules
topics.description: Kirchhoff’s rules are two fundamental laws used to analyze complex electrical circuits: the junction rule (sum of currents entering a junction equals the sum leaving) and the loop rule (sum of potential differences around a closed loop is zero).

topics.title: Kirchhoff’s Second Rule (Loop Rule)
topics.description: The algebraic sum of changes in potential around any closed circuit path (loop) must be zero.

topics.title: Laminar Flow
topics.description: A type of fluid flow in which layers do not mix.

topics.title: Laminar Flow Around Objects
topics.description: Laminar flow around objects occurs when the Reynolds number is less than about 1, resulting in smooth, orderly fluid motion with minimal turbulence.

topics.title: Large Hadron Collider
topics.description: The Large Hadron Collider (LHC) is a large particle accelerator located at CERN, designed to study fundamental particles and their interactions.

topics.title: Laser
topics.description: An acronym for light amplification by stimulated emission of radiation.

topics.title: Laser Vision Correction
topics.description: Laser vision correction is a procedure that uses high-intensity electromagnetic radiation to reshape the cornea, correcting nearsightedness, farsightedness, and astigmatism by altering the cornea's curvature.

topics.title: LASIK
topics.description: LASIK is a laser vision correction procedure where the top layer of the cornea is peeled back, and the underlying tissue is ablated using an excimer laser to reshape the cornea and correct vision.

topics.title: LASIK Procedure
topics.description: LASIK is a laser vision correction procedure where the top layer of the cornea is peeled back, and the underlying tissue is ablated using an excimer laser to reshape the cornea and correct vision.

topics.title: Latent Heat
topics.description: Heat related to the phase change of a substance rather than a change of temperature.

topics.title: Latent Heat Coefficient
topics.description: A physical constant equal to the amount of heat transferred for every 1 kg of a substance during a phase change.

topics.title: Latent Heat of Fusion
topics.description: The latent heat of fusion is the energy required to change 1 kilogram of a substance from solid to liquid without changing its temperature.

topics.title: Latent Heat of Vaporization
topics.description: The latent heat of vaporization is the energy required to change 1 kilogram of a substance from liquid to gas without changing its temperature.

topics.title: Law
topics.description: A description, using concise language or a mathematical formula, of a generalized pattern in nature that is supported by scientific evidence and repeated experiments.

topics.title: Law of Conservation of Angular Momentum
topics.description: Angular momentum is conserved, i.e., the initial angular momentum is equal to the final angular momentum when no external torque is applied to the system.

topics.title: Law of Conservation of Charge
topics.description: The law of conservation of charge states that electric charge cannot be created or destroyed in an isolated system, meaning the net charge remains constant before and after any interaction.

topics.title: Law of Conservation of Energy
topics.description: The general law that total energy is constant in any process; energy may change in form or be transferred from one system to another, but the total remains the same.

topics.title: Law of Conservation of Energy in Rotational Motion
topics.description: The Law of Conservation of Energy in rotational motion states that the total mechanical energy in a closed system remains constant, with energy converting between rotational kinetic energy and other forms such as gravitational potential energy.

topics.title: Law of Conservation of Momentum
topics.description: The total momentum of an isolated system remains constant before and after an event, such as a collision or explosion.

topics.title: Law of Reflection
topics.description: The law of reflection states that the angle of reflection equals the angle of incidence, both measured relative to the perpendicular to the surface.

topics.title: Law of Refraction (Snell’s Law)
topics.description: Snell’s Law states that the ratio of the sine of the incident angle to the sine of the refracted angle is equal to the ratio of the indices of refraction of the two media.

topics.title: Laws of Physics
topics.description: The laws of physics are fundamental principles that describe how the universe operates, from the smallest particles to the largest structures.

topics.title: Leakage Current
topics.description: Current driven by an induced emf on the case of an appliance that can cause a shock if the case is not grounded.

topics.title: Length Contraction
topics.description: Length contraction is the phenomenon where objects moving at relativistic speeds appear shorter in the direction of motion to an observer in a different inertial frame.

topics.title: Lens/Mirror Equation (Reciprocal Version)
topics.description: The reciprocal version of the lens/mirror equation relates the focal length, image distance, and object distance using reciprocals.

topics.title: Lens/Mirror Equation (Solved Version)
topics.description: The solved version of the lens/mirror equation expresses the focal length as the product of image distance and object distance divided by their sum.

topics.title: Lenses
topics.description: Lenses are transparent objects with curved surfaces that refract light to focus or diverge it.

topics.title: Lenz’s Law
topics.description: The minus sign in Faraday’s law, indicating that the induced emf opposes the change in magnetic flux.

topics.title: Lepton
topics.description: Leptons are a group of fundamental particles not bound by the strong nuclear force, including electrons and neutrinos.

topics.title: Lever
topics.description: A lever is a rigid bar pivoted at a fixed point called the fulcrum, used to amplify force by applying it at a distance from the pivot.

topics.title: Lever Arm
topics.description: The distance between the point of rotation (pivot point) and the location where force is applied.

topics.title: Lever Arm and Mechanical Advantage
topics.description: The lever arm is the perpendicular distance from the pivot point to the line of action of a force, and it determines the mechanical advantage of a lever system.

topics.title: Lever Systems in the Body
topics.description: The body functions as a lever system, where muscles, bones, and joints work together to produce movement with specific mechanical advantages.

topics.title: Lift in Airplane Wings
topics.description: Lift in airplane wings is generated by the pressure difference between the upper and lower surfaces of the wing, where the faster-moving air above creates lower pressure, resulting in an upward force.

topics.title: Light Ray
topics.description: A light ray is a straight line that originates at a point and is used to model the path of light traveling through space or media.

topics.title: Light Travel Methods
topics.description: Light can travel from a source to another location directly through empty space, through various media like air and glass, or after being reflected by objects like a mirror.

topics.title: Light Year
topics.description: A light year is the distance that light travels in one year.

topics.title: Lightning Rod Function
topics.description: A lightning rod is a pointed conductor that facilitates the transfer of charge from a building to the atmosphere, preventing dangerous lightning strikes.

topics.title: Limits of Resolution: The Rayleigh Criterion
topics.description: The Rayleigh criterion defines the minimum angular separation at which two objects can be distinguished as separate.

topics.title: Linear Accelerator
topics.description: An accelerator that accelerates particles in a straight line.

topics.title: Linear and Angular Quantity Relationships
topics.description: The direct analogs between linear motion quantities (displacement, velocity, acceleration) and their rotational counterparts (angle, angular velocity, angular acceleration).

topics.title: Linear Expansion
topics.description: Linear expansion is the increase in length of an object due to a temperature change, calculated using the coefficient of linear expansion.

topics.title: Linear Hypothesis
topics.description: An assumption that risk is directly proportional to risk from high doses.

topics.title: Linear Momentum
topics.description: Linear momentum is the product of an object's mass and its velocity.

topics.title: Linear Relationship
topics.description: A linear relationship is a type of relationship between two variables that can be represented by a straight line on a graph, with the equation y = mx + b.

topics.title: Liquid Drop Model
topics.description: A model of a nucleus where nucleons act like atoms in a drop, used to understand some of its features.

topics.title: Liter
topics.description: A unit of volume, equal to 10−3 m3.

topics.title: Load Resistance
topics.description: Load resistance is the resistance of the component or device connected to a voltage source, which affects the current and terminal voltage.

topics.title: Log-Log Plot
topics.description: A log-log plot is a graph where both axes use a logarithmic scale, often used to represent power-law relationships.

topics.title: Logarithmic Scale
topics.description: A graphing scale in which each major tick on an axis is the previous tick multiplied by some value; minor ticks are often included at intermediate values which are logarithmically spaced.

topics.title: Longitudinal Wave
topics.description: A wave in which the disturbance is parallel to the direction of propagation.

topics.title: Loop Rule
topics.description: Kirchhoff’s second rule, which states that in a closed loop, whatever energy is supplied by emf must be transferred into other forms by devices in the loop.

topics.title: Loudness
topics.description: The perception of sound intensity.

topics.title: Low Dose
topics.description: A dose less than 100 mSv (10 rem).

topics.title: Low Dose Irradiation
topics.description: Low dose irradiation refers to the use of ionizing radiation at levels sufficient to prevent or reduce the growth of microorganisms without significantly altering the food's quality.

topics.title: Lumens
topics.description: A unit of measure for luminous flux.

topics.title: Luminous Flux
topics.description: Luminous flux is the total amount of light energy emitted by a source, measured in lumens.

topics.title: Lux
topics.description: A unit of measure for illuminance.

topics.title: MACHOs
topics.description: MACHOs are massive compact halo objects; microlensing objects of huge mass.

topics.title: Macrostate
topics.description: A macrostate is an overall property of a system that describes its general state without specifying the detailed arrangement of its components.

topics.title: Magic Numbers
topics.description: A number that indicates a shell structure for the nucleus in which closed shells are more stable.

topics.title: Magnetic Confinement
topics.description: Magnetic confinement is a technique used to confine plasma in a magnetic field to achieve and sustain nuclear fusion reactions.

topics.title: Magnetic Damping
topics.description: Magnetic damping is the drag force produced by eddy currents that opposes the motion of a conductor moving in a magnetic field.

topics.title: Magnetic Dipole
topics.description: Magnetic dipoles are objects that have two opposite magnetic poles, such as magnets, and their properties are analogous to electric dipoles.

topics.title: Magnetic Domains
topics.description: Magnetic domains are regions within a ferromagnetic material where the magnetic poles of individual atoms are aligned, acting like small bar magnets.

topics.title: Magnetic Effects in Materials
topics.description: Magnetic effects in materials refer to the complex and often unexplained magnetic behaviors observed in certain materials, which are studied in condensed matter physics.

topics.title: Magnetic Field
topics.description: A magnetic field is a region around a magnet or moving charge where a magnetic force is exerted on other magnets or moving charges.

topics.title: Magnetic Field and Charged Particle Motion
topics.description: The motion of a charged particle in a magnetic field is perpendicular to the field, resulting in circular or helical paths.

topics.title: Magnetic Field and Force on a Moving Charge
topics.description: A magnetic field exerts a force on a moving charge, with the direction determined by the right-hand rule.

topics.title: Magnetic Field Inside a Solenoid
topics.description: The magnetic field inside a solenoid is uniform and strong, directly proportional to the number of turns per unit length and the current flowing through the solenoid.

topics.title: Magnetic Field Line Density
topics.description: The strength of a magnetic field is proportional to the closeness (or density) of the magnetic field lines, with closer lines indicating a stronger field.

topics.title: Magnetic Field Lines
topics.description: A pattern of continuous, imaginary lines that emerge from and enter into opposite magnetic poles.

topics.title: Magnetic Field of a Current-Carrying Loop
topics.description: The magnetic field at the center of a current-carrying loop is proportional to the current and inversely proportional to the radius of the loop, given by the equation B = μ₀I/(2R).

topics.title: Magnetic Field of a Long Straight Wire
topics.description: The magnetic field created by a long, straight current-carrying wire is directly proportional to the current and inversely proportional to the distance from the wire.

topics.title: Magnetic Field Produced by a Long Straight Wire
topics.description: The magnetic field around a long straight current-carrying wire forms circular loops and its strength is directly proportional to the current and inversely proportional to the distance from the wire.

topics.title: Magnetic Field Steering
topics.description: The use of magnetic fields to change the direction of charged particles, such as electrons, in devices like cathode ray tubes.

topics.title: Magnetic Field Strength
topics.description: Magnetic field strength, measured in teslas, is defined by the force experienced by a moving charge in a magnetic field, calculated using the equation F = qvB sine theta.

topics.title: Magnetic Field Strength (Magnitude) of a Long Straight Current-Carrying Wire
topics.description: The magnetic field strength produced by a long straight current-carrying wire, defined as B = μ₀I / 2πr.

topics.title: Magnetic Field Strength at the Center of a Circular Loop
topics.description: The magnetic field strength at the center of a circular loop, defined as B = μ₀I / 2R.

topics.title: Magnetic Field Strength Inside a Solenoid
topics.description: The magnetic field strength inside a solenoid, defined as B = μ₀nI.

topics.title: Magnetic Field Strength: Force on a Moving Charge in a Magnetic Field
topics.description: Magnetic field strength is a measure of the force experienced by a moving charge in a magnetic field.

topics.title: Magnetic Fields and Magnetic Field Lines
topics.description: A magnetic field is the region around a magnet where magnetic forces are exerted, and magnetic field lines are used to visualize the direction and strength of the field.

topics.title: Magnetic Fields Produced by Currents: Ampere’s Law
topics.description: Ampere’s law relates the magnetic field around a closed loop to the electric current passing through the loop.

topics.title: Magnetic Flux
topics.description: Magnetic flux is the product of the magnetic field strength, the area through which the field passes, and the cosine of the angle between the field and the perpendicular to the area.

topics.title: Magnetic Force
topics.description: The force on a charge moving in a magnetic field.

topics.title: Magnetic Force Between Two Parallel Conductors
topics.description: Parallel conductors carrying currents experience a magnetic force that is attractive if the currents are in the same direction and repulsive if they are in opposite directions.

topics.title: Magnetic Force Equation
topics.description: The formula used to calculate the magnetic force on a current-carrying conductor, given by F = IlB sin(theta), where I is the current, l is the length of the conductor, B is the magnetic field, and theta is the angle between the current and the magnetic field.

topics.title: Magnetic Force on a Charge
topics.description: The magnetic force on a moving electric charge is given by the product of the charge, its velocity, the magnetic field strength, and the sine of the angle between the velocity and the magnetic field.

topics.title: Magnetic Force on a Current-Carrying Conductor
topics.description: A magnetic force acts on a current-carrying conductor placed in a magnetic field, perpendicular to both the current and the magnetic field.

topics.title: Magnetic Force on a Current-Carrying Loop
topics.description: The magnetic force on a current-carrying loop in a magnetic field produces a torque that depends on the current, the magnetic field, and the angle between the loop and the field.

topics.title: Magnetic Force on a Current-Carrying Wire
topics.description: The magnetic force on a current-carrying wire is the force exerted by a magnetic field on the wire, which depends on the current, the length of the wire, and the magnetic field strength.

topics.title: Magnetic Force on a Moving Charge
topics.description: The magnetic force acting on a moving charge is perpendicular to both the velocity of the charge and the magnetic field.

topics.title: Magnetic Induction
topics.description: Magnetic induction is the process by which a magnetic field generates an electromotive force (emf) and, consequently, a current in a conductor.

topics.title: Magnetic Monopoles
topics.description: An isolated magnetic pole; a south pole without a north pole, or vice versa.

topics.title: Magnetic Monopoles Do Not Exist
topics.description: It is impossible to isolate a single magnetic pole; magnetic poles always occur in pairs of north and south.

topics.title: Magnetic Pole
topics.description: Magnetic poles are the two distinct ends of a magnet, with the north pole and south pole being the fundamental components of any magnet.

topics.title: Magnetic Pole Naming Convention
topics.description: The north magnetic pole is named for its attraction toward the geographic North Pole, while the south magnetic pole is named for its attraction toward the geographic South Pole.

topics.title: Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI)
topics.description: A medical imaging technique that uses magnetic fields to create detailed images of internal tissues and organs.

topics.title: Magnetism
topics.description: Magnetism is the force that attracts or repels objects made of certain materials, such as iron, and is responsible for phenomena like the Aurora Borealis and the operation of compasses.

topics.title: Magnetism in Technology
topics.description: Magnetism is essential in the engineering of technologies like iPods, enabling functions such as data storage and retrieval.

topics.title: Magnetized
topics.description: To be turned into a magnet; to be induced to be magnetic.

topics.title: Magnetized Material
topics.description: A material that is induced to be magnetic or made into a permanent magnet.

topics.title: Magnetocardiogram (MCG)
topics.description: A recording of the heart’s magnetic field as it beats.

topics.title: Magnetoencephalogram (MEG)
topics.description: A measurement of the brain’s magnetic field.

topics.title: Magnets
topics.description: Magnets are objects that produce a magnetic field and can attract or repel other magnetic materials.

topics.title: Magnification
topics.description: Magnification is the ratio of the height of an image to the height of the object, indicating whether the image is upright or inverted and its relative size.

topics.title: Magnification Equation
topics.description: The magnification equation relates the ratio of image height to object height with the ratio of negative image distance to object distance.

topics.title: Magnification in Microscopes
