topics.description: The magnification of a microscope is the product of the magnification of the objective lens and the magnification of the eyepiece, resulting in a larger overall magnification of the object.

topics.title: Magnification in Mirror Image Formation
topics.description: Magnification in mirror image formation is the ratio of the image height to the object height, and it can be positive (upright) or negative (inverted).

topics.title: Magnification in Mirrors
topics.description: Magnification in mirrors is the ratio of the image height to the object height, indicating whether the image is enlarged, reduced, or the same size as the object.

topics.title: Magnitude
topics.description: Size or amount.

topics.title: Magnitude of a Resultant Vector
topics.description: The magnitude of a resultant vector is calculated using the Pythagorean theorem, which relates the magnitudes of its x and y components.

topics.title: Magnitude of a Vector
topics.description: The length or size of a vector; magnitude is a scalar quantity.

topics.title: Magnitude of Centripetal Acceleration
topics.description: The magnitude of centripetal acceleration is given by the formula $ a_c =  rac{v^2}{r} $, where $ v $ is the speed of the object and $ r $ is the radius of the circular path.

topics.title: Magnitude of Kinetic Friction
topics.description: The force calculated as f_k = μ_kN, where μ_k is the coefficient of kinetic friction and N is the magnitude of the normal force.

topics.title: Magnitude of Static Friction
topics.description: The force that is less than or equal to μ_sN, where μ_s is the coefficient of static friction and N is the magnitude of the normal force.

topics.title: Magnitude of the Intrinsic Spin Angular Momentum
topics.description: Given by a specific equation involving the spin quantum number and Planck's constant.

topics.title: Malus’s Law
topics.description: Malus’s law states that the intensity of light transmitted through a polarizing filter is proportional to the square of the cosine of the angle between the light's polarization direction and the filter's axis.

topics.title: Manometer
topics.description: A manometer is a device that measures pressure using a U-shaped tube filled with a fluid, where the difference in fluid levels indicates the pressure difference.

topics.title: Manometer and Fluid Velocity Measurement
topics.description: A manometer connected to tubes measuring fluid velocity uses the pressure difference caused by fluid speed to determine the velocity, where the height difference in the manometer is proportional to the square of the fluid velocity.

topics.title: Mass
topics.description: A measure of the amount of matter in an object, which determines its inertia and remains constant regardless of location.

topics.title: Mass and Volume Relationship
topics.description: The mass of an object can be calculated using its density and volume.

topics.title: Mass Defect
topics.description: The difference in mass between a bound system and its separate constituents, which is related to the binding energy through Einstein's equation.

topics.title: Mass Number
topics.description: The number of nucleons in a nucleus.

topics.title: Mass Ratio in Rocket Propulsion
topics.description: The mass ratio of a rocket is the ratio of its initial mass to its remaining mass after fuel is exhausted, which determines the maximum velocity it can achieve.

topics.title: Mass Spectrometer
topics.description: A device that measures the mass of charged particles by using magnetic fields to cause them to move in circular paths, with the radius of the path proportional to the mass.

topics.title: Mass vs. Weight
topics.description: Mass is the amount of matter in an object, while weight is the gravitational force acting on that mass, which varies depending on the gravitational field.

topics.title: Mass-Energy Equivalence
topics.description: Mass-energy equivalence is the principle that mass and energy are interchangeable, expressed by the equation E = mc², showing that mass can be converted into energy and vice versa.

topics.title: Massive Compact Halo Objects (MACHOs)
topics.description: MACHOs are hypothetical massive, compact objects, such as black holes or brown dwarfs, that could exist in galactic halos and potentially account for dark matter.

topics.title: Mathematical Representation of SHM
topics.description: The displacement of an object in simple harmonic motion as a function of time can be described by a cosine function.

topics.title: Matter and Antimatter
topics.description: Matter and antimatter are particles and their corresponding antiparticles, which have opposite charges but are otherwise identical in properties such as mass and spin.

topics.title: Matter-Antimatter Asymmetry
topics.description: The observed dominance of matter over antimatter in the universe, which is thought to have originated from a small asymmetry in the interactions of fundamental particles.

topics.title: Maximum Field Strength
topics.description: The amplitude of an electromagnetic wave is its maximum electric or magnetic field strength.

topics.title: Maximum Height
topics.description: Maximum height is the highest vertical position reached by a projectile during its motion.

topics.title: Maximum Height (of a Projectile)
topics.description: The highest altitude, or maximum displacement in the vertical position reached in the path of a projectile.

topics.title: Maximum Height in Projectile Motion
topics.description: The maximum vertical height reached by a projectile calculated using the initial vertical velocity and the acceleration due to gravity.

topics.title: Maximum Kinetic Energy of a Photoelectron
topics.description: The maximum kinetic energy of photoelectrons is the energy an ejected electron possesses after absorbing a photon’s energy, calculated as the photon energy minus the binding energy of the electron.

topics.title: Maximum Kinetic Energy of an Ejected Electron
topics.description: The maximum kinetic energy of an ejected electron is the energy of the photon minus the binding energy of the electron in the material, given by KE_e = hf - BE.

topics.title: Maximum Magnetic Field Strength in an Electromagnetic Wave
topics.description: The maximum strength of the magnetic field in an electromagnetic wave can be calculated using the maximum electric field strength and the speed of light.

topics.title: Maximum Number of Electrons in a Shell
topics.description: The maximum number of electrons that can occupy a shell is determined by the principal quantum number n and is given by the formula 2n².

topics.title: Maximum Number of Electrons in a Subshell
topics.description: The maximum number of electrons that can occupy a subshell is determined by the angular momentum quantum number l and is given by the formula 2(2l + 1).

topics.title: Maximum Speed of a Simple Harmonic Oscillator
topics.description: The maximum speed of an oscillating system occurs at the equilibrium position and is determined by the amplitude, spring constant, and mass of the system.

topics.title: Maxwell’s Equations
topics.description: Maxwell’s Equations are a set of four fundamental equations that describe how electric and magnetic fields are generated and altered by charges and currents.

topics.title: Measurement Affects the System
topics.description: Measurement of a quantum system affects the system being observed, often altering its state and introducing uncertainty in its properties.

topics.title: Measurement Inaccuracy
topics.description: Measuring voltage or current in a circuit can never be exact because the meter itself alters the circuit.

topics.title: Mechanical Advantage
topics.description: Mechanical advantage (MA) is the ratio of the output force to the input force for a simple machine, indicating how much a machine multiplies the force applied.

topics.title: Mechanical Advantage in Muscles
topics.description: Skeletal muscles attached close to joints provide greater mechanical advantage, allowing smaller forces to produce larger movements.

topics.title: Mechanical Advantage in Muscles and Joints
topics.description: Skeletal muscles attached close to joints provide mechanical advantages less than one, requiring muscles to exert large forces to move limbs.

topics.title: Mechanical Advantage of Pulley Systems
topics.description: The mechanical advantage of a pulley system is the number of cables pulling upward on the load, which determines how much the force is multiplied.

topics.title: Mechanical Advantage of Pulleys
topics.description: The mechanical advantage of a pulley system is the ratio of the output force to the input force, determined by the number of cables pulling upward on the system of interest.

topics.title: Mechanical Energy
topics.description: The sum of kinetic energy and potential energy.

topics.title: Mechanical Energy Conservation
topics.description: Mechanical energy is conserved in a system when only conservative forces act, but it may not be conserved when nonconservative forces are present.

topics.title: Mechanical Equivalent of Heat
topics.description: The work needed to produce the same effects as heat transfer.

topics.title: Mechanical Wave
topics.description: A mechanical wave is a disturbance that travels through a medium, transferring energy without transferring mass.

topics.title: Medical Applications of Radioactivity
topics.description: Medical applications of radioactivity involve using radioactive substances for diagnostic imaging and radiation therapy.

topics.title: Medium
topics.description: A medium is a material through which a mechanical wave propagates, such as a solid, liquid, or gas.

topics.title: Melting
topics.description: A phase change from solid to liquid.

topics.title: Meson
topics.description: A class of subatomic particles that includes pions and are responsible for mediating the strong nuclear force.

topics.title: Mesons and Baryons
topics.description: Mesons are hadrons that can decay into leptons and have a baryon number of 0, while baryons are hadrons that always decay into other baryons and have a baryon number of +1 for matter and -1 for antimatter.

topics.title: Metabolic Rate
topics.description: The rate at which the body uses food energy to sustain life and perform different activities.

topics.title: Metastable
topics.description: A state whose lifetime is an order of magnitude longer than the most short-lived states.

topics.title: Metastable State
topics.description: A metastable state is an excited state of an atomic nucleus that is unstable and can decay, emitting radiation such as gamma rays.

topics.title: Meter
topics.description: The SI unit for length, abbreviated (m).

topics.title: Method of Adding Percents
topics.description: The percent uncertainty in a quantity calculated by multiplication or division is the sum of the percent uncertainties in the items used to make the calculation.

topics.title: Metric Prefixes
topics.description: Metric prefixes are standardized multipliers used with SI units to denote multiples or fractions of a unit, such as kilo (10^3) or milli (10^-3).

topics.title: Metric System
topics.description: A system in which values can be calculated in factors of 10.

topics.title: Michelson-Morley Experiment
topics.description: An investigation performed in 1887 that proved the speed of light in a vacuum is the same in all frames of reference from which it is viewed.

topics.title: Microgravity
topics.description: An environment in which the apparent net acceleration of a body is small compared with that produced by Earth at its surface.

topics.title: Microlensing
topics.description: Microlensing is a gravitational lensing effect where a massive compact object, such as a dark matter candidate, bends light from a distant star, causing it to appear brighter temporarily.

topics.title: Microscopes
topics.description: Microscopes are optical instruments used to magnify small objects, allowing detailed observation of microscopic structures.

topics.title: Microscopy Enhanced by Wave Characteristics
topics.description: Microscopy uses wave properties of light both as a limit on resolution, because diffraction obscures details smaller than the probe wavelength, and as a means to improve contrast through interference and related imaging methods.

topics.title: Microshock Sensitivity
topics.description: A condition in which a person’s skin resistance is bypassed, rendering the person vulnerable to electrical shock at currents about 1/1000 the normally required level.

topics.title: Microstate
topics.description: A microstate is a detailed description of every element of a system, specifying the exact configuration of its components.

topics.title: Microtubules and Electrostatic Fields
topics.description: Microtubules are hollow protein tubes within cells that can extend electrostatic fields over larger distances despite screening, aiding in cellular processes like chromosome movement.

topics.title: Microwave Applications
topics.description: Microwaves are used for communication, cooking, and radar systems, and they can penetrate materials more than other radio waves due to their shorter wavelengths.

topics.title: Microwaves
topics.description: Microwaves are a type of electromagnetic wave with shorter wavelengths than radio waves, used for communication, cooking, and radar.

topics.title: Micturition Reflex
topics.description: A reflex that stimulates the feeling of needing to urinate, triggered by bladder pressure.

topics.title: Millikan Oil Drop Experiment
topics.description: The Millikan oil drop experiment measured the charge of an electron by balancing the gravitational and electric forces on charged oil droplets, showing that charge is quantized in units of the elementary charge.

topics.title: Mirror
topics.description: A smooth surface that reflects light at specific angles, forming an image of an object.

topics.title: Mirror Image
topics.description: A mirror image is the visual representation of an object formed by light reflecting off a smooth surface.

topics.title: Model
topics.description: A model is a simplified representation of a complex system or phenomenon, used to explain and predict behavior under specific conditions.

topics.title: Model vs. Theory
topics.description: A model is a simplified representation of a complex system used to explain observations, while a theory is a well-substantiated explanation of natural phenomena supported by extensive evidence.

topics.title: Moderate Dose
topics.description: A dose ranging from 0.1 Sv to 1 Sv (10 to 100 rem).

topics.title: Modern Physics
topics.description: Modern physics includes revolutionary theories like relativity and quantum mechanics, which describe phenomena outside the range of everyday experience, such as the very fast and the very small.

topics.title: Modern Relativity
topics.description: Modern relativity is a theory developed by Albert Einstein that revolutionized our understanding of the universe, particularly the relationship between space and time.

topics.title: Molar Mass
topics.description: Molar mass is the mass of one mole of a substance, typically expressed in grams per mole, and can be calculated using the periodic table.

topics.title: Mole
topics.description: The quantity of a substance whose mass (in grams) is equal to its molecular mass.

topics.title: Molecular Size
topics.description: Molecular size refers to the physical dimensions of a molecule, which can be determined through observations like Brownian motion.

topics.title: Molecular Transport Phenomena
topics.description: Molecular transport phenomena refer to the movement of particles through a medium due to diffusion, osmosis, or other similar processes.

topics.title: Moment of Inertia
topics.description: Moment of inertia is a measure of an object's resistance to changes in its rotational motion, depending on the mass distribution relative to the axis of rotation.

topics.title: Momentum
topics.description: Momentum is a property of a moving object that depends on its mass and velocity.

topics.title: Momentum as a Vector Quantity
topics.description: Momentum is a vector quantity that has the same direction as the velocity of the object.

topics.title: Momentum Change in Collisions
topics.description: In a collision between two objects, the change in momentum of one object is equal and opposite to the change in momentum of the other object.

topics.title: Momentum Components in Two Dimensions
topics.description: Momentum along the x and y axes is resolved using trigonometric components (cosine and sine).

topics.title: Momentum Conservation in Different Dimensions
topics.description: Momentum is conserved independently along each dimension (e.g., horizontal and vertical) in the absence of external forces in that direction.

topics.title: Momentum Conservation in Two-Dimensional Collisions
topics.description: In a two-dimensional collision, the total momentum along the x-axis before and after the collision remains the same.

topics.title: Momentum of a Photon
topics.description: The momentum of a photon, which is related to its wavelength by the equation p = h / lambda, where h is Planck's constant and lambda is the wavelength.

topics.title: Monochromatic
topics.description: Light of a single color or wavelength.

topics.title: Monochromator
topics.description: A device that separates incoming light into its component wavelengths and allows only a specific wavelength to pass through.

topics.title: Monochromator and Spectral Analysis in Microscopy
topics.description: Monochromators and spectral analyzers isolate specific wavelength bands of light to provide detailed chemical information about a sample through scattered light.

topics.title: Monochromators and Spectral Analysis in Microscopy
topics.description: Monochromators and spectral analyzers isolate specific wavelengths of light to provide detailed chemical information about a sample through scattered light analysis.

topics.title: More Applications of Magnetism
topics.description: Magnetism has various applications, including in motors, generators, and magnetic storage devices.

topics.title: Motion
topics.description: Displacement of an object as a function of time.

topics.title: Motional Emf
topics.description: Motional emf is the voltage induced in a conductor moving through a magnetic field, calculated as the product of the magnetic field, length of the conductor, velocity, and the sine of the angle between the velocity and the field.

topics.title: Motor
topics.description: A loop of wire in a magnetic field; when current is passed through the loops, the magnetic field exerts torque on the loops, which rotates a shaft.

topics.title: Motor Operation
topics.description: Motor operation involves the conversion of electrical energy into mechanical energy through the interaction of magnetic fields and current-carrying coils.

topics.title: Motors
topics.description: A motor is a device that converts electrical energy into mechanical energy using the interaction between magnetic fields and current-carrying conductors.

topics.title: Multiple Slit Diffraction
topics.description: The diffraction pattern produced by multiple slits results in sharper and more intense maxima compared to a double slit.

topics.title: Muon Family Number
topics.description: The number ±1 assigned to all members of the muon family, or the number 0 assigned to all particles not in the muon family.

topics.title: Muscle and Joint Complexities
topics.description: Real systems involving muscles, bones, and joints have complexities such as changing pivot points and varying mechanical advantages.

topics.title: Muscle Force Exertion
topics.description: Muscles exert forces to move body parts, often much greater than the external forces applied by limbs.

topics.title: Mutual Inductance
topics.description: Mutual inductance is the effect of Faraday’s law of induction where a change in current in one coil induces an emf in another nearby coil.

topics.title: Myelin Sheaths
topics.description: Myelin sheaths are insulating layers around some axons that increase the speed of nerve impulse transmission and reduce energy consumption.

topics.title: Myelin Sheaths and Signal Propagation
topics.description: Myelin sheaths are insulating layers around axons that increase the speed of signal propagation and reduce energy consumption by allowing the signal to jump between gaps called nodes of Ranvier.

topics.title: Myopia
topics.description: A visual defect where distant objects appear blurred because their images are focused in front of the retina.

topics.title: Natural Convection
topics.description: Natural convection is the transfer of heat caused by buoyant forces, where hot fluid rises and cold fluid sinks.

topics.title: Natural Frequency
topics.description: The frequency at which a system would oscillate if there were no driving and no damping forces.

topics.title: Neap Tides
topics.description: Tides that occur when the Sun is at a 90° angle to the Earth-Moon alignment, resulting in the lowest tides due to the opposing gravitational pulls.

topics.title: Near Point
topics.description: The closest point at which an object can be accurately focused on the retina with full accommodation.

topics.title: Nearsightedness
topics.description: A visual defect where distant objects appear blurred because their images are focused in front of the retina.

topics.title: Nearsightedness (Myopia)
topics.description: Nearsightedness is the inability to see distant objects clearly while close objects are clear, caused by the eye overconverging light rays from distant objects, making them focus in front of the retina.

topics.title: Negative Acceleration
topics.description: A component of acceleration in the negative direction of the component axis.

topics.title: Negative Exponential Formula
topics.description: A formula representing exponential decay, written as y = a^(-x), where a is a positive constant and x is the exponent.

topics.title: Negative of a Vector
topics.description: The negative of a vector is a vector with the same magnitude but opposite direction, which is used in vector subtraction.

topics.title: Negatively Curved Universe
topics.description: A negatively curved universe is an open universe that expands forever.

topics.title: Nerve Conduction
topics.description: Nerve conduction is the process by which electric signals are transmitted along a neuron through the movement of ions across the cell membrane.

topics.title: Net External Force
topics.description: Net external force is the vector sum of all external forces acting on a system, and for equilibrium, it must be zero.

topics.title: Net Force
topics.description: The net force is the vector sum of all external forces acting on a system.

topics.title: Net Force in Different Directions
topics.description: The net force in a particular direction is determined by the sum of forces in that direction, which can be zero if there is no acceleration in that direction.

topics.title: Net Heat Transfer by Radiation
topics.description: Net heat transfer by radiation is the difference between the energy absorbed and emitted by an object, which depends on the temperatures of the object and its surroundings.

topics.title: Net Rate of Heat Transfer by Radiation
topics.description: The rate of heat transfer by radiation calculated using the formula involving emissivity, surface area, and temperature difference.

topics.title: Net Work
topics.description: Work done by the net force, or vector sum of all the forces, acting on an object.

topics.title: Neutral Equilibrium
topics.description: A state of equilibrium that is independent of a system’s displacements from its original position.

topics.title: Neutralinos
topics.description: Neutralinos are a type of WIMPs with masses several orders of magnitude greater than nucleon masses.

topics.title: Neutrino
topics.description: An electrically neutral, weakly interacting elementary subatomic particle.

topics.title: Neutrino Mass
topics.description: Neutrino mass refers to the question of whether neutrinos, which were once thought to be massless, actually have a small but non-zero mass.

topics.title: Neutrino Oscillations
topics.description: Neutrino oscillations are the phenomenon where neutrinos change flavor (e.g., from electron to muon) as they travel, which can only occur if neutrinos have mass.

topics.title: Neutron
topics.description: A neutral particle that is found in a nucleus.

topics.title: Neutron Initiator
topics.description: A device that releases neutrons at the precise moment to initiate a nuclear chain reaction in a bomb.

topics.title: Neutron Stars
topics.description: Neutron stars are stars composed primarily of neutrons.

topics.title: Neutron-Induced Fission
topics.description: Neutron-induced fission is a process in which a neutron is absorbed by a nucleus, causing it to split into two fission fragments and release additional neutrons.

topics.title: Newton's First Law
topics.description: Newton's first law states that an object moves at constant velocity unless acted upon by a net external force.

topics.title: Newton's First Law of Motion
topics.description: A body at rest remains at rest, or, if in motion, remains in motion at a constant velocity unless acted on by a net external force.

topics.title: Newton’s First Law of Motion: Inertia
topics.description: An object at rest stays at rest, and an object in motion stays in motion with the same speed and direction unless acted upon by an unbalanced force.

topics.title: Newton's Law of Universal Gravitation
topics.description: A law stating that every object in the universe attracts every other object with a force proportional to the product of their masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them.

topics.title: Newton's Laws of Motion
topics.description: Newton's laws of motion are fundamental principles that describe the relationship between a body and the forces acting upon it, and the body's motion in response to those forces.

topics.title: Newton's Second Law
topics.description: The relationship between the net force acting on an object, its mass, and its acceleration, expressed as F_net = ma.

topics.title: Newton's Second Law Application
topics.description: Using Newton's second law (F_net = ma) to relate the net external force on a system to its acceleration, which is essential for solving dynamics problems.

topics.title: Newton’s Second Law in Multi-Directional Systems
topics.description: The principle that the net force acting on an object is equal to its mass multiplied by its acceleration, applicable in systems where forces act in multiple directions.

topics.title: Newton’s Second Law in Terms of Momentum
topics.description: Newton’s second law in terms of momentum states that the net external force on a system is equal to the rate of change of its momentum over time.

topics.title: Newton’s Second Law in Two Dimensions
topics.description: The application of Newton’s second law to systems where forces act in multiple directions, requiring resolution of forces into components along axes.

topics.title: Newton’s Second Law of Motion
topics.description: Newton's second law of motion states that the force acting on an object is equal to its mass multiplied by its acceleration.

topics.title: Newton’s Second Law of Motion in Terms of Momentum
topics.description: Newton’s second law states that the net external force on a system is equal to the change in momentum of the system divided by the time over which the change occurs.

topics.title: Newton’s Second Law of Motion: Concept of a System
topics.description: The acceleration of an object is directly proportional to the net force acting on it and inversely proportional to its mass, with the direction of the acceleration being in the direction of the net force.

topics.title: Newton’s Third Law of Motion
topics.description: For every action force, there is an equal and opposite reaction force.

topics.title: Newton’s Third Law of Motion: Symmetry in Forces
topics.description: For every action force, there is an equal and opposite reaction force.

topics.title: Newton’s Universal Law of Gravitation
topics.description: Newton’s universal law of gravitation states that every particle attracts every other particle with a force that is proportional to the product of their masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them.

topics.title: Node
topics.description: A point of zero displacement in a wave.

topics.title: Nodes
topics.description: Nodes are points in a standing wave where the displacement is always zero, meaning the wave does not move at these locations.

topics.title: Non-Conservative Forces
topics.description: Non-conservative forces are forces that remove mechanical energy from a system, typically converting it into thermal energy, and are responsible for damping in oscillatory systems.

topics.title: Non-Inertial Frame of Reference
topics.description: A non-inertial frame of reference is a frame of reference that is accelerating or rotating, where fictitious forces appear to act on objects.

topics.title: Non-Reflective Coatings
topics.description: Non-reflective coatings are thin films applied to surfaces to reduce unwanted reflections, commonly used in optics and photography.

topics.title: Non-Uniform Circular Motion
topics.description: Non-uniform circular motion is motion in a circle where the angular velocity changes, resulting in angular acceleration.

topics.title: Nonconservative Force
topics.description: A force whose work depends on the path followed between the given initial and final configurations.

topics.title: Nonlinear Phenomena
topics.description: Nonlinear phenomena are physical processes where the output is not directly proportional to the input, making their analysis and understanding more complex.

topics.title: Nonohmic Material
topics.description: A material that does not follow Ohm’s law.

topics.title: Nonrenewable Energy Sources
topics.description: Nonrenewable energy sources are those that cannot be replenished naturally within a human timescale, such as oil, natural gas, and coal.

topics.title: Normal Force
topics.description: The force that a surface applies to an object to support the weight of the object; acts perpendicular to the surface on which the object rests.

topics.title: Normal Force and Scale Reading
topics.description: The force exerted by a surface perpendicular to the object in contact, which can be measured by a scale as the apparent weight of an object.

topics.title: Normal, Tension, and Other Examples of Forces
topics.description: Normal force is the perpendicular force exerted by a surface on an object, and tension is the force transmitted through a rope or cable when pulled by forces acting on its ends.

topics.title: North Magnetic Pole
topics.description: The end or side of a magnet that is attracted toward Earth’s geographic north pole.

topics.title: North Pole
topics.description: The part of a magnet that orients itself toward the geographic North Pole of Earth.

topics.title: Note
topics.description: A basic unit of music with specific names, combined to generate tunes.

topics.title: Nuclear Decay
topics.description: Nuclear decay is the process by which an unstable nucleus transforms into a more stable nucleus, often emitting particles or energy.

topics.title: Nuclear Decay and Conservation Laws
topics.description: Nuclear decay is the process by which an unstable nucleus transforms into a more stable one, obeying conservation laws such as conservation of energy and momentum.

topics.title: Nuclear Density
topics.description: Nuclear density is the mass of the nucleus divided by its volume, which is extremely high due to the compact nature of the nucleus.

topics.title: Nuclear Energy
topics.description: Energy released by changes within atomic nuclei, such as the fusion of two light nuclei or the fission of a heavy nucleus.

topics.title: Nuclear Energy Production
topics.description: Nuclear energy production involves using nuclear reactions, such as fission, to generate power, as seen in fission power reactors.

topics.title: Nuclear Fission
topics.description: Nuclear fission is the process in which a heavy nucleus splits into two smaller nuclei, releasing energy.

topics.title: Nuclear Force
topics.description: Nuclear force is the strong attractive force that holds protons and neutrons together within the nucleus, overcoming the repulsive Coulomb force between protons.

topics.title: Nuclear Fusion
topics.description: Nuclear fusion is the process in which two light nuclei combine to form a heavier nucleus, releasing energy.

topics.title: Nuclear Imaging
topics.description: Nuclear imaging is a medical technique that uses radioactive substances to create images of the body's internal structures and functions.

topics.title: Nuclear Magnetic Resonance (NMR)
topics.description: A phenomenon in which an externally applied magnetic field interacts with the nuclei of certain atoms.

topics.title: Nuclear Medicine
topics.description: Nuclear medicine involves the use of radioactive substances for diagnosing and treating medical conditions, such as bone scans and radioiodine treatments.

topics.title: Nuclear Phenomena
topics.description: Nuclear phenomena refer to processes and effects that occur within the nucleus of an atom, such as energy production in the sun and the Earth's core remaining molten.

topics.title: Nuclear Physics
topics.description: Nuclear physics involves the study of the nuclei of atoms and the processes that occur within them, such as nuclear fission, which is the basis for nuclear power and weapons.

topics.title: Nuclear Proliferation
topics.description: The spread of nuclear weapons and technology to additional countries or non-state actors.

topics.title: Nuclear Radiation
topics.description: Rays that originate in the nuclei of atoms, the first examples of which were discovered by Becquerel.

topics.title: Nuclear Radioactivity
topics.description: Nuclear radioactivity is the spontaneous emission of radiation from the nucleus of an atom due to instability.

topics.title: Nuclear Reaction Energy
topics.description: The energy created in a nuclear reaction.

topics.title: Nuclear Reactor Accidents
topics.description: Nuclear reactor accidents are incidents that occur in nuclear power plants, which can have severe consequences for human health and the environment.

topics.title: Nuclear Structure
topics.description: Nuclear structure refers to the composition of a nucleus made up of protons and neutrons, which determines the stability and properties of elements.

topics.title: Nuclear Weapon Yield
topics.description: The amount of energy released by a nuclear weapon, typically measured in kilotons or megatons of TNT equivalent.

topics.title: Nuclear Weapons
topics.description: Weapons that derive their destructive power from nuclear reactions, either fission, fusion, or a combination.

topics.title: Nuclear Weapons and Their Destructive Potential
topics.description: Nuclear weapons are weapons of mass destruction that use nuclear reactions to release enormous amounts of energy, posing significant threats to human life and safety.

topics.title: Nucleon
topics.description: A nucleon is a proton or neutron found in the nucleus of an atom.

topics.title: Nucleon Composition
topics.description: Nucleons are protons and neutrons, which are composed of quarks and are part of the nucleus of an atom.

topics.title: Nucleons
topics.description: The particles found inside nuclei.

topics.title: Nucleus
topics.description: A region consisting of protons and neutrons at the center of an atom.

topics.title: Nuclide
topics.description: A type of atom whose nucleus has specific numbers of protons and neutrons.

topics.title: Null Measurement
topics.description: Null measurements are a method of measuring electrical quantities with high precision by balancing a circuit so that no current flows through the measuring device, thereby eliminating the effect of the device's resistance.

topics.title: Numerical Aperture
topics.description: The numerical aperture (NA) of a microscope objective lens is a measure of its light-gathering ability and resolution, calculated using the refractive index of the medium and the angle of acceptance of light rays.

topics.title: Numerical Aperture (NA)
topics.description: The numerical aperture of a microscope objective lens is a measure of its light-gathering ability, calculated using the refractive index of the medium and the angle of acceptance of light rays.

topics.title: Nutrient Loss
topics.description: Nutrient loss refers to the reduction in vitamins and other nutrients in food caused by high-level irradiation, similar to losses from freezing and cooking.

topics.title: Objective Lens
topics.description: The lens nearest to the object being examined in an optical instrument.

topics.title: Observation
topics.description: A step where a scientist observes a pattern or trend within the natural world.

topics.title: Observation in Science
topics.description: Observation is the process of gathering empirical evidence through direct or indirect means, which is essential for verifying scientific theories and understanding natural phenomena.

topics.title: Observer’s Measured Time
topics.description: Observer’s measured time is the time interval between two events as measured by an observer who is moving relative to the events.

topics.title: Ohm
topics.description: The unit of resistance, given by 1Ω = 1 V/A.

topics.title: Ohm’s Law
topics.description: An empirical relation stating that the current I is proportional to the potential difference V, often written as I = V/R, where R is the resistance.

topics.title: Ohm's Law for AC Circuits with Capacitors
topics.description: The relationship between rms voltage, rms current, and capacitive reactance in an AC circuit, given by I = V / X_C.

topics.title: Ohm's Law for AC Circuits with Inductors
topics.description: The relationship between rms voltage, rms current, and inductive reactance in an AC circuit, given by I = V / X_L.

topics.title: Ohmic
topics.description: A type of material for which Ohm's law is valid.

topics.title: Ohmic Material
topics.description: An ohmic material is one that obeys Ohm’s law, meaning its resistance remains constant regardless of the applied voltage or current.

topics.title: Ohmmeter
topics.description: An instrument that applies a voltage to a resistance, measures the current, calculates the resistance using Ohm’s law, and provides a readout of this calculated resistance.

topics.title: One-Dimensional Kinematics
topics.description: One-dimensional kinematics is the study of motion along a straight line, focusing on displacement, velocity, acceleration, and time.

topics.title: One-Dimensional Motion
topics.description: One-dimensional motion is the motion of an object along a straight line without any change in direction.

topics.title: One-Slit Destructive Interference
topics.description: Destructive interference in a single-slit experiment occurs when the ratio of the slit width to the distance from the slit to the screen is an integer multiple of the wavelength.

topics.title: One-Slit First-Order Destructive Interference
topics.description: The first-order destructive interference in a single-slit experiment occurs when the ratio of the slit width to the distance from the slit to the screen is equal to the wavelength.

topics.title: Open and Closed Universe
topics.description: An open universe is one that will expand forever and has negative curvature, while a closed universe is one that will eventually stop expanding and contract, having positive curvature.

topics.title: Open-Pipe Resonator
topics.description: An open-pipe resonator is a tube open at both ends that supports standing waves with resonant frequencies that are integer multiples of the fundamental frequency.

topics.title: Open-Tube Manometer
topics.description: An open-tube manometer is a type of manometer with one side open to the atmosphere, used to measure gauge pressure by comparing fluid levels in the tube.

topics.title: Operation of Meters
topics.description: Meters, such as analog fuel gauges, use the torque on a current-carrying loop in a magnetic field to measure current, with the deflection of a needle proportional to the current.

topics.title: Operation of Motors
topics.description: Motors operate by using the torque on a current-carrying loop in a magnetic field to rotate a shaft, converting electrical energy into mechanical work.

topics.title: Operational Definition of the Ampere
topics.description: The ampere is operationally defined as the current that produces a force of exactly 2 × 10⁻⁷ N/m between two parallel conductors separated by 1 meter in a vacuum, each carrying a current of 1 ampere.

topics.title: Optical Aberration
topics.description: An optical aberration is a distortion in an image caused by imperfections in lenses or mirrors.

topics.title: Optical Activity
topics.description: Optical activity is the property of certain materials to rotate the plane of polarization of light passing through them.

topics.title: Optically Active Substances
topics.description: Substances that rotate the plane of polarization of light passing through them.

topics.title: Optics
topics.description: Optics is the branch of physics that deals with the behavior of visible light and other electromagnetic waves, including their generation, propagation, and interaction with matter.

topics.title: Optics and Imaging
topics.description: Optics and imaging are fields that enable advancements in biosciences by allowing us to visualize and understand structures and processes at microscopic and molecular levels.

topics.title: Orbital Angular Momentum
topics.description: Orbital angular momentum is the angular momentum of an electron due to its motion around the nucleus, which is quantized in magnitude and direction.

topics.title: Orbital Magnetic Field
topics.description: The magnetic field generated due to the orbital motion of electrons.

topics.title: Orbital Motion and Gravitation
topics.description: The motion of celestial bodies in orbits is governed by the gravitational force between them, which provides the necessary centripetal force for circular or elliptical paths.

topics.title: Orbital Period
topics.description: The time it takes for an object to complete one full orbit around another object.

topics.title: Orbital Radius
topics.description: The average distance between the center of an orbiting object and the center of the object it is orbiting.

topics.title: Order
topics.description: The integer used in the equations for constructive and destructive interference for a double slit.

topics.title: Order of Interference
topics.description: The order of interference is an integer that specifies the number of wavelengths corresponding to the path length difference between two waves, determining the position of bright or dark fringes.

topics.title: Order of Magnitude
topics.description: Order of magnitude refers to the power of 10 when numbers are expressed in scientific notation, indicating the scale of a value.

topics.title: Oscillate
topics.description: Moving back and forth regularly between two points.

topics.title: Oscillations
topics.description: Oscillations are repetitive back-and-forth movements between two points.

topics.title: Oscillatory Motion
topics.description: Oscillatory motion is the repetitive movement of an object back and forth between two points.

topics.title: Osmosis
topics.description: Osmosis is the movement of water across a semipermeable membrane from an area of lower solute concentration to an area of higher solute concentration.

topics.title: Osmotic Pressure
topics.description: The back pressure which stops the osmotic process if one solution is pure water.

topics.title: Other Energy (OE)
topics.description: Other energy is a term used to represent all forms of energy not explicitly categorized as kinetic, potential, or work done by nonconservative forces, grouped together for simplicity in energy conservation equations.

topics.title: Otto Cycle
topics.description: The Otto cycle is a thermodynamic cycle used in four-stroke internal combustion engines, consisting of two adiabatic processes and two isochoric processes.

topics.title: Outgassing
topics.description: Outgassing is the process by which molecules dissolved in a material are released into the surrounding space.

topics.title: Output Work
topics.description: Output force multiplied by the distance over which it acts.

topics.title: Over Damping
topics.description: The condition in which damping of an oscillator causes it to return to equilibrium without oscillating; oscillator moves more slowly toward equilibrium than in the critically damped system.

topics.title: Overdamped System
topics.description: An overdamped system is one where the damping is so large that the system does not oscillate and instead returns to equilibrium slowly without overshooting.

topics.title: Overtone
topics.description: Multiples of the fundamental frequency of a sound.

topics.title: Overtones
topics.description: Overtones are the higher resonant frequencies of a system, which are multiples of the fundamental frequency and are also referred to as harmonics.

topics.title: Pair Production
topics.description: Pair production is the process in which a photon creates an electron and a positron, demonstrating the existence of antimatter.

topics.title: Pair Production Near Black Holes
topics.description: Pair production near black holes involves the creation of particle-antiparticle pairs in the strong gravitational field, with one particle escaping and the other falling into the black hole.

topics.title: Parallel
topics.description: The wiring of resistors or other components in an electrical circuit such that each component receives an equal voltage from the power source.

topics.title: Parallel Circuits
topics.description: In a parallel circuit, components are connected across the same two points, providing multiple independent paths for current to flow.

topics.title: Parallel Component of Weight on an Inclined Plane
topics.description: The component of an object's weight acting parallel to an inclined plane, calculated as the product of the object's weight and the sine of the angle of inclination.

topics.title: Parallel Connection of Voltage Sources
topics.description: In a parallel connection of voltage sources, their total internal resistance decreases, allowing for a larger current to be delivered.

topics.title: Parallel Plate Capacitor
topics.description: A capacitor consisting of two parallel conducting plates separated by a distance, with an insulator between them.

topics.title: Parallel Resistors
topics.description: Resistors are connected in parallel when both ends of each resistor are connected directly together, allowing the same voltage across each resistor.

topics.title: Parallel-Plate Capacitor
topics.description: A parallel-plate capacitor is a device consisting of two conducting plates separated by a dielectric, with capacitance dependent on the area of the plates, the distance between them, and the dielectric constant.

topics.title: Parent
topics.description: The original state of a nucleus before decay.

topics.title: Parent and Daughter Nucleus
topics.description: A parent nucleus is the original unstable nucleus that undergoes decay, while a daughter nucleus is the resulting stable or less stable nucleus produced by the decay.

topics.title: Partial Pressure
topics.description: The pressure that a single gas in a mixture would exert if it occupied the entire volume of the container alone.

topics.title: Particle Accelerator
topics.description: A particle accelerator is a device that uses electromagnetic fields to propel charged particles to high speeds and high energies.

topics.title: Particle Colliders
topics.description: Particle colliders are devices that accelerate subatomic particles to very high speeds and collide them to study their properties and interactions, such as the Large Hadron Collider.

topics.title: Particle Creation from Energy
topics.description: The process by which particles are created from energy, as demonstrated in particle accelerators.

topics.title: Particle Physics
topics.description: Particle physics is the study of substructures of atoms and nuclei, focusing on fundamental particles and their interactions.

topics.title: Particle-Wave Duality
topics.description: The concept that all particles, whether massless like photons or having mass like electrons, exhibit both particle and wave properties.

topics.title: Particle-Wave Duality of Light
topics.description: The particle-wave duality of light means that light exhibits both wave-like properties (such as interference and diffraction) and particle-like properties (such as having discrete energy and momentum).

topics.title: Pascal (Unit of Pressure)
topics.description: The pascal is the SI unit of pressure, defined as one newton per square meter.

topics.title: Pascal’s Principle
topics.description: A change in pressure applied to an enclosed fluid is transmitted undiminished to all portions of the fluid and to the walls of its container.

topics.title: Path Independence of Gravitational Potential Energy
topics.description: The change in gravitational potential energy between two points depends only on the initial and final positions, not on the path taken between them.

topics.title: Path Independence of Internal Energy
topics.description: The change in internal energy of a system is independent of the path taken, meaning it depends only on the initial and final states of the system.

topics.title: Path Length Difference
topics.description: Path length difference is the difference in distance traveled by two waves from their sources to a common point, which determines the type of interference.

topics.title: Path Length Difference in Single Slit Diffraction
topics.description: The difference in distance traveled by light waves from different parts of a single slit, which determines whether they interfere constructively or destructively.

topics.title: Path-Length Difference
topics.description: Path-length difference is the difference in distance traveled by two waves, which determines whether they interfere constructively or destructively.

topics.title: Patterns in Spectra Reveal More Quantization
topics.description: Patterns in atomic spectra indicate that energy levels in atoms are quantized, leading to specific wavelengths of emitted or absorbed light.

topics.title: Pauli Exclusion Principle
topics.description: A principle stating that no two electrons can have the same set of quantum numbers, meaning no two electrons can be in the same state.

topics.title: Peak Current
topics.description: Peak current is the maximum current reached by an AC source during one cycle.

topics.title: Peak emf
topics.description: The maximum emf generated in a generator coil, given by emf_0 = NABω.

topics.title: Peak emf in a generator
topics.description: The maximum value of the induced emf in a generator, which occurs when the coil is positioned to produce the highest voltage.

topics.title: Peak Voltage
topics.description: Peak voltage is the maximum value of the voltage in an AC circuit, typically occurring at the peak of the sinusoidal waveform.

topics.title: Penetrating Radiation
topics.description: Penetrating radiation refers to ionizing radiation with high energy per particle, capable of passing through materials and causing ionization in food.

topics.title: Percent Uncertainty
topics.description: Percent uncertainty is the ratio of the uncertainty in a measurement to the measured value, expressed as a percentage.

topics.title: Percussion Point
topics.description: The percussion point is the location on an object where it can be struck without exerting a force on the pivot point, resulting in minimal vibration or reaction force.

topics.title: Perfectly Inelastic Collision
topics.description: A perfectly inelastic collision is a collision in which the colliding objects stick together and move with a common velocity after the collision.

topics.title: Perihelion
topics.description: Perihelion is the point in a planet's orbit where it is closest to the sun.

topics.title: Period
topics.description: The time it takes to complete one oscillation.

topics.title: Period of a Simple Pendulum
topics.description: The time it takes for a simple pendulum to complete one full oscillation, which depends on its length and the acceleration due to gravity.

topics.title: Period of a Wave
topics.description: The time it takes for one complete cycle of a wave to pass a given point.

topics.title: Period of Simple Harmonic Motion
topics.description: The period of simple harmonic motion is the time it takes to complete one full cycle and is given by T = 2π√(m/k), where m is the mass and k is the spring constant.

topics.title: Periodic Motion
topics.description: Motion that repeats itself at regular time intervals.

topics.title: Periodic Wave
topics.description: A periodic wave is a wave that repeats the same oscillation for several cycles, such as the continuous waves in a wave pool.

topics.title: Peripheral Vision and Detail
topics.description: Peripheral images lack detail and color because the fovea, which has the highest concentration of light receptors, is located at the center of the visual field.

topics.title: Permanent Magnet
topics.description: A material that retains its magnetic behavior for a long time, even when exposed to demagnetizing influences.

topics.title: Permeability of Free Space
topics.description: The measure of the ability of a material, in this case free space, to support a magnetic field.

topics.title: Perpendicular Component of Weight on an Inclined Plane
topics.description: The component of an object's weight acting perpendicular to an inclined plane, calculated as the product of the object's weight and the cosine of the angle of inclination.

topics.title: Perpendicular Lever Arm
topics.description: The perpendicular lever arm is the distance from the pivot point to the point where the force is applied, measured perpendicularly to the line of action of the force.

topics.title: Perpendicularity of Electric and Magnetic Fields
topics.description: In an electromagnetic wave, the electric and magnetic fields are perpendicular to each other and to the direction of wave propagation.

topics.title: Phase Angle
topics.description: The angle by which the voltage and current are out of phase in an AC circuit, denoted by φ.

topics.title: Phase Angle in an RLC Circuit
topics.description: The phase angle is the angle by which the voltage leads or lags the current in an RLC series circuit, determined by the relative values of resistance, inductive reactance, and capacitive reactance.

topics.title: Phase Angle in Capacitive Circuits
topics.description: The angle by which voltage lags current in a capacitive circuit, which is 90°.

topics.title: Phase Angle in Inductive Circuits
topics.description: The angle by which voltage leads current in an inductive circuit, which is 90°.

topics.title: Phase Change
topics.description: A phase change is a process where a substance transitions between solid, liquid, or gas states without a change in temperature.

topics.title: Phase Change and Convection
topics.description: Phase change and convection together allow for cooling through evaporation, even when the surrounding air temperature is higher than body temperature.

topics.title: Phase Change and Latent Heat
topics.description: Phase change and latent heat involve the energy required to change the state of a substance without changing its temperature.

topics.title: Phase Change Upon Reflection
topics.description: A phase change of 180° (or λ/2) occurs when light reflects from a medium with a higher index of refraction than the medium it is traveling in.

topics.title: Phase Diagram
topics.description: A graph that shows the states of a substance (solid, liquid, gas) based on temperature and pressure.

topics.title: Phase Relationship in Resistive Circuits
topics.description: The voltage and current in a resistive circuit are in phase, meaning they reach their maximum values at the same time.

topics.title: Phase Relationship of Electric and Magnetic Fields
topics.description: The electric and magnetic fields in an electromagnetic wave are in phase, meaning they reach their maximum and minimum values at the same time.

topics.title: Phase-Contrast Microscope
topics.description: A microscope that utilizes wave interference and differences in phases to enhance contrast.

topics.title: Phase-Contrast Microscopy
topics.description: Phase-contrast microscopy enhances contrast by using a phase plate to create phase differences between light passing through the object and background, resulting in interference.

topics.title: Phon
topics.description: A phon is a unit used to express loudness numerically, representing the perception of sound intensity at different frequencies.

topics.title: Phosphorescence
topics.description: The de-excitation of a metastable state.

topics.title: Photoconductor
topics.description: A substance that is an insulator until it is exposed to light, when it becomes a conductor.

topics.title: Photoelectric Effect
topics.description: The photoelectric effect is the phenomenon where light (or other electromagnetic radiation) ejects electrons from a material.

topics.title: Photoelectron
topics.description: A photoelectron is an electron that has been ejected from a material by a photon of light.

topics.title: Photomultiplier
topics.description: A device that converts light into electrical signals.

topics.title: Photomultiplier Tube
topics.description: A photomultiplier tube is a device that converts light from a scintillator into an electrical signal using the photoelectric effect, amplifying the signal for detection.

topics.title: Photon
topics.description: A quantum, or particle, of electromagnetic radiation.

topics.title: Photon Behavior
topics.description: Photons are massless particles that exhibit both wave-like properties (such as interference and diffraction) and particle-like properties (such as discrete energy and momentum).

topics.title: Photon Emission and Absorption
topics.description: Photon emission and absorption are processes by which electrons in an atom transition between energy levels, releasing or absorbing energy in the form of photons.

topics.title: Photon Energies
topics.description: Photon energies are the energies carried by photons, which depend on their frequency and are related to the electromagnetic spectrum.

topics.title: Photon Energy
topics.description: Photon energy is the energy of a single quantum of electromagnetic radiation, which is proportional to its frequency and given by the equation E = hf, where h is Planck’s constant and f is the frequency.

topics.title: Photon Energy and Bremsstrahlung Radiation
topics.description: Bremsstrahlung radiation is a type of electromagnetic radiation produced when charged particles, such as electrons, are decelerated by a target material.

topics.title: Photon Energy and Characteristic X-rays
topics.description: Characteristic x-rays are emitted when electrons transition between energy levels in atoms, producing discrete spectral lines unique to the material.

topics.title: Photon Energy and Electron Transitions
topics.description: Photon energy is the energy difference between two electron energy levels in an atom, and it is emitted or absorbed when an electron transitions between these levels.

topics.title: Photon Energy and Frequency Relationship
topics.description: The energy of a photon is directly proportional to its frequency, given by the equation E = hf, where E is energy, h is Planck’s constant, and f is frequency.

topics.title: Photon Energy and Infrared Radiation
topics.description: Infrared radiation has lower photon energies than visible light and is associated with molecular vibrations and rotational transitions.

topics.title: Photon Energy and Ionization
topics.description: Photons with sufficient energy can ionize atoms or molecules, which is a key property of high-energy electromagnetic radiation such as gamma rays, x-rays, and ultraviolet light.

topics.title: Photon Energy and Medical Imaging
topics.description: High-energy photons, such as gamma rays and x-rays, are used in medical imaging due to their ability to penetrate materials and produce detailed images of internal structures.

topics.title: Photon Energy and Microwave Radiation
topics.description: Microwave radiation has even lower photon energies than infrared radiation and is associated with rotational transitions in molecules.

topics.title: Photon Energy and Momentum Relationship
topics.description: The energy of a photon is directly related to its momentum through the equation p = E / c, where c is the speed of light.

topics.title: Photon Energy and Power Calculation
topics.description: The number of photons emitted per second by a monochromatic source can be calculated by dividing the power of the source by the energy of a single photon.

topics.title: Photon Energy and Submicroscopic Effects
topics.description: Photon energy is crucial in submicroscopic interactions, such as molecular vibrations, electronic transitions, and ionization, where energy levels are quantized.

topics.title: Photon Energy and the Electromagnetic Spectrum
topics.description: Photon energy varies across the electromagnetic spectrum, with higher energy photons corresponding to shorter wavelengths and higher frequencies.

topics.title: Photon Energy and Visible Light
topics.description: Visible light photons have energies that correspond to transitions between outer electron shells in atoms, typically ranging from about 1.63 eV to 3.26 eV.

topics.title: Photon Energy and Wavelength Relationship
topics.description: The energy of a photon is inversely proportional to its wavelength, given by the equation E = hc/λ, where E is energy, h is Planck’s constant, c is the speed of light, and λ is wavelength.

topics.title: Photon Energy and X-ray Production
topics.description: X-rays are produced when high-energy electrons collide with a target material, converting their kinetic energy into electromagnetic radiation, primarily in the form of x-ray photons.

topics.title: Photon Energy Calculation
topics.description: The process of calculating the energy of a photon emitted or absorbed by an atom based on the difference in energy levels of the atom.

topics.title: Photon Energy in Electron Volts
topics.description: Photon energy can be conveniently expressed in electron volts (eV), where 1 eV is the energy gained by an electron accelerated through a potential difference of 1 volt.

topics.title: Photon Momentum
topics.description: Photon momentum is the momentum carried by a photon, calculated using the equation p = h / λ, where h is Planck's constant and λ is the photon's wavelength.

topics.title: Photon Momentum Conservation
topics.description: Photon momentum is conserved in processes involving the emission, absorption, or reflection of photons, similar to the conservation of momentum in classical physics.

topics.title: Photoreceptors
topics.description: Photoreceptors are light-sensitive cells in the retina that detect light and are responsible for vision.

topics.title: Photoreceptors (Rods and Cones)
topics.description: Photoreceptors are light-sensing cells in the retina; rods are responsible for low-light vision and peripheral vision, while cones are responsible for color vision and high-resolution vision.

topics.title: Physical Characteristics of Gases
topics.description: Gases have neither a definite shape nor a specific volume because their atoms are separated by large distances and move freely.

topics.title: Physical Characteristics of Liquids
topics.description: Liquids have a definite volume but no definite shape because their atoms can slide past one another and change neighbors.

topics.title: Physical Characteristics of Solids
topics.description: Solids have a definite shape and a specific volume because their atoms are in close contact and vibrate but do not move freely.

topics.title: Physical Law
topics.description: A physical law is a concise, generalized description of a pattern in nature that is supported by scientific evidence and repeated experiments.

topics.title: Physical Quantities
topics.description: Physical quantities are measurable properties of objects or phenomena, such as length, mass, and time.

topics.title: Physical Quantities and Units
topics.description: Physical quantities are measurable properties of objects or phenomena, and units are standardized quantities used to express these measurements.

topics.title: Physical Quantity
topics.description: A characteristic or property of an object that can be measured or calculated from other measurements.

topics.title: Physics
topics.description: The science concerned with describing the interactions of energy, matter, space, and time; it is especially interested in what fundamental mechanisms underlie every phenomenon.

topics.title: Physics Applications
topics.description: Physics applications refer to the use of physics principles in other fields of study.

topics.title: Physics of the Eye
topics.description: The physics of the eye involves understanding how light is focused on the retina to form images.

topics.title: Physics: An Introduction
topics.description: Physics is the study of matter, energy, and their interactions to understand the fundamental principles governing the natural world.

topics.title: Physics: Definitions and Applications
topics.description: Physics is the branch of science that studies the fundamental principles of energy, matter, and their interactions in the universe.

topics.title: Pion
topics.description: A particle exchanged between nucleons, transmitting the force between them.

topics.title: Pit
topics.description: A tiny indentation on the spiral track moulded into the top of the polycarbonate layer of CD.

topics.title: Pitch
topics.description: The perception of the frequency of a sound.

topics.title: Pivotal Point
topics.description: A pivotal point is a fixed point around which an object rotates, such as a nail holding a stick in place.

topics.title: Planck Epoch
topics.description: The earliest period of the universe, characterized by extremely high energy and temperature, where all four fundamental forces are thought to have been unified.

topics.title: Planck’s Constant
topics.description: A fundamental physical constant, denoted by 'h', that relates the energy of a photon to its frequency, with a value of approximately 6.626 × 10^-34 J·s.

topics.title: Planetary Model of the Atom
topics.description: The planetary model of the atom describes electrons orbiting the nucleus in fixed, quantized paths, similar to planets orbiting the sun.

topics.title: Plasma
topics.description: An ionized gas that is a combination of the negatively charged free electrons and positively charged ions.

topics.title: Plutonium-239
topics.description: A fissile isotope of plutonium used in nuclear weapons due to its ability to undergo fission with neutrons.

topics.title: Point Charge
topics.description: A charged particle, designated [EQUATION: Q], generating an electric field.

topics.title: Point Masses
topics.description: Structureless particles that cannot rotate or spin, used to simplify collision analysis.

topics.title: Poiseuille’s Law
topics.description: Poiseuille’s Law describes the relationship between the flow rate of a fluid through a tube, the pressure difference, the radius of the tube, and the viscosity of the fluid.

topics.title: Poiseuille’s Law for Resistance
topics.description: The resistance to laminar flow of an incompressible fluid in a tube: R = 8ηl/πr4.

topics.title: Polar Molecule
topics.description: A molecule with an asymmetrical distribution of positive and negative charge.

topics.title: Polarization
topics.description: Polarization is the separation of charges within an object that remains neutral, typically caused by the presence of a nearby charged object.

topics.title: Polarization Microscope
topics.description: A microscope that enhances contrast by utilizing a wave characteristic of light, useful for objects that are optically active.

topics.title: Polarization Microscopy
topics.description: Polarization microscopes enhance contrast by using polarized light and a polarizing filter to observe optically active or birefringent materials.

topics.title: Polarization of Conductors
topics.description: A conductor placed in an electric field becomes polarized, with charges redistributing to neutralize the field inside the conductor.

topics.title: Polarized
topics.description: A state in which the positive and negative charges within an object have collected in separate locations.

topics.title: Polarized Light
topics.description: Light whose electric field component vibrates in a specific plane.

topics.title: Polarized Waves
topics.description: Waves having the electric and magnetic field oscillations in a definite direction.

topics.title: Polarizing Filter
topics.description: A polarizing filter is a device that absorbs light waves vibrating in certain directions and transmits those vibrating in others.

topics.title: Population Inversion
topics.description: Population inversion is a condition where a majority of atoms are in a metastable state, which is necessary for laser emission.

topics.title: Position
topics.description: The location of an object relative to a specific reference frame at a particular time.

topics.title: Position Equation for Simple Harmonic Motion
topics.description: The position of an object in simple harmonic motion can be described by the equation x(t) = X cos(ωt), where X is the amplitude, ω is the angular frequency, and t is time.

topics.title: Position vs. Time Graphs
topics.description: A graph that plots position on the vertical axis and time on the horizontal axis, showing how an object's position changes over time.

topics.title: Positive and Negative Electric Charges
topics.description: Positive and negative electric charges are two types of electric charge that cause objects to attract or repel each other, with like charges repelling and unlike charges attracting.

topics.title: Positive Charge
topics.description: Positive charge is a deficiency of electrons in an object, resulting in an imbalance of electrical charge.

topics.title: Positive Exponential Formula
topics.description: A formula representing exponential growth, written as y = a^x, where a is a positive constant and x is the exponent.

topics.title: Positive Feedback in Convection
topics.description: Positive feedback in convection is a mechanism where the process reinforces itself, such as in the formation of thunderheads, where condensation releases heat that further drives convection.

topics.title: Positive Feedback Mechanism
topics.description: A positive feedback mechanism is a process that reinforces and accelerates itself, such as the formation of thunderheads driven by convection and phase change.

topics.title: Positive, Negative, and Zero Work
topics.description: Positive work is done when the force and displacement are in the same direction, negative work is done when they are in opposite directions, and zero work is done when the force is perpendicular to the displacement.

topics.title: Positively Curved Universe
topics.description: A positively curved universe is a closed universe that eventually contracts.

topics.title: Positron
topics.description: The particle that results from positive beta decay; also known as an antielectron.

topics.title: Positron Decay
topics.description: A type of beta decay in which a proton is converted to a neutron, releasing a positron and a neutrino.

topics.title: Positron Emission Tomography (PET)
topics.description: PET is a medical imaging technique that uses positron-emitting isotopes to produce detailed images of the body's internal structures and functions by detecting gamma rays from electron-positron annihilation.

topics.title: Postulate
topics.description: A postulate is a statement that is assumed to be true for the purposes of reasoning in a scientific or mathematical argument.

topics.title: Postulate of Special Relativity
topics.description: A fundamental assumption in special relativity that the speed of light is the same in all inertial reference frames and is not affected by the speed of its source.

topics.title: Postulates of Special Relativity
topics.description: The two fundamental principles that form the basis of Einstein's theory of special relativity, stating that the laws of physics are the same for all inertial frames and the speed of light is constant in all inertial frames.

topics.title: Potential Barrier
topics.description: A potential barrier is a region in space where the potential energy is higher than the energy of a particle, preventing it from classically passing through, but allowing quantum tunneling.

topics.title: Potential Change Across a Resistor
topics.description: When traversing a resistor in the same direction as the current, the potential change is negative; when traversing in the opposite direction, the potential change is positive.

topics.title: Potential Change Across a Voltage Source
topics.description: When traversing a voltage source from negative to positive (same direction as the emf), the potential change is positive; when traversing from positive to negative, the potential change is negative.

topics.title: Potential Difference
topics.description: The difference in electric potential energy per unit charge between two points.

topics.title: Potential Difference (or Voltage)
topics.description: The change in potential energy of a charge moved from one point to another, divided by the charge; units of potential difference are joules per coulomb, known as volt.

topics.title: Potential Energy
topics.description: Potential energy is the energy an object possesses due to its position or configuration.

topics.title: Potential Energy of a Spring
topics.description: The stored energy of a spring as a function of its displacement; when Hooke’s law applies, it is given by the expression one half kx² where x is the distance the spring is compressed or extended and k is the spring constant.

topics.title: Potentiometer
topics.description: A potentiometer is a null measurement device that measures voltage by adjusting a contact point along a resistive wire until a galvanometer reads zero, indicating no current flow through the device.

topics.title: Power
topics.description: Power is the rate at which work is done or energy is transferred.

topics.title: Power and Energy Relationship
topics.description: Power is the rate at which energy is transferred, and it is related to energy through the equation P = E/t.

topics.title: Power and Focal Length
topics.description: The power of a lens or mirror is the reciprocal of its focal length, measured in diopters.

topics.title: Power Dissipation
topics.description: Power dissipation is the conversion of electrical energy into heat energy due to the resistance in a circuit, calculated as P = I²R.

topics.title: Power Dissipation in Motors
topics.description: Power dissipation in motors refers to the energy lost as heat due to the resistance of the motor coils when current flows through them.

topics.title: Power Dissipation in Resistors
topics.description: Power dissipation in resistors refers to the energy converted into heat by a resistor, calculated using the formulas P = IV, P = V²/R, or P = I²R.

topics.title: Power Factor
topics.description: The ratio of actual power to the theoretical maximum power in a circuit due to voltage and current being out of phase, calculated by cosφ.

topics.title: Power Factor in an RLC Circuit
topics.description: Power factor is the ratio of real power to apparent power in an RLC circuit, representing how effectively electrical power is converted into useful work.

topics.title: Power Fluctuation in AC Circuits
topics.description: Power fluctuation in AC circuits refers to the variation of power over time, which is a function of the product of instantaneous voltage and current.

topics.title: Power in Circuits
topics.description: Electric power in circuits can be calculated using the formulas P = IV, P = V²/R, and P = I²R, which relate power to voltage, current, and resistance.

topics.title: Power in Fluid Flow
topics.description: Power in fluid flow is the rate at which energy is transferred by a fluid, calculated by multiplying the total energy per unit volume (from Bernoulli’s equation) by the flow rate.

topics.title: Power in Watts
topics.description: The SI unit for power is the watt, where 1 watt equals 1 joule per second.

topics.title: Power of a Lens
topics.description: The power of a lens is the inverse of its focal length and is measured in diopters (D).

topics.title: Power Transmission and Voltage Regulation
topics.description: Power is transmitted over long distances at high voltages to reduce current and minimize energy loss due to Joule heating in transmission lines.

topics.title: Precession of a Gyroscope
topics.description: Precession is the circular motion of the axis of a spinning gyroscope caused by an external torque, which changes the direction of the angular momentum vector without altering its magnitude.

topics.title: Precision
topics.description: Precision refers to how close repeated measurements are to each other under the same conditions.

topics.title: Presbyopia
topics.description: A condition where the eye's lens becomes less able to focus on close objects over time.

topics.title: Pressure
topics.description: Pressure is the force applied perpendicular to the surface of an object divided by the area over which the force is distributed.

topics.title: Pressure Amplitude
topics.description: The maximum variation in pressure of a sound wave, measured in pascals (Pa).

topics.title: Pressure and Velocity Relationship
topics.description: The pressure in a fluid decreases as the velocity of the fluid increases, as described by Bernoulli’s principle.

topics.title: Pressure Due to Fluid Weight
topics.description: The pressure exerted by a fluid at a certain depth is caused by the weight of the fluid above that depth.

topics.title: Pressure in a Fluid
topics.description: Pressure in a fluid is defined as the force per unit area exerted by the fluid, which can result from the weight of the fluid above.

topics.title: Pressure in the Chest Cavity
topics.description: The pressure within the chest cavity, which can be negative and helps maintain the attachment of the lungs to the chest wall.

topics.title: Pressure in the Digestive Tract
topics.description: The pressure variations within the digestive system that aid in the movement of food and waste, influenced by muscle actions and fluid dynamics.

topics.title: Pressure in the Human Body
topics.description: The force per unit area exerted by fluids or gases within the body, which can vary across different organs and systems.

topics.title: Pressure in the Lungs
topics.description: The pressure within the lungs that changes during inhalation and exhalation, with negative gauge pressure during inhalation and positive gauge pressure during exhalation.
