topics.title: Pressure in the Spinal Column
topics.description: The pressure exerted by cerebrospinal fluid surrounding the brain and spinal cord, which helps support and protect these structures.

topics.title: Pressure Variation in Sound Waves
topics.description: Pressure variation in sound waves refers to the changes in pressure within a medium, such as air, that propagate as compressions and rarefactions.

topics.title: Pressure-Volume Work
topics.description: Pressure-volume work is the work done by a gas when it expands or contracts against a constant external pressure.

topics.title: Pressures in the Body
topics.description: Pressures in the body refer to the various pressures exerted by fluids within the circulatory and respiratory systems.

topics.title: Pressure–Volume Work
topics.description: Pressure–volume work is the work done by or on a system due to a change in volume at constant pressure, calculated as W = PΔV.

topics.title: Principal Quantum Number
topics.description: The principal quantum number (n) labels the basic energy states of a system and can take positive integer values starting from 1.

topics.title: Principle
topics.description: A principle is a fundamental rule or truth that guides understanding in a specific context.

topics.title: Principle of a Cyclotron
topics.description: A cyclotron uses a magnetic field to cause particles to move in circular orbits and a fixed-frequency alternating electric field to accelerate them.

topics.title: Principle of a Synchrotron
topics.description: A synchrotron uses a ring of magnets and accelerating tubes to guide particles in fixed-radius orbits, with the frequency of the accelerating voltage and magnetic field strength increased as the particles gain energy.

topics.title: Principle vs. Law
topics.description: A principle is a general rule or guideline, while a law is a fundamental, well-established rule that describes a consistent pattern in nature.

topics.title: Prism and Dispersion
topics.description: A prism disperses white light into its component colors due to the variation in the index of refraction with wavelength, producing a sequence of colors from red to violet.

topics.title: Probability Cloud Model
topics.description: The probability cloud model describes the electron's position in an atom as a region of probability, rather than a fixed orbit, due to the wave nature of matter.

topics.title: Probability Distribution
topics.description: The overall spatial distribution of probabilities to find a particle at a given location.

topics.title: Problem-Solving Steps for One-Dimensional Kinematics
topics.description: A structured approach to solving physics problems involving motion in one dimension, including identifying knowns, unknowns, and applying relevant equations.

topics.title: Problem-Solving Strategies
topics.description: A systematic approach to solving physics problems, including identifying knowns and unknowns, selecting appropriate equations, and checking units and significant figures.

topics.title: Problem-Solving Strategies in Statics
topics.description: A systematic approach to solving statics problems, including identifying equilibrium conditions, drawing free body diagrams, applying equilibrium equations, and verifying solutions.

topics.title: Problem-Solving Strategy for Forces
topics.description: A structured approach to solving physics problems involving forces, including identifying principles, drawing free-body diagrams, and applying Newton's laws.

topics.title: Problem-Solving Strategy for Integrated Concepts
topics.description: A systematic approach to solving physics problems that involve multiple concepts, such as kinematics and dynamics, by identifying principles and applying known strategies.

topics.title: Production of Electromagnetic Waves
topics.description: Electromagnetic waves are produced by various mechanisms, including accelerating charges, thermal agitation, and electronic transitions in atoms and molecules.

topics.title: Projectile
topics.description: An object that travels through the air and experiences only acceleration due to gravity.

topics.title: Projectile Components
topics.description: Projectile components refer to the horizontal and vertical parts of a projectile's velocity and displacement, which are analyzed separately in projectile motion.

topics.title: Projectile Motion
topics.description: The motion of an object that is projected into the air and moves under the influence of gravity alone, typically following a curved path.

topics.title: Projection of Uniform Circular Motion
topics.description: The projection of a point undergoing uniform circular motion onto a straight line results in simple harmonic motion.

topics.title: Propagation of Electromagnetic Waves
topics.description: Electromagnetic waves can travel through a vacuum and do not require a medium to propagate.

topics.title: Propagation of Waves
topics.description: The propagation of waves refers to the movement of waves through a medium or space, carrying energy from one location to another.

topics.title: Proper Length
topics.description: The length of an object within its own frame of reference, as opposed to the length observed by an observer moving relative to that frame of reference.

topics.title: Proper Time
topics.description: Proper time is the time measured by an observer at rest relative to the event being observed.

topics.title: Proportionality
topics.description: Proportionality describes the relationship between two quantities where one quantity changes in a consistent ratio to another, such as force being directly proportional to acceleration.

topics.title: Prosthesis
topics.description: A prosthesis is an artificial device used to replace or support a missing or damaged body part, such as a joint in the case of a hip replacement.

topics.title: Protection by Metal Car During Lightning
topics.description: A metal car protects passengers inside from dangerous electric fields caused by a downed line touching the car, as the car acts as a Faraday cage.

topics.title: Proton
topics.description: A particle in the nucleus of an atom and carrying a positive charge equal in magnitude and opposite in sign to the amount of negative charge carried by an electron.

topics.title: Proton Decay
topics.description: A predicted phenomenon in some Grand Unified Theories where protons, typically stable, decay over an extremely long timescale, which can be tested experimentally.

topics.title: Proton Stability
topics.description: Proton stability refers to the question of whether protons are truly stable or if they have a very long lifetime, which is related to the unification of fundamental forces.

topics.title: Proton-Proton Chain
topics.description: The proton-proton chain is a series of nuclear reactions that convert hydrogen into helium, releasing energy in the process.

topics.title: Proton-Proton Cycle
topics.description: The proton-proton cycle is a sequence of fusion reactions that converts hydrogen into helium, releasing energy, and is the primary energy-producing process in stars like the Sun.

topics.title: Protons
topics.description: The positively charged nucleons found in a nucleus.

topics.title: Ptolemaic Model
topics.description: A geocentric model of the universe where Earth is at the center and celestial bodies move in complex circular paths.

topics.title: Pulley
topics.description: A pulley is a simple machine consisting of a wheel with a grooved rim, used to change the direction of a force or provide mechanical advantage when multiple pulleys are used together.

topics.title: Pulse Wave
topics.description: A pulse wave is a sudden disturbance that generates only one or a few waves, such as when a pebble is dropped into water.

topics.title: Pure Rotational Motion
topics.description: Pure rotational motion occurs when all points in an object move in circular paths centered on a single point.

topics.title: Pure Translational Motion
topics.description: Pure translational motion is motion where an object moves without any rotation.

topics.title: PV Diagram
topics.description: A graph of pressure vs. volume.

topics.title: Pythagorean Theorem in Two-Dimensional Motion
topics.description: The Pythagorean theorem is used to calculate the straight-line distance (hypotenuse) in a right triangle formed by horizontal and vertical components of motion.

topics.title: Quadratic Formula
topics.description: A formula used to solve quadratic equations of the form ax² + bx + c = 0, given by x = (-b ± √(b² - 4ac)) / (2a).

topics.title: Quadratic Relationship
topics.description: A quadratic relationship is a type of relationship between two variables where one variable is squared, often represented by a parabolic curve on a graph.

topics.title: Quality Factor
topics.description: A measure of the relative biological effectiveness of ionizing radiation.

topics.title: Quantization of Angular Momentum
topics.description: Angular momentum in an atom is quantized, meaning it can only take on discrete values determined by the electron's orbit.

topics.title: Quantization of Energy
topics.description: Quantization of energy refers to the idea that energy can only exist in discrete, specific amounts rather than a continuous range.

topics.title: Quantization of Energy Levels
topics.description: The wave nature of matter causes energy levels in bound systems, such as atoms, to be quantized, meaning only specific energy states are allowed.

topics.title: Quantized
topics.description: The fact that certain physical entities exist only with particular discrete values and not every conceivable value.

topics.title: Quantized Angular Momentum
topics.description: Quantized angular momentum refers to the restriction that the angular momentum of an electron in an atom can only take on specific, discrete values.

topics.title: Quantized Entities
topics.description: Quantized entities are physical quantities that can only take on specific, discrete values rather than a continuous range of values.

topics.title: Quantum
topics.description: A quantum is a discrete packet or bundle of a physical entity such as energy.

topics.title: Quantum Chromodynamics
topics.description: Quantum Chromodynamics is the theory that describes the strong nuclear force and the interactions between quarks and gluons.

topics.title: Quantum Electrodynamics
topics.description: The theory of electromagnetism on the particle scale.

topics.title: Quantum Electrodynamics (QED)
topics.description: The quantum theory of electromagnetism that describes how charged particles interact through the exchange of photons.

topics.title: Quantum Energy
topics.description: Quantum energy is the energy of a quantum of light, calculated as the product of Planck's constant and the frequency of the light.

topics.title: Quantum Gravity
topics.description: Quantum gravity is a theoretical framework that attempts to unify quantum mechanics and general relativity, particularly in extreme conditions where both theories are required.

topics.title: Quantum Mechanical Tunneling
topics.description: A quantum mechanical effect whereby a particle has a nonzero probability to cross through a potential energy barrier despite not having sufficient energy to pass over the barrier.

topics.title: Quantum Mechanics
topics.description: A branch of physics that describes the behavior of matter and energy at the atomic and subatomic level, where energy and other properties are quantized.

topics.title: Quantum Mechanics Foundations
topics.description: Quantum mechanics foundations refer to the basic principles and theories that describe the behavior of particles at the smallest scales, which Einstein contributed to.

topics.title: Quantum Mechanics in Atomic Physics
topics.description: Quantum mechanics is the branch of physics that describes the behavior of atoms and their substructures using probabilistic principles.

topics.title: Quantum Model of the Atom
topics.description: A model of the atom that describes electrons as existing in probability clouds rather than fixed orbits, based on quantum mechanics.

topics.title: Quantum Nature of Light
topics.description: The quantum nature of light refers to the behavior of light as both particles (photons) and waves, challenging classical intuitions about its properties.

topics.title: Quantum Number
topics.description: A quantum number is a value that quantizes a physical characteristic, such as energy, charge, or angular momentum, and is used to label the states of a system.

topics.title: Quantum Numbers and Rules
topics.description: Quantum numbers are used to describe the state of an electron in an atom, and they follow specific rules that define the allowed values for each electron.

topics.title: Quantum Numbers for Electrons
topics.description: Electrons in an atom are described by four quantum numbers: principal quantum number n, azimuthal quantum number l, magnetic quantum number m_l, and spin quantum number m_s.

topics.title: Quantum Numbers from Quark Composition
topics.description: Quantum numbers from quark composition are calculated by summing the individual quantum numbers of the constituent quarks.

topics.title: Quantum States
topics.description: Quantum states are discrete energy levels that particles, such as photons, can occupy, meaning energy and other properties are quantized rather than continuous.

topics.title: Quantum Tunneling
topics.description: Quantum tunneling is the phenomenon where a particle can pass through a potential barrier that it classically cannot surmount due to insufficient energy.

topics.title: Quark
topics.description: Quarks are elementary particles that are the building blocks of protons and neutrons, and they interact via the strong force.

topics.title: Quark and Lepton Families
topics.description: Quark and lepton families refer to the question of why there are three families of quarks and leptons, and whether this implies a deeper underlying symmetry or relationship.

topics.title: Quark Composition of Hadrons
topics.description: The quark composition of hadrons refers to the specific combination of quarks and antiquarks that make up particles like protons and neutrons.

topics.title: Quark Era
topics.description: A phase in the early universe when quarks began to form and interact, marking the separation of all four fundamental forces and the beginning of particle formation.

topics.title: Quark Flavor
topics.description: One of the distinct types or categories of quarks, such as up, down, strange, charm, bottom, or top.

topics.title: Quark Substructure
topics.description: Quark substructure refers to the idea that quarks, like electrons, may be fundamental particles without further substructure, though this is still under investigation.

topics.title: Quasar Energy Mechanism
topics.description: The quasar energy mechanism refers to the process by which quasars, which are extremely luminous galactic cores, generate and emit vast amounts of energy.

topics.title: Quasars
topics.description: Quasars are extremely luminous active galactic nuclei powered by supermassive black holes accreting matter.

topics.title: R Factor
topics.description: The ratio of thickness to the conductivity of a material.

topics.title: Rad
topics.description: A unit of radiation dose representing the ionizing energy deposited per kilogram of tissue.

topics.title: Radar Antenna
topics.description: A radar antenna is a device used to transmit and receive electromagnetic waves for detecting and tracking objects.

topics.title: Radian
topics.description: A radian is a unit of angular measure defined as the ratio of the arc length to the radius of a circle, and is dimensionless.

topics.title: Radians
topics.description: A unit of angle measurement.

topics.title: Radiant Energy
topics.description: The energy carried by electromagnetic waves.

topics.title: Radiation
topics.description: Radiation is the transfer of heat through electromagnetic waves, such as infrared radiation or visible light, without requiring a medium.

topics.title: Radiation as a Form of Heat Transfer
topics.description: Radiation is the transfer of heat through electromagnetic waves, which do not require a medium to propagate.

topics.title: Radiation Detection and Detectors
topics.description: Radiation detection involves identifying and measuring ionizing radiation using specialized devices called detectors.

topics.title: Radiation Detector
topics.description: Radiation detectors are instruments that detect ionizing radiation by measuring its effects on materials, such as ionization or light emission.

topics.title: Radiation Dose
topics.description: Radiation dose is the amount of energy deposited by ionizing radiation in a given mass of tissue, measured in units such as rad or rem.

topics.title: Radiation Dose (Sv)
topics.description: Radiation dose is the amount of ionizing radiation absorbed by tissue, measured in sieverts (Sv), and is used to determine the effectiveness and safety of radiotherapy treatments.

topics.title: Radiation Dose Unit (Rad)
topics.description: A unit of radiation dose defined as 0.01 joules of ionizing energy deposited per kilogram of tissue.

topics.title: Radiation Exposure Time
topics.description: Radiation exposure time is the duration for which food is exposed to ionizing radiation, with longer times resulting in higher doses of radiation.

topics.title: Radiation Heat Transfer
topics.description: Heat transfer that occurs when microwaves, infrared radiation, visible light, or other electromagnetic radiation is emitted or absorbed.

topics.title: Radiation Localization
topics.description: Radiation localization is the ability to concentrate ionizing radiation in specific areas of the body, such as tumors, to maximize its effect on cancer cells while minimizing damage to surrounding healthy tissue.

topics.title: Radiation Output
topics.description: The proportion of energy released by a nuclear weapon in the form of ionizing radiation, which can be adjusted for different tactical purposes.

topics.title: Radiation Shielding
topics.description: Radiation shielding is the use of materials like water to protect people and the environment from ionizing radiation during food irradiation.

topics.title: Radiation Source Storage
topics.description: Radiation source storage refers to the safe containment of radioactive isotopes like Cobalt-60 and Cesium-137 in deep pools of water when not in use.

topics.title: Radiation Therapy
topics.description: Radiation therapy is the use of radioactive substances or radiation to treat cancer by destroying cancerous cells.

topics.title: Radiative Heat Transfer
topics.description: Radiative heat transfer is the process by which heat is transferred through electromagnetic waves, such as infrared radiation, without requiring a medium.

topics.title: Radio and X-ray Telescopes
topics.description: Telescopes can operate with different frequencies of the electromagnetic spectrum, such as radio waves and X-rays, requiring specialized designs to capture and focus these waves.

topics.title: Radio Wave Applications
topics.description: Radio waves are used for communication, broadcasting, and navigation, including applications such as AM/FM radio, television, and mobile phone signals.

topics.title: Radio Waves
topics.description: Radio waves are a type of electromagnetic wave with the longest wavelengths and lowest frequencies, used for communication and broadcasting.

topics.title: Radioactive
topics.description: A substance or object that emits nuclear radiation.

topics.title: Radioactive Activity
topics.description: Activity is the rate of decay of radioactive nuclei, measured in decays per unit time.

topics.title: Radioactive Dating
topics.description: Radioactive dating is a method used to determine the age of an object by measuring the amount of a radioactive isotope remaining in it.

topics.title: Radioactive Decay
topics.description: A process by which an atomic nucleus of an unstable atom loses mass and energy by emitting ionizing particles.

topics.title: Radioactive Half-Life
topics.description: The radioactive half-life is the time it takes for half of a sample of a radioactive substance to decay.

topics.title: Radioactive Implants
topics.description: Radioactive implants are small radioactive sources placed directly into or near a tumor to deliver a concentrated dose of radiation to cancerous tissue.

topics.title: Radioactive Isotope
topics.description: A form of an element that has an unstable nucleus and decays over time, emitting radiation that can be used for medical imaging and diagnostics.

topics.title: Radioactive Nuclide
topics.description: A radioactive nuclide is an atom with an unstable nucleus that undergoes radioactive decay, emitting radiation and being used in medical imaging and diagnostics.

topics.title: Radioactive Substance
topics.description: A substance or object that emits nuclear radiation.

topics.title: Radioactive Tagging of Compounds
topics.description: The process of attaching a radioactive substance to a chemical compound.

topics.title: Radioactivity
topics.description: Radioactivity is the spontaneous emission of radiation from the nucleus of an unstable atom.

topics.title: Radioactivity and Heat
topics.description: Radioactivity is the process by which unstable atomic nuclei release energy, and it provides a continuous source of heat within the Earth's interior.

topics.title: Radioimmunoassay
topics.description: A technique that uses radioactive isotopes to measure the amount of a target substance by analyzing the binding of antibodies to the substance.

topics.title: Radiolytic Products
topics.description: Radiolytic products are chemical compounds formed when ionizing radiation breaks molecules into ions and free radicals, leading to various chemical reactions.

topics.title: Radiometric Dating
topics.description: Radiometric dating is a method used to determine the age of materials by measuring the decay of radioactive isotopes.

topics.title: Radiopharmaceutical
topics.description: A compound that contains a radioactive isotope and is used in medical imaging to detect and monitor specific body functions or conditions.

topics.title: Radiopharmaceuticals
topics.description: Radiopharmaceuticals are radioactive substances used in cancer therapy to target and destroy cancer cells while minimizing damage to healthy tissue.

topics.title: Radiotherapy
topics.description: Radiotherapy is the use of ionizing radiation to treat cancer by targeting and destroying cancer cells while minimizing damage to healthy tissue.

topics.title: Radius and Focal Length Relationship
topics.description: The radius of curvature of a mirror or lens is twice the focal length.

topics.title: Radius of a Nucleus
topics.description: The radius of a nucleus is calculated as r = r₀A^(1/3).

topics.title: Radius of Curvature
topics.description: The radius of a circular path.

topics.title: Radius of Curvature of a Charged Particle in a Magnetic Field
topics.description: The radius of curvature of the path of a charged particle moving perpendicular to a magnetic field is determined by its mass, velocity, charge, and the magnetic field strength.

topics.title: Radius of Curvature of a Spherical Mirror
topics.description: The radius of curvature of a spherical mirror is the radius of the sphere from which the mirror is made, and it is twice the focal length of the mirror.

topics.title: Rainbow
topics.description: The dispersion of sunlight into a continuous distribution of colors according to wavelength, caused by refraction and reflection in water droplets.

topics.title: Rainbow Formation
topics.description: Rainbows are formed by a combination of refraction and reflection of light within water droplets, resulting in the dispersion of white light into a spectrum of colors.

topics.title: Range
topics.description: The horizontal distance traveled by a projectile on level ground before it returns to the same vertical position.

topics.title: Range of a Projectile
topics.description: The horizontal distance traveled by a projectile calculated using the initial velocity, the launch angle, and the acceleration due to gravity.

topics.title: Range of Radiation
topics.description: The distance radiation can travel through a material before losing its energy, which depends on its type, energy, and the material it encounters.

topics.title: Rarefaction
topics.description: A low-pressure region in a sound wave.

topics.title: Rate of Conductive Heat Transfer
topics.description: For a slab, the conductive heat-transfer rate is \(\frac{Q}{t}=\frac{kA(T_h-T_c)}{d}\), where \(k\) is thermal conductivity, \(A\) is area, \(T_h-T_c\) is the temperature difference across the slab, and \(d\) is its thickness.

topics.title: Rate of Heat Transfer
topics.description: The rate of heat transfer by conduction is directly proportional to the temperature difference, the surface area, and the thermal conductivity of the material, and inversely proportional to the thickness of the material.

topics.title: Ray
topics.description: A straight line representing the path of light from a point.

topics.title: Ray Aspect of Light
topics.description: Light can be modeled as rays that travel in straight lines through a uniform medium.

topics.title: Ray Diagram
topics.description: A ray diagram is a visual representation used to predict the path of light rays and determine the location and nature of an image formed by a mirror.

topics.title: Ray Diagrams for Spherical Mirrors
topics.description: Ray diagrams for spherical mirrors use the law of reflection to trace the paths of light rays and determine the location and characteristics of the image formed.

topics.title: Ray Tracing for Thin Lenses
topics.description: Ray tracing is the technique of determining or following the paths that light rays take through a lens by using specific rules to predict how light bends.

topics.title: Rayleigh Criterion
topics.description: The Rayleigh criterion is a standard used to determine the diffraction limit to resolution, stating that two images are just resolvable when the center of the diffraction pattern of one is directly over the first minimum of the diffraction pattern of the other.

topics.title: RC Circuit
topics.description: A circuit that contains both a resistor and a capacitor.

topics.title: RC Circuit Timing Applications
topics.description: RC circuits are used in timing applications because the time constant (τ = RC) determines how quickly a capacitor charges or discharges, allowing precise control over time intervals.

topics.title: Reactance
topics.description: Reactance is the opposition to the flow of alternating current (AC) caused by inductance or capacitance in a circuit.

topics.title: Real Image
topics.description: A real image is an image that can be projected onto a screen, film, or the retina of an eye, as light rays actually converge at the image location.

topics.title: Real Image Formed by a Concave Mirror
topics.description: A real image formed by a concave mirror is an image that can be projected onto a screen, located in front of the mirror, and is inverted relative to the object.

topics.title: Real Image in Mirrors
topics.description: A real image in mirrors is an image that can be projected onto a screen and is formed on the same side of the mirror as the object.

topics.title: Rearranged Thin-Lens Equation
topics.description: The rearranged thin-lens equation expresses the image distance in terms of the focal length and object distance.

topics.title: Reasonableness Check of Physical Results
topics.description: Evaluating whether a calculated result makes sense by checking its magnitude, sign, and units to ensure it accurately describes the physical situation.

topics.title: Recoil
topics.description: The backward motion of an object or person exerting force on another object, as a result of conservation of momentum.

topics.title: Recoil Velocity
topics.description: Recoil velocity is the velocity of an object after it has collided with another object, typically in the opposite direction of the incoming object's motion.

topics.title: Red Shift Proportionality
topics.description: Red shift is proportional to distance, as evidenced by the consistent red shift observed in gravitational lensing.

topics.title: Reference Frame
topics.description: A coordinate system from which the positions of objects are described.

topics.title: Reference Intensity
topics.description: Reference intensity is the lowest intensity of sound that a person with normal hearing can perceive at a frequency of 1000 Hz, which is defined as 1 × 10⁻¹² W/m².

topics.title: Reference Intensity (I₀)
topics.description: The lowest intensity of sound that a person with normal hearing can perceive, defined as 10⁻¹² W/m².

topics.title: Reference Level for Gravitational Potential Energy
topics.description: A chosen point in space where the gravitational potential energy is defined to be zero, typically Earth's surface, used to calculate changes in potential energy.

topics.title: Reference Level for Potential Energy
topics.description: A reference level is a chosen point where gravitational potential energy is set to zero, typically Earth's surface, allowing for the calculation of potential energy differences.

topics.title: Reflected Light
topics.description: Light that is completely polarized when reflected at the angle of reflection known as Brewster’s angle.

topics.title: Reflection
topics.description: Reflection is the change in direction of a wave when it bounces off a barrier, such as a fixed end, often resulting in an inversion of the wave.

topics.title: Reflection of Light
topics.description: Reflection is the phenomenon where light bounces off a surface and changes direction.

topics.title: Refracted Ray
topics.description: The light ray that bends and continues into the second medium after refraction.

topics.title: Refraction
topics.description: Refraction is the bending of light as it passes from one medium to another due to a change in its speed.

topics.title: Refraction and Dispersion
topics.description: Refraction is responsible for dispersion, as the angle of refraction depends on the wavelength of light and the index of refraction of the medium.

topics.title: Refractive Indices
topics.description: Refractive indices are measures of how much light bends when passing through different materials, such as the cornea and lens of the eye.

topics.title: Refrigerators
topics.description: A refrigerator is a device that removes heat from a cooler interior and expels it to a warmer exterior by doing work on the system.

topics.title: Relationship Between Current, Charge, and Time
topics.description: Electric current is calculated as the amount of charge passing through a given area divided by the time it takes for the charge to pass.

topics.title: Relationship Between Electric and Magnetic Effects
topics.description: Electric and magnetic effects are interconnected, as electromagnetic waves are created by the interaction of changing electric and magnetic fields.

topics.title: Relationship Between Electric and Magnetic Field Strengths
topics.description: In an electromagnetic wave, the electric field strength (E) and magnetic field strength (B) are directly proportional, with their ratio equal to the speed of light (c).

topics.title: Relationship Between Electric Field and Force
topics.description: The electric field at a point is defined as the force experienced by a positive test charge at that point divided by the magnitude of the test charge.

topics.title: Relationship Between Electric Potential and Work
topics.description: The work done to move a charge in an electric field is related to the change in electric potential, where work equals the charge multiplied by the change in electric potential.

topics.title: Relationship Between Electricity and Magnetism
topics.description: Electricity and magnetism are interconnected, as electric currents can produce magnetic fields, and this relationship is fundamental to the concept of electromagnetism.

topics.title: Relationship Between emf, Terminal Voltage, and Internal Resistance
topics.description: Terminal voltage is equal to the electromotive force (emf) minus the product of the current and the internal resistance of the source.

topics.title: Relationship Between Frequency and Period
topics.description: Frequency and period are inversely related, with frequency being the reciprocal of the period.

topics.title: Relationship Between Frequency and Wavelength
topics.description: The frequency and wavelength of an electromagnetic wave are inversely related, such that higher frequency corresponds to shorter wavelength.

topics.title: Relationship Between Linear and Angular Acceleration
topics.description: Linear acceleration (tangential acceleration) is directly proportional to angular acceleration and is related by the equation a_t = r * alpha.

topics.title: Relationship Between Momentum and Force
topics.description: The net external force acting on an object is equal to the rate of change of its momentum over time.

topics.title: Relationship Between Position, Velocity, and Time
topics.description: A graph of position versus time provides a relationship among displacement, velocity, and time, with the slope representing velocity.

topics.title: Relationship Between Pressure and Force
topics.description: Pressure is directly proportional to the force applied and inversely proportional to the area over which the force is distributed.

topics.title: Relationship Between Speed, Frequency, and Wavelength
topics.description: The speed of a sound wave is directly related to its frequency and wavelength by the equation v = fλ, where v is speed, f is frequency, and λ is wavelength.

topics.title: Relationship Between Temperature and Kinetic Energy
topics.description: The temperature of a gas is directly proportional to the average translational kinetic energy of its molecules.

topics.title: Relationship Between Uniform Circular Motion and Simple Harmonic Motion
topics.description: Uniform circular motion and simple harmonic motion are related such that the projection of uniform circular motion onto a straight line exhibits simple harmonic motion.

topics.title: Relationship Between Velocity, Acceleration, and Time
topics.description: A graph of velocity versus time provides a relationship among velocity, acceleration, and time, with the slope representing acceleration.

topics.title: Relationship Between Voltage and Time in RC Circuits
topics.description: The voltage across a capacitor in an RC circuit changes over time according to an exponential function, either increasing or decreasing depending on whether the capacitor is charging or discharging.

topics.title: Relationship Between Voltage, Current, and Resistance
topics.description: The relationship between voltage, current, and resistance in electric power is described by Ohm’s law and the power equations P = IV, P = V²/R, and P = I²R.

topics.title: Relative Biological Effectiveness (RBE)
topics.description: Relative Biological Effectiveness (RBE) is a measure of the biological damage caused by a specific type of ionizing radiation compared to a reference radiation, typically X-rays or gamma rays.

topics.title: Relative Humidity
topics.description: The ratio of the partial pressure of water vapor in the air to the vapor pressure of water at the same temperature, expressed as a percentage.

topics.title: Relative Motion
topics.description: Motion is described relative to the observer's frame of reference.

topics.title: Relative Motion and Frequency
topics.description: Relative motion between a source and an observer affects the perceived frequency of sound, with motion toward the source increasing frequency and motion away decreasing it.

topics.title: Relative Osmotic Pressure
topics.description: The back pressure which stops the osmotic process if neither solution is pure water.

topics.title: Relative Velocity
topics.description: The velocity of an object relative to an observer is the sum of the object's velocity relative to a medium and the medium's velocity relative to the observer.

topics.title: Relativistic
topics.description: Having to do with modern relativity, such as the effects that become significant only when an object is moving close enough to the speed of light for gamma to be significantly greater than 1.

topics.title: Relativistic Addition of Velocities
topics.description: Relativistic addition of velocities is the method used to combine velocities in special relativity, ensuring that the speed of light remains constant in all inertial frames.

topics.title: Relativistic Doppler Effects
topics.description: A change in wavelength of radiation that is moving relative to the observer, resulting in longer wavelengths (red shift) when the source moves away and shorter wavelengths (blue shift) when the source moves toward the observer.

topics.title: Relativistic Doppler Shift
topics.description: The relativistic Doppler shift describes how the observed wavelength or frequency of electromagnetic radiation changes due to the relative motion between the source and the observer, accounting for relativistic effects.

topics.title: Relativistic Energy
topics.description: The total energy of a moving object or particle, which includes both its rest energy mc² and its kinetic energy.

topics.title: Relativistic Factor
topics.description: A factor gamma = 1 / sqrt(1 - (u²/c²)), where u is the velocity of a moving object and c is the speed of light.

topics.title: Relativistic Factor (Gamma)
topics.description: The relativistic factor, gamma, is a factor used in special relativity to account for the effects of high velocities and is given by gamma = 1 / sqrt(1 - v²/c²).

topics.title: Relativistic Kinetic Energy
topics.description: Relativistic kinetic energy is the energy of motion for an object moving at relativistic speeds, given by KE_rel = (gamma − 1) mc², where gamma is the relativistic factor.

topics.title: Relativistic Length Formula
topics.description: The length of an object moving relative to an observer is given by the formula L = L₀√(1 − v²/c²), where L₀ is the proper length, v is the velocity of the object, and c is the speed of light.

topics.title: Relativistic Length Measurement
topics.description: Relativistic length measurement shows that the distance between two events depends on the observer’s relative motion, leading to different measurements of length for different observers.

topics.title: Relativistic Mechanics
topics.description: Relativistic mechanics is the framework that describes the behavior of objects moving at speeds close to the speed of light, where classical mechanics is no longer sufficient.

topics.title: Relativistic Momentum
topics.description: Relativistic momentum is the momentum of an object moving at relativistic speeds, calculated as the product of its rest mass, velocity, and the relativistic factor gamma.

topics.title: Relativistic Quantum Mechanics
topics.description: Relativistic quantum mechanics is an attempt to unify the theories of relativity and quantum mechanics to describe the behavior of subatomic particles in relation to gravity, time, and space.

topics.title: Relativistic Velocity
topics.description: Relativistic velocity refers to the speed of an object approaching the speed of light, where classical mechanics no longer accurately describes its behavior.

topics.title: Relativistic Velocity Addition
topics.description: The method of adding velocities of an object moving at a relativistic speed.

topics.title: Relativity
topics.description: Relativity is a theory developed by Albert Einstein that describes how time, space, and speed are not absolute but can appear different to different observers moving relative to each other.

topics.title: Relaxation Time in MRI
topics.description: The time it takes for protons to return to equilibrium after being exposed to an external magnetic field, which varies depending on tissue type and condition.

topics.title: Renewable Energy Sources
topics.description: Renewable energy sources are those that can be replenished naturally and are not depleted when used, such as water, wind, solar, and biomass.

topics.title: Renewable Forms of Energy
topics.description: Those sources that cannot be used up, such as water, wind, solar, and biomass.

topics.title: Repolarization
topics.description: Repolarization is the process by which the inside of a neuron's membrane returns to its resting negative charge after depolarization.

topics.title: Representation of Vectors
topics.description: Vectors are represented graphically by arrows, where the length of the arrow corresponds to the magnitude of the vector and the direction of the arrow indicates the direction of the vector.

topics.title: Representing Acceleration with Equations
topics.description: Representing acceleration with equations involves using mathematical expressions to describe how velocity changes with time.

topics.title: Representing Acceleration with Graphs
topics.description: Representing acceleration with graphs involves using visual representations, such as velocity-time graphs, to show how acceleration changes over time.

topics.title: Reproducibility in Superconductivity
topics.description: Reproducibility refers to the ability to consistently produce the same results in experiments, which is crucial for validating scientific discoveries in superconductivity.

topics.title: Repulsion of Charges
topics.description: Repulsion of charges is the phenomenon where like charges (such as two positive charges) push each other away.

topics.title: Residual Radioactivity
topics.description: Residual radioactivity is the remaining radioactivity in a material after irradiation, which is not produced by gamma rays or electrons used in food irradiation.

topics.title: Resistance
topics.description: Resistance is a measure of how much a material opposes the flow of electric current.

topics.title: Resistance Arm
topics.description: The resistance arm is the part of a lever between the fulcrum and the point where the resistance force is applied.

topics.title: Resistance Calculation
topics.description: Resistance of a material can be calculated using its resistivity, length, and cross-sectional area with the formula R = resistivity × length / area.

topics.title: Resistance for Voltmeter Range
topics.description: The resistance that must be placed in series with a galvanometer to use it as a voltmeter depends on the maximum voltage to be measured.

topics.title: Resistance in Fluid Flow
topics.description: Resistance in fluid flow is the opposition to the flow of a fluid, which depends on factors such as viscosity, tube length, and radius.

topics.title: Resistivity
topics.description: Resistivity is an intrinsic property of a material that quantifies how strongly it resists the flow of electric current.

topics.title: Resistivity vs. Temperature in Superconductors
topics.description: The resistivity of a superconductor decreases to zero at its critical temperature, and then increases linearly with temperature above that point.

topics.title: Resistor
topics.description: A component that provides resistance to the current flowing through an electrical circuit.

topics.title: Resistors in Parallel
topics.description: Resistors are in parallel when each resistor is connected directly to the same voltage source.

topics.title: Resistors in Series
topics.description: Resistors are in series when the same current flows through each resistor sequentially.

topics.title: Resistors in Series and Parallel
topics.description: Resistors in series are connected end-to-end, resulting in the same current through each resistor, while resistors in parallel are connected across the same voltage, resulting in different currents through each resistor.

topics.title: Resolution
topics.description: The angular resolution of an optical instrument is the angle between two objects that can just be distinguished, and it is proportional to the wavelength of light and inversely proportional to the diameter of the aperture.

topics.title: Resolution of Vectors into Components
topics.description: Resolution of vectors into components involves breaking a vector into horizontal and vertical parts that together represent the original vector.

topics.title: Resolving Power
topics.description: Resolving power is the ability of a lens or optical instrument to distinguish between two closely spaced objects, defined by the smallest distance x between objects that can still be seen as distinct, given by x = 1.22 lambda d / D.

topics.title: Resolving Vectors into Components
topics.description: Resolving vectors into horizontal and vertical components allows for the analysis of two-dimensional motion by breaking it into independent one-dimensional motions.

topics.title: Resolving Weight into Components
topics.description: Resolving weight into components involves breaking the weight vector into perpendicular and parallel components relative to an inclined plane using trigonometric identities.

topics.title: Resonance
topics.description: The phenomenon of driving a system with a frequency equal to the system's natural frequency.

topics.title: Resonance in Electromagnetic Waves
topics.description: Resonance in electromagnetic waves refers to the phenomenon where a wave interacts with a material at its natural frequency, leading to enhanced absorption or emission.

topics.title: Resonant
topics.description: A system that displays enhanced oscillation when subjected to a periodic disturbance of the same frequency as its natural frequency.

topics.title: Resonant Frequencies of a Closed-Pipe Resonator
topics.description: Resonant frequencies of a closed-pipe resonator are the specific frequencies at which standing waves form in a pipe closed at one end.

topics.title: Resonant Frequencies of an Open-Pipe Resonator
topics.description: Resonant frequencies of an open-pipe resonator are the specific frequencies at which standing waves form in a pipe open at both ends.

topics.title: Resonant Frequency
topics.description: The frequency at which the impedance in a circuit is minimized, calculated by f_0 = 1/(2π√(LC)).

topics.title: Resonant Frequency in an RLC Circuit
topics.description: Resonant frequency is the frequency at which the inductive reactance and capacitive reactance in an RLC circuit cancel each other, resulting in minimum impedance and maximum current.

topics.title: Rest Energy
topics.description: Rest energy is the energy an object possesses due to its mass when it is at rest, calculated as E_0 = mc², where m is mass and c is the speed of light.

topics.title: Rest Mass
topics.description: Rest mass is the mass of an object as measured by an observer at rest relative to the object, and it is the only mass that makes sense to discuss in the context of relativistic physics.

topics.title: Resting Potential
topics.description: Resting potential is the stable voltage across a neuron's membrane when it is not transmitting a signal, typically around -90 mV, maintained by ion concentration gradients and the sodium-potassium pump.

topics.title: Restoring Force
topics.description: A restoring force is a force that acts to return an object to its equilibrium position in simple harmonic motion.

topics.title: Resultant Direction
topics.description: The direction of the resultant vector determined by the inverse tangent of the ratio of its y-component to its x-component.

topics.title: Resultant Magnitude
topics.description: The magnitude of the resultant vector calculated using the Pythagorean theorem with the x and y components.

topics.title: Resultant Vector
topics.description: A resultant vector is the vector obtained by adding two or more vectors together, representing the total effect of all the individual vectors.

topics.title: Retarding Voltage
topics.description: Retarding voltage is a voltage applied to stop ejected electrons from reaching a collector, used to measure the energy of the electrons in electron volts.

topics.title: Retinex Theory
topics.description: The retinex theory of color vision suggests that the brain compares images from different parts of the eye to determine the true color of an object, even under varying lighting conditions.

topics.title: Retinex Theory of Color Vision
topics.description: The retinex theory of color vision proposes that color perception arises from the comparison of images formed by different systems of cones in the eye.

topics.title: Reverse Dialysis
topics.description: The process that occurs when back pressure is sufficient to reverse the normal direction of dialysis through membranes.

topics.title: Reverse Osmosis
topics.description: The process that occurs when back pressure is sufficient to reverse the normal direction of osmosis through membranes.

topics.title: Reversible Thermodynamic Process
topics.description: Reversible processes are idealized thermodynamic processes that can be reversed without any change in the system or surroundings, and they are essential for achieving the maximum efficiency of a heat engine.

topics.title: Reynolds Number
topics.description: A dimensionless parameter that can reveal whether a particular flow is laminar or turbulent.

topics.title: Reynolds Number for Object in Fluid
topics.description: The Reynolds number for an object moving in a fluid is a dimensionless quantity that predicts whether the flow around the object is laminar, turbulent, or a combination of both.

topics.title: Right Hand Rule 1 (RHR-1)
topics.description: A rule to determine the direction of the magnetic force on a positive moving charge.

topics.title: Right Hand Rule 2 (RHR-2)
topics.description: A rule to determine the direction of the magnetic field induced by a current-carrying wire.

topics.title: Right-Hand Rule
topics.description: The right-hand rule is a method used to determine the direction of the magnetic field around a current-carrying wire or the direction of the force on a moving charge in a magnetic field.

topics.title: Right-Hand Rule (RHR-1 and RHR-2)
topics.description: A method to determine the direction of the magnetic force on a moving charge or the direction of the induced current in a conductor.

topics.title: Right-Hand Rule 1
topics.description: Right-Hand Rule 1 is a method to determine the direction of the magnetic force on a positive moving charge by aligning the thumb with the velocity, fingers with the magnetic field, and the palm pointing in the direction of the force.

topics.title: Right-Hand Rule 2 (RHR-2)
topics.description: RHR-2 is a method to determine the direction of the magnetic field created by a current-carrying wire by pointing the thumb in the direction of the current and the fingers curling in the direction of the magnetic field.

topics.title: Right-Hand Rule for Angular Momentum
topics.description: The right-hand rule is a method to determine the direction of angular momentum and angular velocity by curling the fingers in the direction of rotation and pointing the thumb in the direction of the vector.

topics.title: Right-Hand Rule for Angular Velocity and Momentum
topics.description: The right-hand rule is a method to determine the direction of angular velocity and angular momentum vectors by curling the fingers in the direction of rotation and pointing the thumb in the direction of the vector.

topics.title: RL Circuit
topics.description: A circuit containing a resistor and an inductor, where the current and voltage change over time due to the interaction between resistance and inductance.

topics.title: RL Circuit Characteristic Time Constant
topics.description: The characteristic time constant of an RL circuit is the time it takes for the current to reach approximately 63.2% of its final value.

topics.title: RL Circuit Current Decay
topics.description: The current in an RL circuit decreases exponentially over time when the circuit is de-energized.

topics.title: RL Circuit Current Growth
topics.description: The current in an RL circuit increases exponentially over time when the circuit is first energized.

topics.title: RLC Circuit
topics.description: An electric circuit that includes a resistor, capacitor, and inductor.

topics.title: RMS Current
topics.description: RMS current is the equivalent DC current that delivers the same power to a resistor as the AC current.

topics.title: RMS Voltage
topics.description: The root mean square of the voltage, V_rms = V0 divided by the square root of 2, where V0 is the peak voltage, in an AC system.

topics.title: Rocket Acceleration Formula
topics.description: The acceleration of a rocket is calculated using the formula a = (v_e) / (m Δm / Δt − g), where v_e is the exhaust velocity, m is the rocket mass, Δm/Δt is the fuel burn rate, and g is the acceleration due to gravity.

topics.title: Rocket Propulsion
topics.description: Rocket propulsion is the process by which a rocket moves by expelling mass in the opposite direction, utilizing conservation of momentum.

topics.title: Rocket Propulsion Principle
topics.description: Rockets move by expelling mass in one direction, which creates an equal and opposite force that propels the rocket in the opposite direction.

topics.title: Rods and Cones
topics.description: Rods and cones are two types of photoreceptors in the retina; rods are responsible for low-light vision and do not detect color, while cones are responsible for color vision and function best in bright light.

topics.title: Roentgen Equivalent Man
topics.description: The roentgen equivalent man (rem) is a unit used to measure the biological effect of radiation exposure, calculated by multiplying the radiation dose in rad by the relative biological effectiveness.

topics.title: Roentgen Equivalent Man (rem)
topics.description: The roentgen equivalent man (rem) is a unit used to measure the biological effect of ionizing radiation, calculated by multiplying the radiation dose in rads by the relative biological effectiveness (RBE).

topics.title: Role of Ions in Biological Systems
topics.description: Ions such as sodium (Na⁺), potassium (K⁺), and chloride (Cl⁻) play a crucial role in biological systems by reducing or screening electrostatic interactions and facilitating processes like nerve impulse transmission.

topics.title: Rolling Resistance
topics.description: Various forces that may impede a rolling wheel, including axle friction, drag, and imperfectly elastic deformation of the wheel and/or surface.

topics.title: Root Mean Square (RMS) Voltage
topics.description: RMS voltage is the equivalent DC voltage that delivers the same power to a resistor as the AC voltage.

topics.title: Root-Mean-Square Distance
topics.description: The root-mean-square distance is the statistical average distance a molecule travels during a random walk in a given time.

topics.title: Rotation Angle
topics.description: Rotation angle is the measure of the angle through which an object rotates about an axis.

topics.title: Rotational Angle
topics.description: The total angle through which an object rotates, denoted by theta.

topics.title: Rotational Dynamics
topics.description: Rotational dynamics is the study of the relationship between torque, moment of inertia, and angular acceleration in rotational motion.

topics.title: Rotational Inertia
topics.description: Rotational inertia is the rotational analog of mass, which measures an object's resistance to changes in its rotational motion.

topics.title: Rotational Kinematic Equations
topics.description: A set of equations that describe the relationships between angular displacement, angular velocity, angular acceleration, and time in rotational motion.

topics.title: Rotational Kinematics
topics.description: Rotational kinematics describes the relationships between angular displacement, angular velocity, angular acceleration, and time.

topics.title: Rotational Kinetic Energy
topics.description: Rotational kinetic energy is the energy an object possesses due to its rotational motion, defined as one-half the moment of inertia multiplied by the square of the angular velocity.

topics.title: Rotational Motion
topics.description: Motion of an object around a fixed axis, characterized by angular displacement, velocity, and acceleration.

topics.title: Rotational Work
topics.description: Rotational work is the work done to rotate an object, calculated as the product of torque and the angular displacement.

topics.title: Rules for Significant Figures in Addition and Subtraction
topics.description: The result of an addition or subtraction calculation should have the same number of decimal places as the quantity with the least number of decimal places.

topics.title: Rules for Significant Figures in Multiplication and Division
topics.description: The result of a multiplication or division calculation should have the same number of significant figures as the quantity with the least significant figures.

topics.title: Rutherford Scattering
topics.description: The phenomenon where alpha particles are scattered by the nucleus of an atom, indicating the nucleus is small and dense.

topics.title: Rutherford's Gold Foil Experiment
topics.description: Rutherford's gold foil experiment demonstrated that the nucleus of an atom is very small, dense, and contains most of the atom's mass, as evidenced by the large-angle scattering of alpha particles.

topics.title: Rutherford's Planetary Model of the Atom
topics.description: Rutherford's planetary model of the atom describes electrons orbiting a small, massive, positively charged nucleus, similar to how planets orbit the Sun, with most of the atom's volume being empty space.

topics.title: Rydberg Constant
topics.description: A physical constant that appears in the formula for the wavelengths of spectral lines emitted by hydrogen-like atoms.

topics.title: Rydberg Formula
topics.description: The Rydberg formula is a mathematical equation used to calculate the wavelengths of spectral lines in the hydrogen spectrum based on the energy levels of the electron.

topics.title: Satellites
topics.description: Satellites are objects that orbit a planet or other celestial body, held in orbit by the gravitational force exerted by the body they orbit.

topics.title: Saturation
topics.description: The condition of 100% relative humidity.

topics.title: Saturation Vapor Density
topics.description: The maximum amount of water vapor that air can hold at a specific temperature, measured in grams per cubic meter.

topics.title: Scalar
topics.description: A physical quantity with magnitude but no direction.

topics.title: Scalar Quantity
topics.description: A scalar quantity is a physical quantity that has only magnitude, not direction.

topics.title: Scaling
topics.description: Scaling is the method of using known quantities to estimate unknown quantities by proportionally increasing or decreasing measurements.

topics.title: Scanning Tunneling Electron Microscope
topics.description: A microscope that uses quantum tunneling effects to produce high-resolution images of surfaces at the atomic level.

topics.title: Schwarzschild Radius
topics.description: The Schwarzschild radius is the radius of the event horizon of a black hole, calculated using the mass of the object and the speed of light.

topics.title: Science
topics.description: The study or knowledge of how the physical world operates, based on objective evidence determined through observation and experimentation.

topics.title: Scientific Communication
topics.description: Scientific communication is the process by which scientists share their findings and results with others.

topics.title: Scientific Law
topics.description: A scientific law is a description of a pattern in nature that is true in all circumstances that have been studied, often expressed as a concise statement or mathematical equation.

topics.title: Scientific Method
topics.description: The scientific method is a systematic process used to investigate phenomena, acquire knowledge, and test hypotheses through observation, experimentation, and analysis.

topics.title: Scientific Model
topics.description: A scientific model is a representation of a complex system or phenomenon, often used to visualize or understand aspects of the natural world that are difficult to observe directly.

topics.title: Scientific Notation
topics.description: Scientific notation is a way of writing numbers that are too large or small to be conveniently written in decimal form, using the format x × 10^y.

topics.title: Scientific Standards
topics.description: Scientific standards are agreed-upon units and systems used by scientists to ensure consistency and clarity in measurements.

topics.title: Scintillator
topics.description: A scintillator is a material that converts the energy of ionizing radiation into light, which can then be detected and analyzed for information about the radiation.

topics.title: Scintillators
topics.description: A radiation detection method that records light produced when radiation interacts with materials.

topics.title: Screening
topics.description: The dilution or blocking of an electrostatic force on a charged object by the presence of other charges nearby.

topics.title: Screw
topics.description: A simple machine consisting of a spiral inclined plane.

topics.title: Second
topics.description: The SI unit for time, abbreviated (s).

topics.title: Second Condition for Equilibrium
topics.description: The second condition for equilibrium is that the net external torque on a system must be zero, ensuring no accelerated rotation.

topics.title: Second Law of Motion
topics.description: The net external force on a system is equal to the change in momentum of the system divided by the time over which it changes.

topics.title: Second Law of Thermodynamics
topics.description: The second law of thermodynamics states that the total entropy of a system either increases or remains constant in any process; it never decreases.

topics.title: Second Law of Thermodynamics (Entropy Formulation)
topics.description: The total entropy of a system either increases or remains constant; it never decreases.

topics.title: Second Law of Thermodynamics (Statistical Explanation)
topics.description: The second law of thermodynamics states that entropy either remains the same or increases in every process, due to the overwhelming probability of systems moving toward more disordered states.

topics.title: Second Law of Thermodynamics (Third Form)
topics.description: The third form of the second law of thermodynamics states that the maximum efficiency of a heat engine operating between two temperatures is achieved by a Carnot engine, and all reversible engines operating between the same temperatures have the same maximum efficiency.

topics.title: Second Postulate of Special Relativity
topics.description: The idea that the speed of light is a constant, independent of the source.

topics.title: Self-Inductance
topics.description: Self-inductance is the effect of Faraday’s law of induction where a change in current in a coil induces an emf in the same coil.

topics.title: Self-Organization
topics.description: Self-organization is the process by which a system spontaneously organizes itself without external direction, often leading to structured patterns or behaviors.

topics.title: Semi-Log Plot
topics.description: A plot that uses a logarithmic scale on one axis of the graph and a linear scale on the other.

topics.title: Semi-Major Axis
topics.description: The semi-major axis is half the longest diameter of an ellipse, representing the average distance of a planet from the sun in its orbit.

topics.title: Semi-Major Axis of an Ellipse
topics.description: The semi-major axis of an ellipse is the average of the maximum and minimum distances from the center to the ellipse's perimeter.

topics.title: Semi-Minor Axis of an Ellipse
topics.description: The semi-minor axis of an ellipse is the geometric mean of the maximum and minimum distances from the center to the ellipse's perimeter.

topics.title: Semipermeable
topics.description: A type of membrane that allows only certain small molecules to pass through.

topics.title: Semipermeable Membrane
topics.description: A semipermeable membrane is a selectively permeable barrier that allows certain molecules to pass through while blocking others.

topics.title: Series
topics.description: A sequence of resistors or other components wired into a circuit one after the other.

topics.title: Series and Parallel Combinations
topics.description: Complex circuits can be simplified by identifying and reducing series and parallel resistor combinations to a single equivalent resistance.

topics.title: Series and Parallel Connections
topics.description: Series connections of capacitors result in a total capacitance less than any individual capacitor, while parallel connections result in a total capacitance equal to the sum of individual capacitances.

topics.title: Series Circuit
topics.description: A circuit where components are connected end-to-end in a single path, so the same current flows through each component.

topics.title: Series Connection of Voltage Sources
topics.description: In a series connection of voltage sources, their internal resistances and electromotive forces add algebraically.

topics.title: Series RLC Circuit
topics.description: An RLC series circuit is a circuit containing a resistor, inductor, and capacitor connected in series with an AC voltage source.

topics.title: Shear Deformation
topics.description: Shear deformation is the deformation of an object when a force is applied parallel to its surface, causing it to twist or slide.

topics.title: Shear Modulus
topics.description: Shear modulus is a measure of the stiffness of a material under shear stress, defined as the ratio of shear stress to shear strain.

topics.title: Shell
topics.description: A probability cloud for electrons that has a single principal quantum number.

topics.title: Shielding
topics.description: A technique to limit radiation exposure.

topics.title: Shock Hazard
topics.description: A shock hazard occurs when electric current passes through a person, causing effects ranging from painful sensations to potentially lethal ventricular fibrillation.

topics.title: Short Circuit
topics.description: A low-resistance path between terminals of a voltage source.

topics.title: Shorter Wavelengths Improve Resolution
topics.description: Using shorter wavelengths, such as ultraviolet light, allows for better resolution in microscopes, enabling the observation of finer details.

topics.title: Shunt Resistance
topics.description: A small resistance R placed in parallel with a galvanometer G to produce an ammeter.

topics.title: SI Unit of Density
topics.description: The SI unit of density is kilograms per cubic meter (kg/m³).

topics.title: SI Unit of Momentum
topics.description: The SI unit of momentum is kilogram meters per second (kg × m/s).

topics.title: SI Units
topics.description: The International System of Units (SI) is a standardized system of measurement that defines seven fundamental physical units, such as meter, kilogram, and second.

topics.title: SI Units of Torque
topics.description: Newton times meters, usually written as N·m.

topics.title: Sievert
topics.description: The SI equivalent of the rem, used to measure radiation dose.

topics.title: Sievert (Sv)
topics.description: The SI unit for radiation dose equivalent, defined as 1 joule of energy per kilogram of tissue multiplied by the relative biological effectiveness (RBE).

topics.title: Significant Figures
topics.description: Significant figures are the digits in a measured value that indicate the precision of the measurement.

topics.title: Simple Circuit
topics.description: A circuit with a single voltage source and a single resistor.

topics.title: Simple Harmonic Motion
topics.description: Simple harmonic motion is a type of periodic motion where the restoring force is directly proportional to the displacement and acts in the opposite direction of the displacement.

topics.title: Simple Harmonic Oscillator
topics.description: A simple harmonic oscillator is a system that undergoes simple harmonic motion, where the net force is described by Hooke’s law.

topics.title: Simple Machine
topics.description: Simple machines are basic mechanical devices that change the direction or magnitude of a force to make work easier.

topics.title: Simple Pendulum
topics.description: A simple pendulum is a mass (bob) suspended from a fixed point by a string or rod, which swings back and forth under the influence of gravity.

topics.title: Simple Theory of Color Vision
topics.description: The simple theory of color vision suggests that all hues are our eye’s response to different combinations of wavelengths of light.

topics.title: Simplified Theory of Color Vision
topics.description: A theory stating that there are three primary colors corresponding to the three types of cones in the eye.

topics.title: Simultaneity
topics.description: Simultaneity refers to the occurrence of two events at the same time, which can differ depending on the observer's frame of reference.

topics.title: Single Slit Diffraction
topics.description: The diffraction pattern produced by a single slit results in a central bright maximum and alternating dark and bright fringes.

topics.title: Single Slit Diffraction Equation
topics.description: The equation used to calculate the angle of minima in a single slit diffraction pattern, given by D sin(theta) = mλ, where D is the slit width, λ is the wavelength, theta is the angle, and m is the order of the minimum.

topics.title: Single Slit Diffraction Pattern
topics.description: A diffraction pattern formed when light passes through a single slit, characterized by a central maximum that is larger and more intense than the smaller, dimmer maxima on either side.

topics.title: Single-Photon-Emission Computed Tomography (SPECT)
topics.description: An imaging technique that uses gamma rays emitted by radiopharmaceuticals to create three-dimensional images of internal body structures.

topics.title: Single-Slit Diffraction
topics.description: Single-slit diffraction is the wave phenomenon where light passing through a single narrow slit produces a pattern of bright and dark regions due to interference.

topics.title: Sinusoidal variation of emf
topics.description: The emf generated in a rotating coil varies sinusoidally with time, following the equation emf = emf₀ sin(ωt), where emf₀ is the peak emf and ω is the angular velocity.

topics.title: Slope
topics.description: The difference in y-value (the rise) divided by the difference in x-value (the run) of two points on a straight line.

topics.title: Slope in Position vs. Time Graphs
topics.description: The slope of a position vs. time graph represents the average velocity of an object over a given time interval.

topics.title: Slope in Velocity vs. Time Graphs
topics.description: The slope of a velocity vs. time graph represents the acceleration of an object.

topics.title: Slope Intercept Form
topics.description: A linear equation written as y = mx + b, where m is the slope and b is the y-intercept.

topics.title: Slope of a Graph
topics.description: The slope of a graph represents the rate of change of the dependent variable with respect to the independent variable.

topics.title: Slope of a Position vs. Time Graph
topics.description: The slope of a position vs. time graph represents the average velocity of an object over that time interval.

topics.title: Slope of a Velocity vs. Time Graph
topics.description: The slope of a velocity vs. time graph represents the average acceleration of an object over that time interval.

topics.title: Small Angle Approximation
topics.description: An approximation used in pendulum motion where the sine of the angle is nearly equal to the angle itself for small angles (less than about 15°), simplifying the equations of motion.

topics.title: Snell's Law
topics.description: Snell’s Law describes the relationship between the indices of refraction of two media and the angles of incidence and refraction, stated as n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂.

topics.title: Snell’s Law in Terms of Speed
topics.description: Snell’s law can also be expressed in terms of the speeds of light in the two media, relating the sine of the angles to the ratio of the speeds.

topics.title: Solar Energy
topics.description: Energy derived from the Sun's radiation.

topics.title: Solar Storms
topics.description: Solar storms are intense bursts of radiation and charged particles emitted by the Sun, which can interact with Earth's magnetic field.

topics.title: Solenoid
topics.description: A thin wire wound into a coil that produces a magnetic field when an electric current is passed through it.

topics.title: Solid-State Radiation Detectors
topics.description: Semiconductors fabricated to directly convert incident radiation into electrical current.

topics.title: Some Questions We Know to Ask
topics.description: A list of fundamental questions that physicists are currently exploring to deepen our understanding of the universe and its underlying principles.

topics.title: Sonic Boom
topics.description: A sonic boom is a loud sound caused by an object moving through the air faster than the speed of sound.

topics.title: Sound
topics.description: A disturbance of matter that is transmitted from its source outward.

topics.title: Sound as a Mechanical Wave
topics.description: Sound is a mechanical wave that propagates through a medium due to the vibration of particles.

topics.title: Sound as a Physical Phenomenon
topics.description: Sound is a disturbance of the atoms in matter transmitted from its origin outward, which is a wave.

topics.title: Sound Intensity
topics.description: Sound intensity is the power of sound waves transmitted through a unit area per unit time.

topics.title: Sound Intensity and Amplitude Relationship
topics.description: The intensity of a sound wave is proportional to the square of its pressure amplitude.

topics.title: Sound Intensity and Pressure Amplitude
topics.description: Sound intensity is proportional to the square of the pressure amplitude of the sound wave, as described by the equation I = (Δp)² / (2ρv_w).

topics.title: Sound Intensity Level
topics.description: The logarithmic measure of sound intensity relative to a reference intensity, expressed in decibels (dB).

topics.title: Sound Interference
topics.description: Sound interference is the phenomenon where two or more sound waves superpose to form a resultant wave of greater, equal, or lesser amplitude.

topics.title: Sound Level
topics.description: Sound level is a measure of the intensity of sound, typically expressed in decibels.

topics.title: Sound Pressure Level
topics.description: Sound pressure level is a measure of the loudness of a sound, expressed in decibels (dB), and is related to the ratio of the sound pressure to a reference pressure.

topics.title: Sound Wave
topics.description: A sound wave is a disturbance that travels through a medium like air, water, or other matter, causing particles to vibrate in a wave-like fashion.

topics.title: South Magnetic Pole
topics.description: The end or side of a magnet that is attracted toward Earth’s geographic south pole.

topics.title: South Pole
topics.description: The part of a magnet that orients itself toward the geographic South Pole of Earth.

topics.title: Space Quantization
topics.description: Space quantization is the quantization of the direction of orbital angular momentum, meaning only certain angles are allowed between the angular momentum vector and an external magnetic field.

topics.title: Space Shuttle Function
topics.description: The space shuttle is a reusable spacecraft designed to carry astronauts and cargo into space, with components like solid fuel boosters and an external fuel tank.

topics.title: Space-Time Continuum
topics.description: The space-time continuum is the concept that space and time are interwoven into a single entity, where gravity can distort both space and time.

topics.title: Special Relativity
topics.description: A theory based on two postulates: the laws of physics are the same in all inertial reference frames, and the speed of light is constant in all inertial reference frames regardless of the motion of the source.

topics.title: Specific Gravity
topics.description: The ratio of the density of an object to the density of a reference fluid, usually water.

topics.title: Specific Heat
topics.description: Specific heat is the amount of heat required to raise the temperature of 1.00 kg of a substance by 1.00 °C.

topics.title: Specular Reflection
topics.description: Specular reflection is the reflection of light from a smooth surface, where light is reflected at specific angles, forming a clear image.

topics.title: Speed
topics.description: Speed is the magnitude of velocity, a scalar quantity that describes how fast an object is moving without regard to direction.

topics.title: Speed of Light
topics.description: The speed at which electromagnetic waves travel in a vacuum, calculated using the equation c = 1 / sqrt(μ₀ε₀).

topics.title: Speed of Light in a Medium
topics.description: The speed of light in a medium is less than its speed in a vacuum and depends on the material's index of refraction.

topics.title: Speed of Light in a Vacuum
topics.description: The speed of light in a vacuum is a constant, [EQUATION: c = 3.00 × 10^8 m/s].

topics.title: Speed of Light in Terms of Frequency and Wavelength
topics.description: The speed of light in a vacuum is equal to the product of its frequency and wavelength.

topics.title: Speed of Light, Frequency, and Wavelength
topics.description: The speed of light in a medium is equal to the product of its frequency and wavelength.

topics.title: Speed of Sound
topics.description: The speed of sound is the rate at which sound waves travel through a medium, which varies depending on the medium's properties.

topics.title: Spherical Aberration
topics.description: Spherical aberration is an optical distortion where rays converging from different parts of a lens focus at different distances from the lens.

topics.title: Spin
topics.description: Rotation about an axis that goes through the center of mass of the object.

topics.title: Spin and Trajectory
topics.description: The rotation of an object, such as a tennis ball, affects its trajectory and motion through the air, often resulting in curved paths.

topics.title: Spin Projection Quantum Number
topics.description: The spin projection quantum number (m_s) specifies the z-component of spin angular momentum and can take values of +1/2 or −1/2 for electrons.

topics.title: Spin Quantum Number
topics.description: The quantum number that parameterizes the intrinsic angular momentum (or spin angular momentum) of a given particle.

topics.title: Spinal Column Pressure
topics.description: The pressure exerted on the spinal column, often due to forces between vertebrae, which can be harmful if excessive.

topics.title: Spontaneous Symmetry Breaking
topics.description: A process in which a system transitions from a symmetric state to a less symmetric state, often observed in the early universe as forces separated after unification.

topics.title: Spring Tides
topics.description: Tides that occur when the Sun, Earth, and Moon are aligned, resulting in the highest tidal range.

topics.title: Stability
