topics.description: Stability refers to the ability of an object to return to its original position after being displaced, often determined by the position of its center of mass relative to its base of support.

topics.title: Stable Equilibrium
topics.description: A system is in stable equilibrium if, when displaced from equilibrium, it experiences a net force or torque in a direction opposite to the direction of the displacement.

topics.title: Standard Force
topics.description: A standard force is a defined reference force used to measure and compare the magnitude of other forces.

topics.title: Standard Force Unit
topics.description: A standard force unit is a reproducible force used to measure the magnitude of other forces, such as the force exerted by a stretched spring.

topics.title: Standard Model
topics.description: A theoretical framework that combines quantum chromodynamics and electroweak theory to describe the fundamental particles and forces, except for gravity.

topics.title: Standing Wave
topics.description: A standing wave is a wave pattern formed by the superposition of two identical waves moving in opposite directions, resulting in fixed points of no motion called nodes.

topics.title: Standing Waves in Air Columns
topics.description: A wave pattern formed in a confined air column where certain frequencies cause constructive and destructive interference, resulting in nodes and antinodes.

topics.title: Static Electricity
topics.description: Static electricity is the buildup of electric charge on the surface of objects, often caused by friction or induction.

topics.title: Static Equilibrium
topics.description: A state of equilibrium in which the net external force and torque acting on a system is zero.

topics.title: Static Equilibrium in Conductors
topics.description: In static equilibrium, the electric field inside a conductor is zero, and all excess charge resides on the surface.

topics.title: Static Friction
topics.description: Static friction is the friction that acts between two surfaces that are stationary relative to each other.

topics.title: Statistical Analysis
topics.description: Using statistics to examine data, such as counting microstates and macrostates.

topics.title: Statistical Interpretation of Entropy
topics.description: The statistical interpretation of entropy explains that entropy is a measure of the number of microstates corresponding to a macrostate, with higher entropy indicating a greater number of possible microstates.

topics.title: Steady State
topics.description: A condition in a circuit where the current and voltage remain constant over time, typically after all transient effects have settled.

topics.title: Stefan-Boltzmann Law
topics.description: The Stefan-Boltzmann law states that the power radiated by an object is proportional to the fourth power of its absolute temperature and its emissivity.

topics.title: Stefan-Boltzmann Law of Radiation
topics.description: The law that states the rate of heat transfer by radiation is proportional to the fourth power of the absolute temperature and the emissivity of the object.

topics.title: Step-Down Transformer
topics.description: A step-down transformer decreases the voltage from the primary coil to the secondary coil by having fewer turns in the secondary coil than in the primary coil.

topics.title: Step-Up Transformer
topics.description: A step-up transformer increases the voltage from the primary coil to the secondary coil by having more turns in the secondary coil than in the primary coil.

topics.title: Stimulated Emission
topics.description: Emission by an atom or molecule in which an excited state is stimulated to decay, most readily caused by a photon of the same energy.

topics.title: Stokes’ Law
topics.description: A formula for drag force on a spherical object in a viscous fluid, expressed as F_s = 6πrηv, where r is the radius, η is the viscosity, and v is the velocity.

topics.title: Strain
topics.description: Strain is the measure of deformation in a material resulting from an applied stress, expressed as the ratio of change in dimension to original dimension.

topics.title: Strange Quark
topics.description: The third lightest of all quarks.

topics.title: Strangeness
topics.description: Strangeness (S) is a quantum number assigned to particles according to their decay patterns; it is conserved in strong interactions but not in weak interactions.

topics.title: Strategic Nuclear Weapons
topics.description: Nuclear weapons designed for use against large military targets or cities, typically with a long range and high destructive power.

topics.title: Stress
topics.description: Stress is the internal force per unit area within a material that arises in response to an applied external force.

topics.title: String Size and Wavelength
topics.description: The size or wavelength of strings in Superstring theory is thought to be on the order of 10^-35 meters, which is the scale at which quantum gravity effects are expected to dominate.

topics.title: Strong Nuclear Force
topics.description: A short-range force that binds protons and neutrons together within the nucleus of an atom, overcoming the repulsive electromagnetic force between protons.

topics.title: Structure of the Atom
topics.description: The structure of the atom refers to the arrangement of protons, neutrons, and electrons within an atom.

topics.title: Subatomic Particles
topics.description: Subatomic particles are particles smaller than atoms, such as protons, neutrons, and electrons, which make up the structure of atoms.

topics.title: Subatomic Structure
topics.description: Subatomic structure refers to the hierarchical organization of matter, starting from molecules, atoms, nuclei, nucleons, and finally quarks.

topics.title: Sublimation
topics.description: The process by which a substance transitions directly from the solid phase to the gas phase without passing through the liquid phase.

topics.title: Submicroscopic World
topics.description: The submicroscopic world refers to the realm of objects such as atoms, molecules, and fundamental particles like electrons and protons, which require quantum mechanics for accurate description.

topics.title: Subshell
topics.description: A probability cloud for electrons that has a single angular momentum quantum number.

topics.title: Substructure of Matter
topics.description: The substructure of matter refers to the smaller components that make up atoms, nuclei, and other structures, such as electrons, protons, neutrons, and quarks.

topics.title: Substructure of the Nucleus
topics.description: The substructure of the nucleus refers to the composition and arrangement of protons and neutrons within the nucleus.

topics.title: Super Space
topics.description: Super space is a theoretical concept where each independent quantum number is considered a separate dimension, analogous to the independent dimensions of space.

topics.title: Superconducting Magnet
topics.description: A magnet made from superconducting materials that generates strong, stable magnetic fields used in MRI machines to create detailed images of the body.

topics.title: Superconductors
topics.description: Superconductors are materials that have zero resistivity, allowing electric current to flow without energy loss.

topics.title: Supercriticality
topics.description: Supercriticality is a condition in which the rate of fission reactions increases exponentially, leading to an uncontrolled release of energy.

topics.title: Superforce
topics.description: Superforce is a hypothetical unified force in the TOE epoch.

topics.title: Supernova Remnant
topics.description: A supernova remnant is the remains of a star that has exploded, often forming structures like the Veil Nebula, which can span vast distances in space.

topics.title: Superposition
topics.description: Superposition is the phenomenon where two or more waves combine by adding their disturbances at the same point in space.

topics.title: Superposition and Interference
topics.description: Superposition is the principle that when two or more waves overlap, the resultant wave is the sum of the individual waves, leading to interference patterns.

topics.title: Superstring Theory
topics.description: Superstring theory is a theory to unify gravity with the other three forces, considering fundamental particles as one-dimensional vibrating strings.

topics.title: Superstrings
topics.description: A theoretical framework proposing that fundamental particles are tiny, vibrating strings rather than point-like particles.

topics.title: Surface Tension
topics.description: Surface tension is the property of a liquid's surface that allows it to resist external forces, due to the cohesive forces between its molecules.

topics.title: Symmetry in Physics
topics.description: Symmetry in physics refers to the property of a system that remains unchanged under certain transformations, such as rotations or reflections.

topics.title: Synchrotron
topics.description: A synchrotron is a type of particle accelerator that uses a fixed-radius orbit and synchronized accelerating voltages to increase the energy of particles.

topics.title: Synchrotron Radiation
topics.description: Radiation caused by a magnetic field accelerating a charged particle perpendicular to its velocity.

topics.title: Synchrotron Source
topics.description: A synchrotron source is a type of device that produces electromagnetic radiation by accelerating charged particles in a magnetic field.

topics.title: System
topics.description: A defined boundary of an object or collection of objects being observed; all forces originating from outside of the system are considered external forces.

topics.title: System of Interest
topics.description: A defined set of objects or parts of an object that is analyzed to determine the forces acting on it.

topics.title: Systolic Blood Pressure
topics.description: The maximum pressure in the arteries when the heart contracts, representing the highest blood pressure during a heartbeat.

topics.title: Systolic Pressure
topics.description: Systolic pressure is the maximum blood pressure in the arteries, measured when the heart contracts and pumps blood.

topics.title: Tactical Nuclear Weapons
topics.description: Nuclear weapons designed for use in smaller-scale military operations, typically with a shorter range and lower yield compared to strategic weapons.

topics.title: Tail
topics.description: The start point of a vector; opposite to the head or tip of the arrow.

topics.title: Tail (of a Vector)
topics.description: The starting point of a vector; the point opposite to the head or tip of the arrow.

topics.title: Tangent
topics.description: A line that touches another at exactly one point.

topics.title: Tangential Acceleration
topics.description: Tangential acceleration is the linear acceleration of an object in circular motion that is tangent to the circle and related to the change in the magnitude of the velocity.

topics.title: Tangential Speed
topics.description: Tangential speed is the linear speed of an object moving along a circular path, related to angular velocity and the radius of the path.

topics.title: Tangential Velocity
topics.description: Tangential velocity is the instantaneous linear velocity of an object in rotational motion, perpendicular to the radius at the point of rotation.

topics.title: Tau Family Number
topics.description: The number ±1 assigned to all members of the tau family, or the number 0 assigned to all particles not in the tau family.

topics.title: Telescope Function
topics.description: A telescope is an optical instrument designed to view distant objects by producing an image larger than what can be seen with the unaided eye.

topics.title: Telescope Lens Configuration
topics.description: A telescope typically uses two convex lenses: a convex objective lens that forms an image and a convex eyepiece lens that magnifies this image.

topics.title: Telescope with Concave Mirror
topics.description: A telescope can use a concave mirror as its objective, which focuses light similarly to a convex lens but avoids chromatic aberrations.

topics.title: Telescope with Mirrors
topics.description: A telescope can use a concave mirror as its objective, which focuses light similarly to a convex lens, allowing for larger and more efficient light collection.

topics.title: Telescopes
topics.description: Telescopes are optical instruments designed to gather and focus light from distant objects, making them appear closer and clearer.

topics.title: Temperature
topics.description: Temperature is the quantity measured by a thermometer, operationally defined to be what we measure with a thermometer.

topics.title: Temperature Change
topics.description: Temperature change is the difference in temperature of a substance before and after heat transfer occurs.

topics.title: Temperature Change and Heat Capacity
topics.description: Temperature change and heat capacity describe how much heat is required to change the temperature of a substance.

topics.title: Temperature Coefficient of Resistivity
topics.description: An empirical quantity, denoted by α, which describes the change in resistance or resistivity of a material with temperature.

topics.title: Temperature Conversion
topics.description: Temperature conversion is the process of expressing a temperature value in one scale (such as Celsius, Fahrenheit, or Kelvin) to another scale using defined equations.

topics.title: Temperature Dependence of Resistance
topics.description: The resistance of a material changes with temperature, following the equation R = R₀ × (1 + αΔT), where α is the temperature coefficient of resistivity.

topics.title: Temperature Difference
topics.description: Temperature difference is the difference in temperature between two regions, which drives the rate of heat transfer through conduction.

topics.title: Temperature Scales
topics.description: Temperature scales are standardized systems used to measure temperature, such as Celsius, Fahrenheit, and Kelvin.

topics.title: Tensile Deformation
topics.description: Tensile deformation is the elongation of a material when subjected to a force pulling it apart, resulting in a change in length.

topics.title: Tensile Strength
topics.description: Tensile strength is the maximum stress that a material can withstand while being stretched or pulled before breaking.

topics.title: Tension
topics.description: The force transmitted through a string, rope, or cable when it is pulled tight by forces acting on its ends.

topics.title: Tension Force
topics.description: Tension is a force transmitted through a flexible medium, such as a rope or cable, pulling along the length of the medium.

topics.title: Tension in Strings or Wires
topics.description: The force transmitted through a string, rope, or wire when it is pulled by forces acting on opposite ends.

topics.title: Terminal Speed
topics.description: Terminal speed is the constant speed an object reaches when the viscous drag force equals the net force acting on it, resulting in zero acceleration.

topics.title: Terminal Velocity
topics.description: The constant speed an object reaches when the drag force equals the gravitational force acting on it, resulting in zero net force and no acceleration.

topics.title: Terminal Voltage
topics.description: Terminal voltage is the voltage measured across the terminals of a battery or power source when it is connected to a circuit, which is less than its electromotive force due to internal resistance.

topics.title: Tesla
topics.description: The SI unit of the magnetic field strength.

topics.title: Tesla (Unit of Magnetic Field Strength)
topics.description: The tesla is the SI unit of magnetic field strength, defined as 1 N/(A·m), derived from the equation B = F/(qv sine theta).

topics.title: Test Charge
topics.description: A test charge is a small positive charge used to measure the electric field at a point in space without significantly disturbing the existing electric field.

topics.title: The Four Basic Forces—An Introduction
topics.description: The fundamental forces in nature are gravitational, electromagnetic, strong nuclear, and weak nuclear forces.

topics.title: The Four Fundamental Forces
topics.description: The four fundamental forces are the basic interactions that govern all physical phenomena in the universe.

topics.title: The Hall Effect
topics.description: The Hall effect is the production of a voltage difference across an electrical conductor when a magnetic field is applied perpendicular to the current.

topics.title: The Pauli Exclusion Principle
topics.description: The Pauli Exclusion Principle states that no two electrons in an atom can have the same set of quantum numbers.

topics.title: Theory
topics.description: An explanation for patterns in nature that is supported by scientific evidence and verified multiple times by various groups of researchers.

topics.title: Theory of Everything (TOE)
topics.description: A Theory of Everything is a hypothetical framework that aims to unify all fundamental forces and particles into a single, coherent theory.

topics.title: Theory of Quark Confinement
topics.description: A theory that explains how quarks can exist and yet never be isolated or directly observed.

topics.title: Theory of Relativity
topics.description: A theory constructed by Albert Einstein which describes how space, time and energy are different for different observers in relative motion.

topics.title: Therapeutic Ratio
topics.description: The therapeutic ratio is the ratio of abnormal cells killed to normal cells killed in radiotherapy, which is a measure of the effectiveness and safety of radiation treatment.

topics.title: Therapeutic Uses of Ionizing Radiation
topics.description: The application of ionizing radiation to treat diseases, particularly cancer, by targeting and destroying malignant cells.

topics.title: Thermal Agitation
topics.description: The thermal motion of atoms and molecules in any object at a temperature above absolute zero, which causes them to emit and absorb radiation.

topics.title: Thermal Agitation and Electromagnetic Waves
topics.description: Thermal agitation refers to the random motion of atoms and molecules, which can produce and absorb electromagnetic waves, particularly in the infrared and microwave regions.

topics.title: Thermal Conductivity
topics.description: The property of a material’s ability to conduct heat.

topics.title: Thermal Conductivity Equation
topics.description: The thermal conductivity equation relates the rate of heat transfer through a material to its thermal conductivity, temperature difference, surface area, and thickness.

topics.title: Thermal Conductivity of Materials
topics.description: The thermal conductivity of materials varies, with metals generally being good conductors and insulators like wood and Styrofoam being poor conductors.

topics.title: Thermal Efficiency
topics.description: Thermal efficiency is the ratio of the useful work output to the heat input, indicating how effectively a heat engine converts heat into work.

topics.title: Thermal Efficiency of a Heat Engine
topics.description: The thermal efficiency of a heat engine is the ratio of the work output to the heat input from the hot reservoir.

topics.title: Thermal Emissivity of Skin
topics.description: The thermal emissivity of skin is a measure of how effectively skin emits infrared radiation, which is approximately 0.97 in the infrared spectrum.

topics.title: Thermal Energy
topics.description: Thermal energy is the energy associated with the random motion of particles in a substance.

topics.title: Thermal Equilibrium
topics.description: The condition in which heat no longer flows between two objects in contact; the two objects have the same temperature.

topics.title: Thermal Expansion
topics.description: The change in size or volume of an object with a change in temperature.

topics.title: Thermal Hazard
topics.description: A thermal hazard is an electrical hazard where excessive electric power causes undesired thermal effects, such as starting a fire in the wall of a house.

topics.title: Thermal Radiation
topics.description: Thermal radiation is the electromagnetic radiation emitted by an object due to its temperature, with higher temperatures emitting more radiation.

topics.title: Thermal Stress
topics.description: Thermal stress is the internal stress created in a material when it is prevented from expanding or contracting freely due to a temperature change.

topics.title: Thermodynamics
topics.description: Thermodynamics is the branch of physics that studies heat transfer and its relationship to work and energy.

topics.title: Thermodynamics Engineer
topics.description: A thermodynamics engineer applies principles of thermodynamics to design, test, and optimize systems that involve heat, work, pressure, temperature, and volume.

topics.title: Thermometer
topics.description: A thermometer is a device used to measure temperature by observing the expansion or contraction of a substance.

topics.title: Thermonuclear Bomb
topics.description: A bomb that uses both nuclear fission and fusion reactions to release energy, typically involving a fission trigger to initiate fusion.

topics.title: Thermonuclear Power
topics.description: Thermonuclear power is the use of controlled nuclear fusion as an energy source.

topics.title: Thin Film Interference
topics.description: Interference between light reflected from different surfaces of a thin film.

topics.title: Thin Films
topics.description: Thin films are very thin layers of material that can be deposited on a surface, often used to manipulate light properties such as reflection and refraction.

topics.title: Thin Lens
topics.description: A thin lens is a lens whose thickness allows light rays to refract but does not significantly affect properties such as dispersion and aberrations.

topics.title: Thin Lens Equation
topics.description: The thin lens equation relates the object distance, image distance, and focal length of a lens, used to calculate the magnification and image formation in a microscope.

topics.title: Thin Lens Equation for Mirrors
topics.description: The thin lens equation for mirrors relates the object distance, image distance, and focal length, allowing for quantitative analysis of image formation.

topics.title: Thin-Film Interference
topics.description: Thin-film interference is the phenomenon where light waves reflect off the top and bottom surfaces of a thin film, leading to interference patterns that depend on the film's thickness and the wavelength of light.

topics.title: Thin-Lens Equation
topics.description: The thin-lens equation is a formula used to calculate the relationship between the object distance, image distance, and focal length of a lens.

topics.title: Thought Experiment
topics.description: A thought experiment is a mental analysis of carefully and clearly defined situations to develop an idea.

topics.title: Three-Dimensional Kinematics
topics.description: The study of motion not confined to a single plane, such as a car following a winding road.

topics.title: Three-Primary-Color Theory
topics.description: The three-primary-color theory states that all colors can be created by combining red, green, and blue light in different proportions.

topics.title: Three-Wire System
topics.description: A wiring system with live, neutral, and ground wires used for safety in modern electrical systems.

topics.title: Threshold Frequency
topics.description: Threshold frequency is the minimum frequency of electromagnetic radiation required to eject electrons from a material, below which no electrons are ejected regardless of intensity.

topics.title: Thrust
topics.description: A reaction force that pushes a body forward in response to a backward force.

topics.title: Thrust of a Rocket
topics.description: Thrust is the force exerted on a rocket by the expulsion of gas, calculated as the product of the exhaust velocity and the rate of mass ejection.

topics.title: Tidal Forces
topics.description: The differential gravitational force experienced by different parts of an object due to the gravitational pull of another massive body.

topics.title: Tides
topics.description: The periodic rise and fall of sea levels caused by the gravitational pull of the Moon and the Sun on Earth.

topics.title: Timbre
topics.description: Timbre is the perception of the quality of a sound, determined by the number and relative intensity of multiple frequencies.

topics.title: Time
topics.description: Time is the duration during which an event occurs, measured in seconds.

topics.title: Time Constant Formula for an RL Circuit
topics.description: The time constant (τ) of an RL circuit is calculated as τ = L/R, where L is the inductance and R is the resistance.

topics.title: Time Constant in RC Circuits
topics.description: The time constant (τ) in an RC circuit is the product of resistance (R) and capacitance (C), representing the time it takes for the voltage across the capacitor to reach about 63.2% of its final value during charging.

topics.title: Time Dilation
topics.description: Time dilation is the phenomenon where time passes more slowly for an object traveling at high speeds or in a strong gravitational field, as described by Einstein's theory of relativity.

topics.title: Time Interval
topics.description: The difference between the ending time and the beginning time of an event.

topics.title: TOE Epoch
topics.description: The TOE epoch is the period before 10−43 after the Big Bang.

topics.title: Tone
topics.description: A tone is the perception of a sound characterized by its frequency and intensity.

topics.title: Top Quark
topics.description: The top quark is the heaviest of the six quark flavors.

topics.title: Tornado Formation
topics.description: A tornado is a violently rotating column of air that extends from a thunderstorm to the ground.

topics.title: Tornado Structure
topics.description: Tornado structure describes the funnel-like shape of a tornado, which extends from storm clouds to the ground and spins violently, especially at its narrowest point.

topics.title: Tornado Wind Speed
topics.description: Tornado wind speed refers to the extremely high velocity of air within a tornado, which can reach up to 500 km/h near the bottom of the funnel.

topics.title: Torque
topics.description: Torque is the rotational effect of a force about a pivot point, calculated as the product of the force and the perpendicular distance from the pivot to the line of action of the force.

topics.title: Torque and Angular Momentum Relationship
topics.description: Torque is the rate of change of angular momentum, expressed as the net torque equals the change in angular momentum over time.

topics.title: Torque and Change in Angular Momentum
topics.description: Torque causes a change in angular momentum, and the direction of this change is the same as the direction of the torque, as described by the equation net torque equals the rate of change of angular momentum.

topics.title: Torque and Force in Muscles
topics.description: Torque is the rotational effect of forces exerted by muscles, which can be calculated using the lever arm and the force applied.

topics.title: Torque Equation
topics.description: The magnitude of torque is calculated as the product of the force, the perpendicular lever arm, and the sine of the angle between the force and the lever arm.

topics.title: Torque Equation for a Current Loop
topics.description: The torque on a current-carrying loop in a magnetic field is calculated using the equation tau = NIAB sine theta, where N is the number of turns, I is the current, A is the area of the loop, B is the magnetic field, and theta is the angle between the loop and the field.

topics.title: Torque on a Current Loop
topics.description: The torque experienced by a current-carrying loop in a magnetic field is the rotational force that causes the loop to rotate.

topics.title: Torque on a Current Loop: Motors and Meters
topics.description: Torque on a current loop in a magnetic field causes rotation, which is the principle behind electric motors and meters.

topics.title: Torque on a Current-Carrying Loop
topics.description: The torque experienced by a current-carrying loop in a magnetic field is the rotational force that causes the loop to rotate, calculated by the equation tau = N I A B sine theta.

topics.title: Torricelli’s Theorem
topics.description: Torricelli's theorem states that the speed of fluid flowing out of an opening in a container is the same as the speed it would have if it fell freely from the height of the fluid surface to the opening.

topics.title: Total Capacitance in Parallel
topics.description: The total capacitance of capacitors connected in parallel is simply the sum of the individual capacitances.

topics.title: Total Capacitance in Series
topics.description: The total capacitance of capacitors connected in series is calculated by taking the reciprocal of the sum of the reciprocals of the individual capacitances.

topics.title: Total Energy
topics.description: Total energy is the energy of a relativistic object, calculated as E = gamma mc², where gamma is the relativistic factor, m is mass, and c is the speed of light.

topics.title: Total Energy in Relativity
topics.description: Total energy is the energy of an object in motion, calculated as E = gamma mc², where gamma is the relativistic factor, m is the object's mass, and c is the speed of light.

topics.title: Total Internal Reflection
topics.description: Light reflects entirely back into the original medium when it strikes a boundary at an angle greater than the critical angle.

topics.title: Total Resistance in Parallel
topics.description: The total resistance of resistors in parallel is found by taking the reciprocal of the sum of the reciprocals of the individual resistances.

topics.title: Total Resistance in Series
topics.description: The total resistance of resistors in series is the sum of their individual resistances.

topics.title: Trajectory
topics.description: The path followed by a projectile under the influence of gravity.

topics.title: Transfer of Charge
topics.description: Transfer of charge is the process by which electric charge moves from one object to another.

topics.title: Transformer
topics.description: A transformer is a device that transfers electrical energy between two circuits through electromagnetic induction, typically changing the voltage level.

topics.title: Transformer and AC
topics.description: Transformers only work with alternating current (AC) because they rely on changing magnetic fields to induce voltage in the secondary coil.

topics.title: Transformer and Power Conservation
topics.description: Transformers conserve power (assuming 100% efficiency), meaning the input power equals the output power.

topics.title: Transformer Current Ratio
topics.description: The ratio of the secondary current to the primary current in a transformer is inversely proportional to the ratio of the number of turns in the secondary coil to the number of turns in the primary coil.

topics.title: Transformer Efficiency
topics.description: Transformer efficiency is the ratio of the output power to the input power, and it is nearly 100% for well-designed transformers.

topics.title: Transformer Equation
topics.description: The equation showing that the ratio of secondary to primary voltages in a transformer equals the ratio of the number of turns in their coils, V_s/V_p = N_s/N_p.

topics.title: Transformer Function
topics.description: A transformer is a device that changes the voltage of an alternating current (AC) by using electromagnetic induction between two coils.

topics.title: Transformer Operation
topics.description: A transformer changes the voltage of an alternating current (AC) by using electromagnetic induction between two coils, with the voltage ratio depending on the number of turns in the coils.

topics.title: Transformer Power Relationship
topics.description: In an ideal transformer, the electrical power input equals the electrical power output, meaning the product of current and voltage remains constant.

topics.title: Transformers
topics.description: A transformer is a device that transfers electrical energy between two circuits through electromagnetic induction, typically changing the voltage level.

topics.title: Transitive Property in Thermodynamics
topics.description: The transitive property in thermodynamics is a fundamental principle that if system A is in thermal equilibrium with system B, and system B is in thermal equilibrium with system C, then system A is also in thermal equilibrium with system C.

topics.title: Translational Kinetic Energy
topics.description: Translational kinetic energy is the kinetic energy of an object moving in a straight line, calculated as one-half the mass of the object multiplied by the square of its velocity.

topics.title: Transmutation
topics.description: Transmutation is the process by which one element is transformed into another through nuclear reactions, such as radioactive decay.

topics.title: Transverse Nature of Electromagnetic Waves
topics.description: Electromagnetic waves are transverse waves, meaning the electric and magnetic fields oscillate perpendicular to each other and to the direction of wave propagation.

topics.title: Transverse Wave
topics.description: A wave in which the disturbance is perpendicular to the direction of propagation.

topics.title: Trigonometric Analysis of Forces
topics.description: The use of trigonometric functions to resolve forces into their horizontal and vertical components for analysis.

topics.title: Trigonometric Relationships in Vector Components
topics.description: The sine, cosine, and tangent of an angle are used to relate the magnitude of a vector to its x and y components.

topics.title: Triple Point
topics.description: The pressure and temperature at which a substance exists in equilibrium as a solid, liquid, and gas.

topics.title: Turbulence
topics.description: Fluid flow in which layers mix together via eddies and swirls.

topics.title: Turbulent Flow
topics.description: A type of fluid flow characterized by chaotic, irregular motion with eddies and vortices.

topics.title: Turbulent Flow Around Objects
topics.description: Turbulent flow around objects occurs when the Reynolds number exceeds about 10^6, resulting in chaotic, irregular fluid motion with significant mixing and energy dissipation.

topics.title: Twin Paradox
topics.description: A scenario where a twin traveling at a relativistic speed ages less than the Earth-bound twin due to acceleration, which makes special relativity inapplicable to accelerating frames of reference.

topics.title: Two-Dimensional Collisions
topics.description: Collisions where objects scatter to the side, requiring analysis along both x and y axes.

topics.title: Two-Dimensional Kinematics
topics.description: The study of motion in a plane, involving both horizontal and vertical components.

topics.title: Two-Dimensional Motion
topics.description: Motion in two dimensions involves movement along both horizontal and vertical directions simultaneously.

topics.title: Two-Dimensional Vector Problems
topics.description: Two-dimensional vector problems involve both horizontal and vertical components of motion.

topics.title: Two-Slit Constructive Interference
topics.description: Constructive interference in a two-slit experiment occurs when the path difference between the two slits is an integer multiple of the wavelength.

topics.title: Two-Slit Destructive Interference
topics.description: Destructive interference in a two-slit experiment occurs when the path difference between the two slits is a half-integer multiple of the wavelength.

topics.title: Types of Electric Charge
topics.description: There are two types of electric charge: positive and negative, which interact by attracting opposite charges and repelling like charges.

topics.title: Types of Electromagnetic Waves
topics.description: Electromagnetic waves include a range of types such as radio waves, microwaves, infrared, visible light, ultraviolet, X-rays, and gamma rays.

topics.title: Types of Radiation
topics.description: The three main forms of nuclear radiation: alpha emission, beta emission, and gamma emission.

topics.title: Types of Waves
topics.description: Waves are disturbances that transfer energy through a medium or space, and they can be classified into different types such as water waves, sound waves, light waves, and waves on strings.

topics.title: Ultimate Speed Limit
topics.description: The ultimate speed limit is the speed of light, which no object with mass can reach, as it would require infinite energy to accelerate to this speed.

topics.title: Ultracentrifuge
topics.description: A centrifuge optimized for spinning a rotor at very high speeds.

topics.title: Ultrasound
topics.description: Ultrasound refers to sound waves with frequencies above 20,000 Hz, which are not perceived by the human ear.

topics.title: Ultrasound Imaging
topics.description: Ultrasound imaging is a medical technique that uses high-frequency sound waves to create images of internal body structures by analyzing the reflections of the sound waves.

topics.title: Ultraviolet (UV) Microscopes
topics.description: Microscopes constructed with special lenses that transmit UV rays and utilize photographic or electronic techniques to record images.

topics.title: Ultraviolet Catastrophe
topics.description: A prediction of classical physics that the energy emitted by a blackbody would become infinite at high frequencies, which contradicted experimental results and led to the development of quantum mechanics.

topics.title: Ultraviolet Radiation
topics.description: Ultraviolet radiation is a type of electromagnetic wave with wavelengths shorter than visible light but longer than X-rays, used for sterilization and vitamin D production.

topics.title: Ultraviolet Radiation (UV)
topics.description: Electromagnetic radiation in the range extending upward in frequency from violet light and overlapping with the lowest X-ray frequencies.

topics.title: Unavailability of Energy
topics.description: Unavailability of energy refers to the portion of energy in a system that cannot be used to do work, often due to the increase in entropy.

topics.title: Uncertainty
topics.description: Uncertainty is a measure of the confidence in a measurement, representing the range of values that could be consistent with the measured value.

topics.title: Uncertainty in Energy
topics.description: Lack of precision or lack of knowledge of precise results in measurements of energy.

topics.title: Uncertainty in Energy and Time
topics.description: The uncertainty in energy (ΔE) and the uncertainty in time (Δt) of a system are related such that their product is always greater than or equal to Planck's constant divided by four times π.

topics.title: Uncertainty in Momentum
topics.description: Lack of precision or lack of knowledge of precise results in measurements of momentum.

topics.title: Uncertainty in Position
topics.description: Lack of precision or lack of knowledge of precise results in measurements of position.

topics.title: Uncertainty in Position and Momentum
topics.description: The uncertainty in position (Δx) and the uncertainty in momentum (Δp) of a particle are related such that their product is always greater than or equal to Planck's constant divided by four times π.

topics.title: Uncertainty in Time
topics.description: Lack of precision or lack of knowledge of precise results in measurements of time.

topics.title: Uncontrolled Chain Reaction
topics.description: An uncontrolled chain reaction is a process in which neutrons from one fission event cause subsequent fission events without regulation, leading to a rapid and potentially dangerous increase in energy release.

topics.title: Under Damping
topics.description: The condition in which damping of an oscillator causes it to return to equilibrium with the amplitude gradually decreasing to zero; the system returns to equilibrium faster but overshoots and crosses the equilibrium position one or more times.

topics.title: Underdamped System
topics.description: An underdamped system is one where the damping is small enough that the oscillations gradually decrease in amplitude but the period and frequency remain nearly the same as in simple harmonic motion.

topics.title: Unidentified Superconducting Objects (USOs)
topics.description: Unidentified superconducting objects (USOs) are materials that exhibit superconductivity under certain conditions but fail to reproduce the effect consistently, raising questions about their validity.

topics.title: Unification of Forces
topics.description: The unification of forces refers to the idea that the fundamental forces of nature may be different manifestations of a single underlying force under certain conditions.

topics.title: Uniform Circular Motion
topics.description: Uniform circular motion is the motion of an object moving at a constant speed along a circular path.

topics.title: Uniform Circular Motion and Simple Harmonic Motion
topics.description: Uniform circular motion can be related to simple harmonic motion, where the projection of circular motion onto a straight line results in periodic oscillatory motion.

topics.title: Uniform Circular Motion in a Magnetic Field
topics.description: A charged particle moving perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field undergoes uniform circular motion because the magnetic force provides the centripetal force.

topics.title: Unit Conversion
topics.description: Unit conversion is the process of changing the units of a physical quantity from one system to another, such as converting meters to kilometers.

topics.title: Units
topics.description: A standard used for expressing and comparing measurements.

topics.title: Units of Measurement
topics.description: Units of measurement are standardized quantities used to express the magnitude of physical quantities.

topics.title: Units of Volume
topics.description: Units of volume include cubic meters (m³), liters (L), and cubic centimeters (cm³), with 1 liter equal to 1000 cubic centimeters.

topics.title: Units of Work and Energy
topics.description: Work and energy are measured in joules (J), which is equivalent to newton-meters (N·m) or kg·m²/s².

topics.title: Unity of Physical Laws
topics.description: The same fundamental laws of physics apply to all phenomena in the universe, from the smallest atoms to the largest galaxies.

topics.title: Universal
topics.description: Applies throughout the known universe.

topics.title: Universal Gas Constant
topics.description: The universal gas constant is a physical constant that appears in the ideal gas law when using moles instead of molecules, with a value of approximately 8.31 J/(mol·K).

topics.title: Universal Gravitational Constant (G)
topics.description: A proportionality factor used in the equation for Newton’s universal law of gravitation; it is a universal constant.

topics.title: Universality of Physical Laws
topics.description: The same fundamental laws of physics apply to all objects, whether they are as large as galaxies or as small as atoms.

topics.title: Unpolarized Waves
topics.description: Waves that are randomly polarized.

topics.title: Unreasonable Results in Physics
topics.description: A type of problem where the solution may produce unrealistic or inconsistent results, often due to incorrect assumptions or inconsistent premises.

topics.title: Unstable Equilibrium
topics.description: A system is in unstable equilibrium if, when displaced, it experiences a net force or torque in the same direction as the displacement from equilibrium.

topics.title: Unstable Flow
topics.description: A type of fluid flow that can oscillate between laminar and turbulent states, typically occurring at intermediate Reynolds numbers.

topics.title: Up Quark
topics.description: The lightest of all quarks.

topics.title: Uranium-235
topics.description: Uranium-235 is a uranium isotope with 92 protons and 143 neutrons that is readily fissile.

topics.title: Use of Equations to Solve for Unknowns
topics.description: Selecting and applying appropriate equations that relate known quantities to unknowns in order to find a solution to a physics problem.

topics.title: Useful Work
topics.description: Work done on the outside world, such as lifting weights, which involves exerting a force through a distance on an external object.

topics.title: Van de Graaff Accelerator
topics.description: An early accelerator: a simple, large-scale version of the electron gun.

topics.title: Van de Graaff Generator
topics.description: A device that uses electrostatic principles to generate and store large amounts of static charge, often used for research and demonstration purposes.

topics.title: Vapor
topics.description: A gas at a temperature below the boiling temperature.

topics.title: Vapor Pressure
topics.description: The pressure exerted by a vapor in equilibrium with its liquid or solid phase at a given temperature.

topics.title: Vapor Pressure of Water
topics.description: The pressure exerted by water vapor in equilibrium with its liquid or solid phase at a given temperature.

topics.title: Vaporization
topics.description: A phase change from liquid to gas.

topics.title: Variation of Pressure with Depth
topics.description: Pressure in a fluid increases linearly with depth due to the increasing weight of the fluid above.

topics.title: Variation of Pressure with Depth in a Fluid
topics.description: The pressure in a fluid increases with depth due to the weight of the fluid above.

topics.title: Vector
topics.description: A physical quantity with both magnitude and direction.

topics.title: Vector Addition
topics.description: The process of combining two or more vectors to find their resultant, which is the total vector that represents the combined effect of all the individual vectors.

topics.title: Vector Addition and Subtraction: Analytical Methods
topics.description: The analytical method of vector addition and subtraction uses mathematical equations and components to add or subtract vectors.

topics.title: Vector Addition and Subtraction: Graphical Methods
topics.description: The graphical method of vector addition and subtraction involves representing vectors as arrows and using geometric techniques to add or subtract them.

topics.title: Vector Addition in Force Systems
topics.description: The process of combining forces acting on an object by adding their vector components to determine the net force.

topics.title: Vector Addition of Forces
topics.description: Forces, like other vectors, can be added using methods such as the head-to-tail technique or trigonometric methods.

topics.title: Vector Addition of Velocities
topics.description: The total velocity of an object is found by adding the individual velocity vectors using vector addition techniques, which involve both magnitude and direction.

topics.title: Vector Addition Using Analytical Methods
topics.description: Vector addition using analytical methods involves breaking vectors into perpendicular components and adding them along each axis to find the resultant vector.

topics.title: Vector Components
topics.description: The parts of a vector that represent its magnitude in perpendicular directions, such as horizontal and vertical, which are used to describe the vector's effect in different directions.

topics.title: Vector Direction
topics.description: The direction of a vector is the angle it makes with a reference axis, indicating the orientation of the vector in space.

topics.title: Vector Magnitude
topics.description: The magnitude of a vector is its length, which represents the size of the vector quantity.

topics.title: Vector Nature of Electrostatic Force
topics.description: The electrostatic force is a vector quantity, meaning it has both magnitude and direction, and it acts along the line joining the two charges.

topics.title: Vector Quantity
topics.description: A vector quantity is a physical quantity that has both magnitude and direction.

topics.title: Vector Subtraction
topics.description: Vector subtraction is the process of finding the difference between two vectors, which is done by adding the negative of the second vector to the first vector, where the negative of a vector has the same magnitude but opposite direction.

topics.title: Vector Subtraction Using Analytical Methods
topics.description: Vector subtraction using analytical methods involves breaking vectors into perpendicular components, negating the components of the vector being subtracted, and then adding them along each axis.

topics.title: Vectors and Scalars
topics.description: Vectors are quantities that have both magnitude and direction, while scalars are quantities that have only magnitude.

topics.title: Vectors in Two Dimensions
topics.description: Vectors in two dimensions are quantities that have both magnitude and direction, and can be represented as arrows with length proportional to magnitude and direction indicated by the arrow's orientation.

topics.title: Vectors vs. Scalars
topics.description: Vectors have both magnitude and direction, while scalars have only magnitude.

topics.title: Velocity
topics.description: Velocity is a vector quantity that describes the rate of change of position with respect to time, including direction.

topics.title: Velocity and Flow Rate Relationship
topics.description: The flow rate of a fluid is directly related to its velocity and the cross-sectional area through which it flows.

topics.title: Velocity Components
topics.description: The horizontal and vertical parts of the velocity vector of a projectile, which can be calculated using trigonometric functions of the launch angle.

topics.title: Velocity in SHM
topics.description: Velocity in simple harmonic motion is the rate of change of displacement and varies sinusoidally with time, reaching maximum at the equilibrium position.

topics.title: Velocity Magnitude
topics.description: The magnitude of velocity calculated using the Pythagorean theorem with the x and y components of velocity.

topics.title: Velocity Selector
topics.description: A region in a mass spectrometer that uses both electric and magnetic fields to allow only particles with a specific velocity to pass through.

topics.title: Velocity with Constant Acceleration
topics.description: The final velocity of an object under constant acceleration, calculated by adding the initial velocity to the product of acceleration and time.

topics.title: Velocity-Time Graph
topics.description: A velocity-time graph shows how velocity changes with time, and its slope represents acceleration.

topics.title: Velocity-versus-Time Graph
topics.description: A velocity vs. time graph visually represents the velocity of an object over time, with the slope indicating acceleration.

topics.title: Vertical Displacement
topics.description: Vertical displacement is the change in position of an object in the vertical direction, represented by the symbol 'y' in kinematic equations.

topics.title: Vertical Motion
topics.description: The motion of a projectile along the vertical axis, influenced by acceleration due to gravity.

topics.title: Vertically Polarized
topics.description: Oscillations that are in a vertical plane.

topics.title: Very High Frequency (VHF)
topics.description: TV channels utilizing frequencies in the two ranges of 54 to 88 MHz and 174 to 222 MHz.

topics.title: Virtual Image
topics.description: A virtual image is an image that cannot be projected onto a screen, as light rays do not actually converge at the image location but appear to originate from it.

topics.title: Virtual Image Formed by a Concave Mirror
topics.description: A virtual image formed by a concave mirror is an image that cannot be projected onto a screen, located behind the mirror, and is upright relative to the object.

topics.title: Virtual Image in Mirrors
topics.description: A virtual image in mirrors is an image that cannot be projected onto a screen and appears to originate from a point behind the mirror.

topics.title: Virtual Particle
topics.description: A particle that cannot be directly observed but whose effects can be observed, often existing temporarily due to the Heisenberg uncertainty principle.

topics.title: Virtual Photon Exchange
topics.description: The process by which the electromagnetic force is transmitted between charged particles through the exchange of a virtual photon.

topics.title: Viscosity
topics.description: Viscosity is a property of fluids that describes their resistance to flow, or the internal friction between layers of the fluid.

topics.title: Viscous Drag
topics.description: A resistance force exerted on a moving object, with a nontrivial dependence on velocity.

topics.title: Viscous Drag Force
topics.description: Viscous drag force is the resistance force exerted by a fluid on a moving object, which depends on the fluid's viscosity, the object's speed, and its size.

topics.title: Visible and Invisible Fluid Flow
topics.description: Visible fluid flow is when the movement of a fluid can be directly observed, while invisible fluid flow occurs when the movement is not easily seen, such as air movement.

topics.title: Visible Light
topics.description: Visible light is the portion of the electromagnetic spectrum that can be detected by the human eye.

topics.title: Vision Correction
topics.description: Vision correction is the process of using lenses or other methods to adjust the focusing ability of the eye so that images are formed clearly on the retina.

topics.title: Vision Correction with Converging Lenses
topics.description: Farsightedness is corrected using a converging spectacle lens that produces an image farther from the eye than the object, allowing the farsighted person to see it clearly.

topics.title: Vision Correction with Diverging Lenses
topics.description: Nearsightedness is corrected using a diverging spectacle lens that produces an image closer to the eye than the object, allowing the nearsighted person to see it clearly.

topics.title: Voltage Across a Charging Capacitor
topics.description: The voltage across a capacitor charging through a resistor increases exponentially over time, approaching the maximum voltage of the source, and is described by the equation V = emf(1 − e^(-t/RC)).

topics.title: Voltage Across a Discharging Capacitor
topics.description: The voltage across a capacitor discharging through a resistor decreases exponentially over time, approaching zero, and is described by the equation V = V₀e^(-t/RC).

topics.title: Voltage and Current Relationship in an RLC Circuit
topics.description: In an RLC series circuit, the voltage and current are out of phase due to the presence of inductive and capacitive reactance, with the total voltage being the vector sum of the individual voltages.

topics.title: Voltage and Work Done by Electric Field
topics.description: The work done by an electric field in moving a charge between two points is equal to the charge multiplied by the potential difference between those points.

topics.title: Voltage Drop
topics.description: Voltage drop is the reduction in voltage across a component in a circuit due to the resistance encountered by the current flowing through it.

topics.title: Voltage Drop Across a Resistor
topics.description: The voltage drop across a resistor is the product of the current through the resistor and its resistance.

topics.title: Voltage Drop in Feeder Lines
topics.description: Voltage drop in feeder lines refers to the reduction in voltage across power lines caused by the large current drawn by a motor when it is first turned on.

topics.title: Voltage in Parallel Circuits
topics.description: In a parallel circuit, the voltage drop across each resistor is the same and equal to the voltage of the battery.

topics.title: Voltage Needed by an Accelerator Between Accelerating Tubes
topics.description: The voltage between accelerating tubes in an accelerator must be sufficient to provide the necessary energy to the particles, with the total voltage across all gaps equal to the desired kinetic energy of the particles.

topics.title: Voltage Transformation in Transformers
topics.description: Transformers increase or decrease voltage by changing the number of turns in the primary and secondary coils, following the transformer equation V_S / V_P = N_S / N_P.

topics.title: Voltage, Current, and Resistance Relationship
topics.description: Voltage, current, and resistance are related through Ohm’s law (V = IR) and are used to calculate electric power in different circuit configurations.

topics.title: Voltmeter
topics.description: An instrument that measures voltage.

topics.title: Voltmeter Connection
topics.description: A voltmeter must be connected in parallel with the circuit to measure the potential difference across a component.

topics.title: Volume
topics.description: Volume is the amount of three-dimensional space occupied by an object or enclosed within a container.

topics.title: Volume Calculation
topics.description: Volume calculation involves determining the space occupied by an object by multiplying its length, width, and height.

topics.title: Volume Deformation
topics.description: Volume deformation is the change in volume of a material when subjected to uniform compressive forces applied on all surfaces.

topics.title: Volume Expansion
topics.description: Volume expansion is the increase in volume of an object due to a temperature change, calculated using the coefficient of volume expansion.

topics.title: Watt
topics.description: The SI unit of power, with 1 W = 1 J/s.

topics.title: Wave
topics.description: A disturbance that moves from its source and carries energy.

topics.title: Wave Amplitude
topics.description: Wave amplitude is the maximum displacement of a particle of the medium from its equilibrium position.

topics.title: Wave Aspect of Light
topics.description: Light exhibits wave-like behavior, such as interference and diffraction.

topics.title: Wave Behavior
topics.description: Waves in the ocean exhibit similar characteristics and behaviors to other types of waves, such as mechanical and electromagnetic waves.

topics.title: Wave Character of Light
topics.description: Light exhibits wave characteristics, such as interference and diffraction, which cannot be fully explained by geometric optics.

topics.title: Wave Characteristics Limit Microscopy
topics.description: The wave nature of light limits the ability to observe details smaller than the wavelength of light due to diffraction.

topics.title: Wave Energy and Time
topics.description: The energy effects of a wave depend on both its amplitude and the duration of the wave's interaction, with longer durations transferring more energy.

topics.title: Wave Frequency
topics.description: Wave frequency is the number of waves that pass a fixed point in a given time, measured in hertz.

topics.title: Wave Intensity
topics.description: The intensity of a wave is the power per unit area carried by the wave, which is proportional to the square of the amplitude of the wave.

topics.title: Wave Interference
topics.description: Wave interference is the phenomenon that occurs when two or more waves meet and combine to form a new wave pattern.

topics.title: Wave Nature of Matter
topics.description: The wave nature of matter refers to the property of particles, such as electrons, to exhibit wave-like behavior, including interference and diffraction.

topics.title: Wave Nature of Matter Causes Quantization
topics.description: The wave nature of matter leads to quantization, meaning that certain physical quantities can only take on discrete values.

topics.title: Wave Optics
topics.description: Wave optics is the branch of physics that studies the behavior of light when it interacts with objects comparable in size to its wavelength, emphasizing wave characteristics like interference.

topics.title: Wave Period
topics.description: Wave period is the time it takes for one complete wave cycle to pass a fixed point, measured in seconds.

topics.title: Wave Properties of Sound
topics.description: The wave properties of sound refer to how sound travels through a medium as a wave, involving vibrations and the transfer of energy.

topics.title: Wave Speed
topics.description: Wave speed is the rate at which a wave propagates through a medium, measured in meters per second.

topics.title: Wave Superposition
topics.description: Wave superposition is the principle that when two or more waves overlap, the resultant wave is the sum of the individual waves.

topics.title: Wave Types
topics.description: Wave types refer to different forms of waves, such as water waves, sound waves, light waves, and waves on strings.

topics.title: Wave Velocity
topics.description: The speed at which the disturbance moves. Also called the propagation velocity or propagation speed.

topics.title: Wave-Like Properties of Matter
topics.description: Wave-like properties of matter indicate that particles such as electrons exhibit behaviors typically associated with waves, such as interference and diffraction.

topics.title: Wave-Particle Analogy
topics.description: Wave-particle analogy is the concept that small-scale phenomena, like EM radiation and matter, are understood by comparing their behaviors to macroscopic wave and particle phenomena.

topics.title: Wave-Particle Duality
topics.description: Wave-particle duality is the concept that fundamental particles, like photons, can exhibit both wave-like and particle-like properties.

topics.title: Wave-Particle Duality in Macroscopic Objects
topics.description: The idea that while all particles have wave properties, the wave nature of macroscopic objects becomes difficult to observe due to their large mass.

topics.title: Wave-Particle Nature of Matter
topics.description: Matter, such as electrons and atoms, can also exhibit wave-like properties, similar to photons, which suggests that all particles have dual characteristics of both waves and particles.

topics.title: Wavefront
topics.description: A wavefront is a line or surface that connects points in a wave that are in phase, such as the crest or trough of a wave.

topics.title: Wavelength
topics.description: The distance between adjacent identical parts of a wave.

topics.title: Wavelength Calculation for Emitted Photons
topics.description: The process of calculating the wavelength of light emitted by an atom based on the energy difference between two energy levels.

topics.title: Wavelength in a Medium
topics.description: The wavelength of light in a medium is shorter than its wavelength in vacuum and is given by λ_n = λ / n, where λ is the vacuum wavelength and n is the refractive index of the medium.

topics.title: Wavelength of an Orbital
topics.description: The wavelength of an orbital is related to the radius of the orbital and the principal quantum number.

topics.title: Wavelength of Light
topics.description: The wavelength of light is the distance between successive crests or troughs of a light wave, and it determines the color and behavior of light.

topics.title: Wavelength of Light Emitted by an Electron Changing States
topics.description: The wavelength of light emitted when an electron transitions between energy levels is related to the difference in the reciprocals of the squares of the final and initial energy levels.

topics.title: Wavelength of Sound
topics.description: The wavelength of a sound wave is the distance between adjacent compressions or rarefactions in the wave.

topics.title: Waves
topics.description: A wave is a disturbance that propagates through a medium or space, transferring energy without the net movement of particles.

topics.title: Weak Nuclear Force
topics.description: A fundamental force responsible for particle decay.

topics.title: Weakly Interacting Massive Particles (WIMPs)
topics.description: WIMPs are hypothetical particles that are thought to make up dark matter, as they are massive, interact weakly with normal matter, and are gravitationally bound to galaxies.

topics.title: Wedge
topics.description: A simple machine consisting of two back-to-back inclined planes.

topics.title: Weight
topics.description: The force due to gravity acting on an object of mass; defined mathematically as the product of mass and the acceleration due to gravity.

topics.title: Weightlessness
topics.description: A state where an object is in free-fall, experiencing no normal force, even though it is still subject to gravitational force.

topics.title: Wheatstone Bridge
topics.description: A null measurement device for calculating resistance by balancing potential drops in a circuit.

topics.title: Wheel and Axle
topics.description: A wheel and axle is a simple machine where the effort is applied to the wheel, and the resistance is applied to the axle, providing mechanical advantage through rotation.

topics.title: Why Massive Particles Cannot Reach the Speed of Light
topics.description: Massive particles cannot reach the speed of light because as their velocity approaches c, their relativistic mass increases, requiring infinite energy to accelerate them further.

topics.title: WIMPs
topics.description: WIMPs are weakly interacting massive particles; chargeless leptons (non-baryonic matter) interacting negligibly with normal matter.

topics.title: Wind-Chill Factors
topics.description: Wind-chill factors are the temperatures of still air that produce the same rate of cooling as air of a given temperature and speed, highlighting the combined effect of convection and conduction.

topics.title: Work
topics.description: The transfer of energy by a force that causes an object to be displaced; the product of the component of the force in the direction of the displacement and the magnitude of the displacement.

topics.title: Work and Energy Relationship
topics.description: Work is the process by which energy is transferred from one system to another or converted from one form to another.

topics.title: Work and Heat as Forms of Energy
topics.description: Work and heat are both forms of energy transfer, capable of changing the internal energy of a system.

topics.title: Work as Energy Transfer
topics.description: Work is the transfer of energy into or out of a system, where energy is transferred by a force acting through a distance.

topics.title: Work Done
topics.description: Work done is energy transferred by a force moving through a distance, representing an organized process.

topics.title: Work Done Against Gravity
topics.description: The energy transferred to an object when a force is applied to lift it against the gravitational force, resulting in an increase in its gravitational potential energy.

topics.title: Work Done by a Constant Force
topics.description: The work done by a constant force on an object is calculated as the product of the magnitude of the force, the magnitude of the displacement, and the cosine of the angle between the force and displacement vectors.

topics.title: Work Done by Heat
topics.description: Work done by heat refers to the conversion of thermal energy into mechanical energy, as seen in devices like steam engines.

topics.title: Work Done by Nonconservative Forces
topics.description: The work done by nonconservative forces equals the change in mechanical energy of a system.

topics.title: Work Done in a Cyclical Thermodynamic Process
topics.description: The total work done in a cyclical thermodynamic process is equal to the area enclosed by the cycle on a PV diagram, representing the net work output or input.

topics.title: Work Equation
topics.description: The work done on a system by a constant force is calculated using the equation W = Fd cos(theta), where F is the force, d is the displacement, and theta is the angle between the force and displacement vectors.

topics.title: Work in the Scientific Sense
topics.description: Work in the scientific sense is the product of the component of a force in the direction of motion and the distance through which the force acts.

topics.title: Work Input in Heat Pumps
topics.description: Work input in a heat pump is the energy required to move heat from a cold reservoir to a hot reservoir, which is converted into heat transfer to the hot reservoir.

topics.title: Work Output
topics.description: Work output is the amount of energy transferred by a heat engine to perform work, calculated as the difference between heat input and heat rejected.

topics.title: Work Output for a Cyclical Process
topics.description: The work output for a cyclical process is the difference between the heat absorbed from the hot reservoir and the heat expelled to the cold reservoir.

topics.title: Work, Energy, and Power in Humans
topics.description: Work, energy, and power in humans refer to how the human body uses energy and performs work during physical activities.

topics.title: Work-Energy Theorem
topics.description: The work-energy theorem states that the net work done on a system is equal to the change in its kinetic energy.

topics.title: Work-Energy Theorem with Nonconservative Forces
topics.description: The work-energy theorem, when including nonconservative forces, states that the net work done on a system equals the change in its kinetic energy.

topics.title: Working Distance
topics.description: The working distance is the distance from the front lens element of a microscope objective to the specimen, which affects the resolution and the risk of damaging the specimen.

topics.title: Work–Energy Theorem
topics.description: States that the net work done on a system equals the change in kinetic energy.

topics.title: World Energy Use
topics.description: World energy use refers to the total amount of energy consumed globally by various sectors such as industry, transportation, and households.

topics.title: X Rays: Atomic Origins and Applications
topics.description: X rays are a form of electromagnetic radiation produced by atomic processes, and they have various applications in science and medicine.

topics.title: X-Component of a Vector
topics.description: The horizontal component of a vector calculated as the product of the vector's magnitude and the cosine of the angle it makes with the horizontal.

topics.title: X-Ray
topics.description: Invisible, penetrating form of very high frequency electromagnetic radiation, overlapping both the ultraviolet range and the gamma-ray range.

topics.title: X-ray Crystallography
topics.description: X-ray crystallography is a technique that uses x-ray diffraction to determine the atomic and molecular structure of crystals and other materials.

topics.title: X-ray Diffraction
topics.description: X-ray diffraction is the phenomenon where x rays interact with the atomic structure of a material, producing patterns that can be analyzed to determine the arrangement of atoms within the material.

topics.title: X-ray Imaging
topics.description: X-ray imaging is the process of creating images of internal structures by using x rays, which penetrate materials and produce shadows based on differences in density.

topics.title: X-ray Production
topics.description: X-rays are produced when high-energy electrons collide with a material, either by ionizing atoms or through bremsstrahlung radiation.

topics.title: X-ray Spectrum
topics.description: An x-ray spectrum is a graph showing the intensity of x rays produced by an x-ray tube as a function of frequency, typically displaying a broad curve of bremsstrahlung radiation and sharp peaks of characteristic x rays.

topics.title: X-ray Tube
topics.description: An x-ray tube is a specialized cathode ray tube that produces x rays by accelerating electrons through a high voltage and allowing them to strike a target material.

topics.title: X-Rays
topics.description: X-rays are a type of electromagnetic wave with very short wavelengths and high energy, used for medical imaging and material analysis.

topics.title: Xerography
topics.description: An electrostatic process used in copy machines to create images by using a charged drum and toner to transfer the image onto paper.

topics.title: Y-Component of a Vector
topics.description: The vertical component of a vector calculated as the product of the vector's magnitude and the sine of the angle it makes with the horizontal.

topics.title: Y-Intercept
topics.description: The y-value when x = 0, or when the graph crosses the y-axis.

topics.title: Y-Intercept of a Position vs. Time Graph
topics.description: The y-intercept of a position vs. time graph represents the initial position of an object at time zero.

topics.title: Young’s Double Slit Experiment
topics.description: An experiment demonstrating the wave nature of light through the formation of interference patterns.

topics.title: Young’s Modulus
topics.description: Young’s modulus is a measure of the stiffness of a material, defined as the ratio of tensile stress to tensile strain.

topics.title: Yukawa Particle
topics.description: A particle proposed by Hideki Yukawa to explain the strong nuclear force between protons and neutrons.

topics.title: Z-Component of Angular Momentum
topics.description: The component of orbital angular momentum of an electron along the z-axis.

topics.title: Z-Component of Spin Angular Momentum
topics.description: The component of intrinsic electron spin along the z-axis.

topics.title: Zeeman Effect
topics.description: The Zeeman effect is the splitting of spectral lines into multiple lines when an external magnetic field is applied, indicating the interaction between magnetic fields and quantized energy levels of electrons.

topics.title: Zeroth Law of Thermodynamics
topics.description: The zeroth law of thermodynamics states that if two systems are each in thermal equilibrium with a third system, they are also in thermal equilibrium with each other.

topics.title: Zircon
topics.description: A natural gemstone with a high index of refraction.

topics.title: Motion of an Object in a Viscous Fluid
topics.description: An object moving through a viscous fluid experiences viscous drag. The Reynolds number characterizes the flow regime, and a falling object reaches terminal velocity when gravitational force, buoyancy, and drag balance.

topics.title: Planck and Quantum Nature of Light
topics.description: Planck proposed that energy is exchanged in discrete quanta, each with energy hf, where h is Planck’s constant and f is frequency. This quantization explains the blackbody radiation spectrum and avoids the ultraviolet catastrophe.
